#3353. ‘SNL’ Writer Jimmy Fowlie Pays Tribute To Late Sister On Her Birthday After 2 Arrested For Her Killing

After the LAPD arrested two people in connection to the killing of his sister Christina Downer, Jimmy Fowlie paid tribute to her for her birthday.

On Thursday, the Saturday Night Live writer shared a video of the two of them posing on a movie theater display for last year’s Tron: Ares the last time they saw each other, noting it brought his family “some relief” that an arrest has been made.

“Today is my sister’s birthday, and so I wanted to share this video of what turned out to be our last moment together,” he wrote on Instagram. “It truly was just an inconsequential night at the movies.

“I’ve always thought those little photo ops at the Grove were so puzzling. I’d see them and try to imagine a world where me and my friends would pose in front of one non-ironically. For some reason on this day, I decided to make @nletreize take one of me and Christina as we were leaving. I just wanted to be extra and make her laugh, and I love how you can see her giggling as she walks up. She’s wearing her slippers which i think is so cute. In this video I feel like you can feel how sweet her energy is. She was one of my favorite people to make laugh. You could argue my whole comedy career was actually born out of sitting at the dinner table as kids and acting dumb while our dad became increasingly irate at me. It was a sacrifice that was always worth it. Watch on Deadline

Fowlie continued, “Thank you to everyone who’s reached out. It brings our family and her friends some relief to know that charges have been filed in connection with Christina’s death. Because this whole experience has been so endlessly depressing, today I want to spend a little time remembering how much fun I had with her and how lucky I am that she was my sister. Happy birthday, Chris!”

Last week, LAPD officers took 41-year-old Delorean Bijon Brandon, who is believed to be Downer’s boyfriend, and Kaylee Markowski, 34, into custody for allegedly murdering and disposing of her body, before concealing their involvement.

Downer’s family reported her missing on Dec. 18, 2025, following a welfare check requested by her ex-husband after he hadn’t heard from her in an extended period of time. Detectives with LAPD’s Robbery-Homicide Division took over the investigation when her cellphone was discovered washed ashore on a Santa Monica beach.

Last December, Fowlie sought help from friends and followers as he searched Downer’s Koreatown neighborhood, noting they were “worried that she isn’t safe.” Fowlie announced in April that LAPD had informed the family that Downer was “no longer alive,” and were treating the case as a homicide.

#3352. These Signature Sony Headphones Are Under $200 Ahead of Black Friday

The Sony WH-1000XM6 headphones are the most recent entry in Sony's 1000X series, which has been around since 2016. They're the best over-ear headphones in terms of audio quality currently on the market—but not everyone can (or needs to) drop nearly half a grand on headphones.

The WH-1000XM5 are a generation older and were at the top of their class until they were supplanted by the XM6. On the plus side, by virtue of being older, they're currently discounted to $198 (down from the original $399.99) during Amazon's early Black Friday sale. That 50% off brings it down to the lowest price they've ever reached, according to price-tracking tools, a good deal for premium headphones that still sound incredible, even in 2026.

I have been a loyal customer of the 1000X line for many years; they're my go-to headphones for most activities. The WH-1000XM5 received an "outstanding" review from PCMag for their top-notch audio quality and exceptional audio when using the best-in-class active noise cancellation. The headphones are also well-designed to be comfortable for long listening sessions. The ear controls use tapping and swiping, which isn't my favorite, but it's what all modern headphones are moving toward. There's a companion app that lets you adjust your EQ settings to your liking, including what the swiping and tapping functions do.

These headphones also have a stereo 3.5mm connection, which is perfect for those who want to use a cable and not worry about battery life. And speaking of battery life, Sony says you can expect about 30 hours, but it will vary depending on your use of ANC. They are compatible with AAC, LDAC, and SBC codecs and have multipoint connection, meaning you can pair them with more than one device at the same time.

Personally, I think the value for the money you get with the XM5 for $198 is better than paying full price for the XM6. If you're looking to get ahead of the Black Friday chaos and secure an amazing deal on great headphones, this is it.

#3350. Chasing China’s Monazite Monopoly

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

Billions are driving a race against Beijing’s decades-long lead

The Baogang Tailings Dam, near the industrial city of Baotou, in Inner Mongolia, is one of the most polluted bodies of water in the world. The 11-square-kilometer artificial lake holds the effluent from decades of rare-earth and other industrial-processing operations.

One of the singular features of Baotou, an industrial city of 2 million people in Inner Mongolia, is a 10-square-kilometer (4-square-mile) lake that is among the most polluted in the world. The artificial lake, referred to by the name of the dam associated with it, Weikuang Dam (or Baogang Tailings Dam), has for decades collected the effluent from minerals processing for China’s globally dominant iron, steel, and rare-earths industries.

Built in the late 1950s, the lake contains a highly toxic stew of industrial chemicals with substantial amounts of radioactive thorium, the latter resulting primarily from the processing of monazite ores for rare-earths. China has since greatly tightened its environmental regulations and restrictions on mining and minerals processing. For example, largely because of the environmental disaster that is Weikuang Dam, the country doesn’t permit the development or operation of stand-alone monazite mines—that is, mines where nothing is mined except monazite ore.

Now, with industrialized nations in North America, Asia, and Europe spending billions to shore up their rare-earths supply chains, and counting on monazite to help them do it, China’s history and experiences with monazite offer important lessons.

This article is a collaboration between Foreign Policy, the global magazine of politics and ideas, and IEEE Spectrum, the flagship magazine of the IEEE.

Monazite ore is a pillar of China’s rare-earths industry because it is a prime source of some less common but extremely important rare-earth elements, notably dysprosium, terbium, yttrium, and erbium. The country mines and processes vast quantities of monazite ore; it also imports huge amounts of monazite ore for processing.

Most of the domestically mined monazite ore comes from a single mine: the mammoth Bayan Obo complex, 150 kilometers north of Baotou, in Inner Mongolia. Bayan Obo, which is primarily an iron-ore mine, also happens to contain the largest known rare-earth deposit in the world. It’s the source of nearly half of all the rare-earth ore mined on the planet in a typical year. Most of the rare-earth ore mined at Bayan Obo is a type called bastnaesite; it’s the mining of that bastnaesite that makes it legal to mine monazite ore at Bayan Obo as well.

Related: Can a Radioactive Ore Break China’s Grip on Rare Earths?

All told, ore from Bayan Obo was used to produce 170,000 tonnes of rare-earth metal last year, according to David Merriman, research director at the minerals intelligence firm Project Blue. Roughly 30 percent to 40 percent of the rare-earth ore mined at Bayan Obo is monazite. That amount alone would be enough to make China the world’s largest processor of monazite for rare-earths.

But a more detailed picture of China’s interest in monazite emerges when you consider the country’s imports of the ore. Last year, they amounted to more than 70,000 tonnes, says Thomas Kruemmer, a Singapore-based consultant on minerals and metals. That figure becomes more impressive when you consider the unique challenges of shipping monazite by sea. Because of its radioactivity, concentrated monazite ore is classified as Class 7 dangerous cargo under the International Maritime Dangerous Goods Code. That means, Kruemmer notes, that the ore can be imported through only four ports in China.

In addition, importation of some kinds of monazite into China is supposed to go through a joint venture consisting of the China National Nuclear Corp. and Shenghe Resources, which are at least partly state-owned. But lots of imported monazite doesn’t go through those organizations, notes Merriman. That’s because heavy mineral sands, which may contain roughly 2 percent or 3 percent monazite by weight, are not subject to the same import controls as concentrated monazite ore. So companies import the heavy mineral sands; separate out various profitable concentrates, including the monazite mineral concentrate; and then process the monazite concentrate to recover the rare-earths.

China has lately stepped up its efforts to secure rare-earth ore around the world. One reason, says Kruemmer, is simply to make up for recently lost supplies. In 2025, the U.S. government invested US $400 million in MP Materials, which operates the Mountain Pass mine and processing facility in California. The deal put an end to long-standing contracts under which MP Materials had been selling tens of thousands of tonnes of rare-earth concentrate annually to a trading affiliate of Shenghe Resources.

But other Westerners speculate that China has strategic reasons for stepping up its efforts to acquire heavy mineral sands or other rare-earth assets abroad. By locking down rights to deposits or projects abroad, Chinese organizations are making them unavailable to non-Chinese developers, according to this reasoning.

Merriman points out that your view of these activities largely depends on where you sit. The U.S. government recently made a conditional loan commitment of up to $725 million to U.S. monazite processor Energy Fuels, which has been aggressively securing substantial monazite supplies in Australia, Brazil, and Madagascar. To a Chinese observer, those moves probably look rather strategic.

China, meanwhile, is doing what it has been doing for decades. “China’s playing its game,” says Merriman.

This article appears in the November 2026 print issue as “Radioactive Realpolitik.”

Glenn Zorpette is editorial director for content development at IEEE Spectrum. A Fellow of the IEEE, he holds a bachelor's degree in electrical engineering from Brown University.

#3349. Five Hacks Every Una Watch User Should Know

The Una watch is pretty much made to be hackable, with its interchangeable parts and open development environment. But it’s also pretty barebones at launch, without many features available yet. However, here are five things I’ve discovered I can do with it—and I hope to expand this list quite a bit as the device and its community mature.

Because the Una watch has a regular USB-C port, you don’t need to remember any specific cable, dongle, or adapter to charge it. I knew that, but it didn’t occur to me until recently that I didn’t need a computer or a wall outlet to plug into the other end. I was able to take a USB-C to USB-C cable—the same kind I might carry around to charge my phone—and plug one end into my watch and the other into my phone. It charged!

(You can also charge some other devices from a phone, including an Apple Watch, but you’d need to carry around that specific adapter, which is why nobody bothers.)

The Una watch doesn’t have any built-in sleep tracking, but a few community-built apps aim to provide it. The Slumber app, for example, will let you know how long you slept and compare your most recent bedtime with when you usually get to bed. There are no sleep stages (honestly: refreshing, since watches are rarely good at this anyway), and the analysis is done on the watch itself.

But if what you’re really hoping for is a recovery score or an overnight HRV reading, the HabitLab app combines that with habit tracking. Every evening, the watch will buzz and ask you to check off which habits or factors played into your day: Alcohol and late meals are among the options, and the watch will automatically detect morning or evening workouts to add them to the list. In the morning, the watch asks you how you slept, and then it gives you a score based on your resting heart rate, HRV, and your subjective rating.

The app is supposed to be able to put together trends and insights from this data, but I haven’t managed to get it to do this. Maybe it’s waiting for more data (I’ve been using it a little over a week), or maybe it’s just buggy.

By contrast, the barcode app worked even better than I expected it to. It’s meant for a parkrun barcode; each participant in the free weekly 5K has a number that you can use to check your results online. But it works just as well for other barcodes.

I installed the Barcode app and entered the number for my library card. Perhaps because of the watch’s MIP screen, I found this barcode scanned more reliably than any barcodes I’ve previously tried to use on a watch. The library scanner picked it up just fine on the first try, and a phone-based scanner also had no problem with it. You can store up to six barcodes, so I’ve also entered a few others, like my grocery discount card.

The app supports QR codes as well as regular barcodes, and to enter a QR code, you just type in a shortened URL. (It needs to be 22 characters or less.) This means that the Barcode app is also a QR code creator, a nifty feature indeed.

Seeing how soon the sun sets is a bit of a downer as we leave daylight saving time and get into the dark winter months, but it’s also helpful in planning. The Sun & Moon Face puts a graphic on your wrist that shows how far along the sun is in its trajectory across the sky for the day. When evening is approaching, you’ll see just how little time you have left.

The app grabs your GPS location once a day, which means that for the first few hours I wore it, the sunrise and sunset times were incorrectly listed as 6 a.m. and 6 p.m. But as long as you aren’t flying to a drastically new location every day, the app does the job just fine. As a bonus, it changes the color of the screen’s sky to show daylight, nighttime, or sunrise/sunset colors.

If you want to hack this hackable watch, you might as well take the plunge and try to build something yourself. Instructions are here to download the development tools for Windows, Mac, or Linux, and there are tutorials for different features you might want to use and implement. There are also about a dozen example apps you can build on, including activity trackers, watch faces, and glances. I'm not much of a coder myself, but this is the friendliest setup I've seen for someone to get into building their own apps for a watch.

#3348. Simulation App Speeds Up Electric Truck Battery Design

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

Using a laser-welding simulation app, Volvo Trucks has accelerated the design of long-lasting, high-performance batteries

A consortium including Volvo Trucks used COMSOL-based multiscale simulation and a custom app to optimize laser-welded battery pack design and manufacturing, improving the robustness and lifetime of batteries for electric trucks to enable longer-range, more reliable heavy-duty electric fleets.

This article is brought to you by COMSOL.

These days, no one blinks an eye at two-day, one-day, and even same-day package deliveries. Despite the plethora of localized fulfillment and distribution centers that have cropped up to meet the demand, delivery trucks still need to make considerably long drives, often over highways. To reduce fuel and maintenance costs as well as carbon emissions, companies are investing in electric trucks for their delivery fleets. While turning to electric trucks is a promising solution, the battery packs incorporated into these automotive designs often fall short in the lifetime needed to make long-distance highway travel feasible.

To help overcome the issue of battery lifetime, a consortium of universities and industry partners incorporated multiscale simulation and a custom simulation app into the battery manufacturing process. The organizations involved in this project were Aurobay, Resolvent, the European Commission, the Technical University of Denmark (DTU), Vinnova (the Swedish Agency for Innovation Systems), Innovation Fund Denmark, and Volvo Group Trucks Operations.

The simulation app, built by Resolvent, a Denmark-based engineering consultancy that specializes in green energy, enables the R&D department at Volvo to easily test battery lifetime performance.

The Multiscale Simulation of Laser Welding for Optimal Battery Pack Manufacturing project — referred to as “LaserBATMAN” — was initiated in May 2022 and wrapped up in May 2025 (Ref. 1). Although BATMAN here refers to battery manufacturing and not the famous masked superhero, the goals for the project also strove for greatness.

The LaserBATMAN project aimed to optimize two key performance metrics for battery packs: robustness and lifetime (Ref. 1). One element of the battery manufacturing process that affects both of these metrics is the laser welding used in component joining processes (for example, to connect battery cells in a pack via a busbar). If done correctly, laser welding can positively impact battery life, but if done incorrectly, laser welding can increase the risk of battery degradation. Computational modeling can be used to analyze and predict the effects of welding and joining processes at different stages of the manufacturing process.

Martin Refslund Nielsen, former chief commercial officer and partner at Resolvent, explained that for this type of multiphysics and multiscale problem, “COMSOL Multiphysics is just the right tool.”

The Resolvent team used the COMSOL Multiphysics software to study how laser welding affects the electrochemistry and degradation of battery cells. At least, that’s how the project started.

“Ambitions grew,” Nielsen said, explaining that the team ended up modeling the performance of the entire battery, from cell to pack level, and even “turned [the model] into a design tool in the end”, in reference to the app.

After training the deep neural network of the battery model, the team built a custom simulation app to efficiently optimize busbar tabs in the configuration of a battery pack.

First, the team built an electrochemical model of a battery cell by inputting the formulas for the relevant chemical reaction kinetics (Figure 2). The resulting cell-layer model was then fed input data, and the output data was used to train a deep neural network (DNN). With this reduced-order model, the team was able to quickly gain insight into cell behavior.

After training the DNN of the battery model, the team built a custom simulation app to efficiently optimize busbar tabs in the configuration of a battery pack.

Figure 2: The Resolvent battery model.COMSOL

The different features of the simulation app, as described by Nielsen, include its options to input dimensions for the pack geometry (Figure 3), the number of cells, and operating conditions such as ambient temperature and charge–discharge current profiles. The app also makes it possible to apply a simple charging current and load customized cycles. Users are then able to see how the battery performs with each set of specific inputs.

Figure 3. The battery pack model developed by Resolvent.COMSOL

Another important aspect of Resolvent’s app is the Busbar Weld Design Tool button, which Nielsen described as “a tool within a tool.” This button can be used to efficiently calculate busbar weld performance after a number of cycles. After clicking the button, a window opens with options for setting different parameters, including the shape of the weld, busbar thickness, and penetration depth of the laser (Figure 4).

“[This button] is interesting from a robust design perspective,” said Nielsen. Users can apply a variant to the input parameters to see what happens in production if the weld does not reach far enough into the busbar.

Figure 4. Resolvent’s simulation app, showing how certain parameters can be customized. The model shows how the busbar weld is affected by a cooling airflow.COMSOL

“We certainly get deep technical insight here, and we can dimension the design in the sweet spot. Deep technical insight is also key to optimizing product performance,” Nielsen said. For example, if the results suggest better cooling, the team could potentially reduce the design by two battery cells and retain the same performance, easily quantifying the tradeoff between cooling and setup.

The app’s user interface also includes a Compute Battery button, which can be used to see the temperature of the weld in a given state, the state of charge, and the solid–electrolyte interface (SEI) layer thickness (Figure 5). The results can help the engineering team further determine if there is room for optimization in the design. For instance, a user can apply a cooling flow in the app and see if turbulence or standing air occurs.

As explained by Nielsen, simulation apps offer more consistent analysis and reporting, and the intuitiveness of custom apps makes it easier to share knowledge. “We are in a much better place to optimize performance and increase robustness,” said Nielsen.

Figure 5. Temperature in the given state (left), state of charge (middle), and SEI layer thickness (right) in the battery pack.COMSOL

The custom simulation app developed by the LaserBATMAN consortium can be used to help produce more robust battery designs with ranges that can support highway travel over longer distances with fewer failures — all while promoting the use of green energy. A heroic project indeed.

#3347. Resident Evil director Zach Cregger explains why the iPhone is vital to his work

There have been a number of high-profile movies technically shot on iPhone, but in most cases they are using the same professional cinematography kit they would use with other cameras, including lenses costing tens of thousands of dollars.

Resident Evil director Zach Cregger uses his own iPhone in a rather different way, taking an approach that could be useful to amateur and professional filmmakers alike …

There’s an ongoing debate about how meaningful it is to claim that a high-profile movie, ad, or keynote video was shot on iPhone. Naysayers argue that the quality is all down to the professional lenses, lighting rigs, and editing employed, while those on the other side of the fence point out that everything was captured by the iPhone sensor.

Cregger mostly sidesteps all of that, describing his own use of an iPhone for shot planning, creating photo boards that accurately represent the image that will be captured by each of the Pro lenses he intends to use.

We grew up with video games informing our visual sense just as much as movies and television did, and I feel like I’m able to make a movie that involves the gameplay. [Here] I have a wide angle lens, our protagonist is in the center of the frame as he’s moving, we’re following locked right behind him when he looks right and we swing, right. His attention is dictating where the camera goes, and I think that the effect of that is is a much more immersive horror experience where you’re feeling informed.

I’m a hyper prepper. I’ve got the iPhone that is, like, always on me. I’ll go to the location with my cinematographer and I’ll use Cadrage, an app that approximates different lenses, and I will basically plan out the sequence. I will know exactly what shot is going to cut to what shot, and I will print out these images and everyone will know we’re using this lens for these shots. This is what’s going to be in the frame, and there’s no guesswork.

He does, however, add that an iPhone is all that you need to make a movie, even if his own budgets give him access to rather more expensive kit.

Anybody can make a movie with what’s in your pocket right now.

At the other end of the scale, I use my iPhone in a similar way to him when planning my own amateur videos. I take still photos to create a photo board so that I have a visual reference for each of my planned shots. The videos themselves may be shot on my Blackmagic rig, my iPhone, or some mix of the two.

You can watch Cregger talk through his process for Apple TV here.

Resident Evil director Zach Cregger counts iPhone among his go-to filmmaking tools.Go inside his unique approach to crafting immersive horror experiences, and watch his latest movie now on the Apple TV app. https://t.co/oOpQL0mJde pic.twitter.com/RHWwlPjFID

#3345. Everything You Should Know About This Year's Black Friday Sales

As is often the case with major sales these days, retailers are increasingly blurring the lines between early deals and the official start of a sale. Black Friday sales appear to be becoming a month-long event, with early deals appearing in the first week of the month. If you haven't been paying attention, major retailers have already put out their plans and even started churning out deals. But you're still in time to make this upcoming Black Friday sale a great one. Here is everything you need to know to prepare you for the big sale.

Black Friday is always the day after Thanksgiving. This year, Black Friday starts at midnight on Nov. 27. Cyber Monday is the Monday following Black Friday, which starts at midnight on Nov. 30.

The major retailers doing sales are the usual: Amazon, Best Buy, Target, Walmart, Home Depot, and many others. Currently, Walmart has publicized its plans already and has early deals available. Best Buy is offering one of the largest Black Friday and Cyber Week sales, with multiple events and early deals. Target has a three-day event. Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Cyber Monday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, November 30, 2026.

Black Friday used to be bigger for major retailers and more expensive tech and appliances, while Cyber Monday was for cheaper tech and gave smaller businesses a chance to compete online. Nowadays, though, the distinction is almost meaningless. Every major retailer will offer sales on both days, and the smart move is to know what you want, use price trackers or refer to guides like our live blog that use price trackers for you, and don’t stress over finding the perfect timing. The “best” deal will always depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers that can afford lower prices: think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot.

Unlike Spring or Summer sales, Black Friday doesn't focus on specific categories, which means everything is fair game for discounts. In previous years, we've seen tech, tools, fitness equipment, outdoor supplies and furniture, bedding, video games, kitchen appliances, and more. This is one of the best times to make a list of what you need and start tracking prices. You're likely to find what you're looking for discounted, and probably at its lowest price it has ever been. If you'd like to avoid having to do all that work, we always do it for you. Just follow our Black Friday coverage.

The WH-1000XM5 were at the top of their class until they were supplanted by the XM6. On the plus side, by virtue of being older, they're currently discounted to $198 (originally $399.99).

Knightley and Ben Whishaw return with razor-sharp banter, tangled conspiracies and plenty of bloodshed

"Black Doves" was one of my favorite surprises of 2024. A spy thriller with a panache for murder, double-crosses and dark comedy? Netflix, you really do know me.

Verdict: "Black Doves" season 2 is a thoroughly entertaining return, with plenty of twists, sharp humor and terrific performances from Keira Knightley and Ben Whishaw. It occasionally gets tangled in its own web of secrets, but the show's winning mix of spy games and genuine friendship makes this another binge-worthy winner.

Release schedule: All 6 episodes now streaming

Now, Keira Knightley and Ben Whishaw are back for another round as secret agent Helen Webb and her hitman best friend, Sam Young. I've watched all six episodes of "Black Doves" season 2, and I'm happy to report that creator Joe Barton has done it again. This is a terrific installment, with plenty of twists, sharp dialogue and wonderfully messy characters.

So what makes this return such a success? Well, there are a few things, starting with deeper insights into the backgrounds of several major players.

Kelly most recently reviewed "The Gilded Age" season 4, "Nobody Wants This" season 3 and "The Diplomat" season 4."

Helen is still feeding government secrets to the Black Doves, the shadowy organization that employs her, while her husband Wallace (Andrew Buchan) is about to become prime minister. You'd think that would be enough to keep her occupied, but there's another crisis brewing. Her handler, Mrs. Reed (Sarah Lancashire), is accused of plotting a coup against the organization, putting Helen and Sam in the middle of yet another sticky situation.

It leads to some fascinating revelations about Mrs. Reed's past, including a family connection that turns out to be rather more complicated (and deadly) than anyone expected. I particularly enjoyed the flashbacks to her earlier life; getting a better sense of how Reed became the woman she is today makes her even more interesting. It also gives the world of "Black Doves" a richer history and texture.

The plotting does get pretty convoluted at times. There are a lot of people with competing agendas, and keeping track of who's working for whom and whose loyalties lie where can feel like a full-time job. But honestly, that's part of the appeal. Just when you think you've figured out what's going on, someone turns out to be working for someone else, usually with a gun on hand. It's all very entertaining.

Sign up to the weekly Tom's Streaming Guide to stay in the loop with the latest releases and top recommendations across your favorite streaming services. We’ve got you covered with a complete guide on what’s worth watching.

The returning cast is in fine form, particularly Knightley and Whishaw, whose chemistry remains one of the best things about the show. Helen and Sam's friendship is the heart of "Black Doves." You can see their genuine affection for each other, even when they're busy shooting at various foes. Sam has his own demons to contend with this season, and as compelling as that storyline is, the show is strongest when the two of them are in a scene together.

Season 2 also brings in some welcome new faces, most notably Ambika Mod as Laila, an acerbic Black Doves agent who helps Helen with a heist (while toting a big gun, of course). Mod is fantastic, bringing a wonderfully snarky energy to the proceedings and delivering some of the season's best lines.

Not everyone makes quite the same impression. Neve Campbell joins as American envoy Cecile Mason, but her character doesn't get much to do. It's a bit of a waste of an actor and I'm still scratching my head about why someone of Campbell's caliber was cast in such a nothingburger of a role.

There's a lot of competition in the spy thriller department these days, but "Black Doves" continues to hold its own. It's got the action and intrigue you'd expect from the genre, but it also has a sense of humor that keeps things from getting too serious.

Season 2 isn't without its shortcomings. A few characters could use more screen time, and the plot occasionally gets tangled in its own web of secrets. But those are relatively minor complaints when you've got the kind of cracking cast that could make a dictionary recital work.

Most of all, I'm just glad we get another six episodes with Helen and Sam. Their friendship gives the show something beyond the usual spy-versus-spy shenanigans. If you enjoyed season 1, season 2 is just as good. And there's plenty of story left for "Black Doves" to continue for at least one more outing, but I hope it's more like three or four.

Kelly is the managing editor of streaming for Tom’s Guide, so basically, she watches TV for a living. Previously, she was a freelance entertainment writer for Yahoo, Vulture, TV Guide and other outlets. When she’s not watching TV and movies for work, she’s watching them for fun, seeing live music, writing songs, knitting and gardening.

#3343. IEEE Offers More Services to Cities That Want to Be Smarter

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

They include webinars, educational resources, and conferences

Georges Zissis is an IEEE Fellow and chair of the IEEE Smart Cities Technical Community.

Satish Sani is an IEEE senior member and chair of the IEEE Smart Grid Technical Track.

More and more city governments are using advanced technologies to improve livability for their residents. Municipalities use data from smartphones and sensors for traffic enforcement, traffic control, and waste management. They also have implemented artificial intelligence and deep learning programs.

Dubai, Paris, and Coral Gables, Fla., are among the cities that have invested heavily in programs to become smarter.

Although many initiatives have delivered real innovations, not all have been successful. Inefficient global coordination has hindered projects with unclear standards, socioeconomic differences, and a lack of worldwide governance, leading to a disconnect between the technologies and the ability to adapt to them.

Smart city projects are complex and expensive endeavors that involve politicians, citizens, technocrats, and engineers. Successful projects require citizens to be fully engaged and to have strong collaborations with the participants, especially engineers, as engineering is the cornerstone.

Collaboration with universities, research institutions, and technology experts can bridge knowledge gaps on the behavior of complex socio-technical systems. What’s missing, though, is a global platform where those involved can discuss their experiences.

To help solve those and other challenges, the IEEE Smart Cities Technical Community (formerly the IEEE Smart Cities Initiative) was launched in 2013 by IEEE Future Directions, which incubates emerging technologies and new applications of current ones. The technical community provides city leaders and others with credible, unbiased information and educational content developed by IEEE experts.

Since then, IEEE Smart Cities has launched services including its flagship International Smart Cities Conference, a media center with educational and technical resources, and a contest to recognize the best smart project completed by city officials. The platforms bring together practicing engineers, academic researchers, policymakers, and city leaders to collaborate and exchange ideas and experiences about moving toward a smart-city model.

In 2021 the IEEE Power & Energy Society began managing the Smart Cities program, which is supported by the IEEE Communications, Industry Applications, and Intelligent Transportation Systems societies and other IEEE entities.

Thanks to volunteers’ dedication and determination, IEEE Smart Cities launched several services. But the initiative’s structure limited the development of long-term projects and the creation of new activities.

To address the situation, the IEEE Technical Activities Board (TAB) created the second-generation technical community ad hoc committee, also in 2021. It was a pilot program whereby IEEE Smart Cities formed a board of governors to oversee the community’s operations and leadership, and created a policies and procedures manual.

In November 2025 IEEE Smart Cities became a TAB technical community.

Today more than 7,000 volunteers collaborate on various aspects of the community within at least one of the following technical tracks:

New webinar series, workshops, conferences, educational resources, and other offerings are being created.

Two events were launched recently: the IEEE European Technology and Engineering Management Summit, held in May 2025 in Belgium, with the next one planned for 2027; and the IEEE Sustainable Smart Lighting World Conference, scheduled for 2 to 6 December in Athens.

The Smart Cities Ambassadors program aims to raise the technical community’s visibility outside IEEE by holding roundtables and other events at non-IEEE functions.

IEEE Smart Cities volunteers are working on launching journals. In addition, standards are being developed in collaboration with the IEEE Standards Association, societies, and councils.

The program is collaborating with the Open and Agile Smart Cities and Communities network, the Instituto de Competitividad e Innovación para el Desarrollo y Transferencia de Tecnología, and the International Project Management Association.

All of those actions have the ultimate objective of boosting IEEE Smart Cities’ growth and sustainability, as well as strengthening the leadership and educational offerings to technical community volunteers.

If you would like to volunteer, visit the Smart Cities website.

Georges Zissis is an IEEE Fellow and chair of the IEEE Smart Cities Technical Community.

Satish Sani is an IEEE senior member and chair of the IEEE Smart Grid Technical Track.

The Apple Watch Ultra 4 combines outstanding smart features with solid sports tracking to be one of the best all-round options on the market.

The Pace 4 Pro is a thin, lightweight sports watch with a bright AMOELD display and impressive battery life.

The Coros Pace 4 Pro and Apple Watch Ultra 4 both launched in September this year and both impressed me in my testing overall. I rate the Coros as one of the best sports watches available, while the Apple Watch Ultra 4 is my favorite sporty smartwatch.

I wore both for my final week of training for the Frankfurt Marathon, and then for race day itself, where I ran 2:25 in my 18th marathon.

With one watch on either wrist, I was keen to see if there were any noticeable differences in their GPS and heart rate accuracy on the day.

I also checked their battery life throughout the weekend to see how fast they were draining, noted any design differences that stood out, and kept in mind how useful they were outside the run itself.

This was a true sports watch vs. smartwatch test, and I’ve picked out the key differences I noticed between the two watches over the marathon weekend below. For more detailed info on either watch, check out our full Apple Watch Ultra 4 review and Coros Pace 4 Pro review.

Before diving into the test, it’s worth noting that the Coros Pace 4 Pro is cheaper than the Apple Watch Ultra 4. It will set you back $449, compared with $799 for the Apple.

Coros rarely reduces its watches, whereas the Ultra 4 is likely to go on sale in time, which will make the gap between them smaller, but the Pace 4 Pro is always going to be the more affordable pick.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

I love the look of both watches, but they have a different feel on the wrist. The Apple Watch Ultra 4 has a full titanium case and is more robust and heavy — it’s a more premium look for sure.

The Coros Pace 4 Pro is delightfully light and slim, and has a sapphire crystal case and a titanium bezel, so it’s also going to be durable.

Both watches have three buttons, one of which is a dial, and bright displays that are easy to read in all conditions, including the wet and windy day we had in Frankfurt.

In the rain, the fact that you have to use the touchscreen on the Ultra 4 to navigate its apps and menus is a little annoying compared to the buttons on the Coros.

Importantly, you can do all the key actions you need during runs, like pause and lap, using buttons on the Apple Watch Ultra 4, but you have to use the screen to actually end your run.

The Frankfurt Marathon is a tough test for GPS accuracy because the first and final 5K of the race involve twisting around the skyscrapers in the city center. In between, it’s easy enough for watches, with a big loop out to the suburbs.

On the day, the Coros Pace 4 Pro logged a total distance of 42.52km (26.42 miles) and the Apple Watch Ultra 4 logged 43.07km (26.76 miles).

The official marathon distance is 42.19km/ 26.21 miles, and although you never run exactly this distance in an event because of weaving around crowds, I certainly think the Coros Pace 4 Pro was more accurate.

I noticed it was closer in line with the kilometer markers on the course, and because I was in the first 100 runners, I was able to stay pretty close to the most direct racing line throughout the event, so the Ultra 4’s total distance seems too much (it also read long for my colleague Jane at the event).

Looking at the GPS tracks of the watches, you can see they both went wrong at various stages in the city center under the tall buildings there, but the Ultra 4 cut corners and tracked me off the road more often.

This was unexpected for me, as I’ve run marathons with every Apple Watch Ultra and generally they have been pretty good on GPS accuracy in city centers.

I actually used the pacer mode on the Apple Watch Ultra 4, and it logged me finishing the marathon in 2:23… if only.

Concerning heart rate accuracy, I’m not going to be too hard on either watch because I didn’t wear a chest strap to get a reading to compare them to, and I wore arm sleeves during the marathon, which had watch holes but might have impacted the sensor accuracy.

Looking at the graph of the readings from the two watches, I’d say two things stood out to me when comparing them with past marathons and what I know my heart rate tends to do during them.

One is that the Coros had a consistent reading, but it looks too high compared with my max heart rate of around 176, and it doesn’t trend up throughout the event, which always happens during marathons in my experience.

The Apple Watch Ultra 4’s readings look more accurate to me, aside from the long section from the one-hour to two-hour mark where it didn’t take a reading, greying out the number on the watch because it wasn’t confident it had it right.

I’ve done a lot of testing of the heart rate sensors on both watches outside the marathon (when not wearing arm sleeves), and both are pretty good, but if you want the most reliable results, I’d always say using a chest strap is better.

The Coros Pace 4 Pro certainly wins the battery life battle between these watches, lasting up to seven days on a charge with the screen always-on, compared with 50 hours on the Apple Watch Ultra 4.

I used the marathon weekend away as a chance to test the real-world battery life performance of the two, taking both off the charger early Friday morning when I flew to Frankfurt.

After short runs with both watches on Friday and Saturday, the Coros was down to 75% on Sunday morning, and the Apple Watch Ultra 4 was at 41% (note that I didn’t sleep with them on, so that saved some battery life).

At that point, I got nervous about the Ultra 4 lasting the marathon and charged it to 75% to match the Coros, which didn’t take long thanks to the fast charging on the Apple.

During the race, I did listen to music on the Apple Watch Ultra 4 for about an hour, which increased how much battery it used, but even so, I could have got by with the 41% it originally had left, as it only drained by 16% in the race.

The Coros only lost 10% of its battery in the race, though, and is certainly the better option for battery life, but the Ultra 4 did impress me over the course of the weekend, and still had 32% of its battery left when I got home on Monday, with only that one short charge over the whole marathon weekend.

The Apple Watch Ultra 4 is clearly a better smartwatch than the Coros, with a full App Store, easy music storage through streaming services and NFC payments. The Coros can store MP3 files for Bluetooth playback, but that’s about it.

This did come across on a weekend away, where the Ultra 4 could do things like show boarding passes for my flights, and I could wirelessly adjust my running playlist on the watch pre-race and listen to music during the event.

The Apple Watch Ultra 4 also has more customization options, especially on watch faces. If it’s smarts you want, it’s definitely the better pick.

The weekend trip showcased the pros and cons of both sports watches and smartwatches, and there still isn’t one device from any brand that manages to nail both sides of the coin.

During the marathon, the Coros Pace 4 Pro was more reliable for GPS accuracy and pacing, which is absolutely crucial for me, and it offers much better battery life than the Ultra 4.

However, the Apple Watch Ultra 4 is certainly a more useful smartwatch, and it does still offer good sports tracking and a very attractive, robust design.

As someone who has made running most of my job and personality, the superior sports tracking of the Coros Pace 4 Pro is what I’d go for, and I love its lighter design too, but the Apple Watch Ultra 4 is a well-rounded pick that handles sports and smarts better than most.

#3339. This TP-Link Wi-Fi 7 Travel Router Is 27% Off for This Early Black Friday Deal

Pradershika Sharma is a tech deals writer for Lifehacker. She has a Master’s degree in English Literature, a B.Ed., and a TESOL certification. A novel solution for connecting to the internet on the go, the TP-Link Roam 7 travel router is now down to $87.99 from $119.99 in an early Black Friday deal—marking its lowest price to date, according to price trackers. This is not a full-size home router but, as the name suggests, a compact travel companion that measures roughly the size of a paperback book, with foldable antennas so it slips easily into a bag.

More about convenience than chasing top speeds, you can use the Roam 7 as a standard router, connect it to public wifi to create a private network, or share your phone's internet through USB tethering. It also supports Ethernet input and USB modems, along with range extender and wireless client modes. That flexibility is particularly useful when you’re juggling a laptop, phone, and maybe a tablet and would prefer not to sign each one into a shaky network separately. Setup is straightforward through the TP-Link Tether app: scan a QR code, choose your connection type, and you’re online in a few minutes.

Once it’s running, the hardware covers the basics, with a 2.5 Gbps port for a wired connection like a hotel’s Ethernet jack, a 1 Gbps port for a wired device, and a USB 3.0 port for a storage drive or phone tethering. And since it draws power over USB-C (5V/3A), a basic power bank can keep it going through a long layover or a camping trip. As handy as it is on the road, though, it’s not meant to replace a full-size home router—even with its 5 GHz band and Wi-Fi 7 support—which will generally offer better coverage and more consistent speeds. Real-world performance also depends heavily on your connection and setup. USB tethering, for example, can feel slower than using your phone directly. It also leaves out features like automatic band steering, so you may end up managing networks yourself. Still, if you travel often or need a portable network hub for multiple devices, you’ll find it holds up pretty well.

#3338. Nintendo Switch games running natively on Apple TV using Claude Code port

A Redditor has just released an open-source project allowing Switch and Switch 2 games to run natively on Apple TV.

So far, both Super Mario Odyssey and Animal Crossing: New Horizons are running, with work ongoing on The Legend of Zelda: Tears of the Kingdom …

We’ve seen people using Claude Code to do some pretty wild things, like reverse engineering Adobe’s pro apps in order to create open-source versions of them. The latest example is a Redditor who’s created an open-source project called TVport to recompile Nintendo games from the Switch and Switch 2 to Apple TV.

Redditor FloatingFalafel shared the work on GitHub. They’ve so far ported three games to Apple TV, with one of them still a work in progress.

I have been working on a fork of nxnative that recompiles your OG Switch and Switch 2 dumps for AppleTV. Currently, this only works on a game-by-game basis. Most games run essentially the same on the switch, but some load textures into memory differently and need to be diagnosed and fixed before the game will run properly. My hope is to find outliers during this beta so more fixes can be added into the program, making it a seamless experience […]

Super Mario Odyssey – Runs at 60FPS, very slight stutters on occasion, and some audio issues around waterfalls specifically.

Animal Crossing: Horizon – Runs at 30FPS, zero issues so far on my plays.

Zelda: TOTK – Still being worked on, runs at 30FPS, gets thermal throttled. I have a work around for the thermal throttle. I have a render scale selection set at 75% and I am working on adding MetalFX upscaling.

They note you’ll need the 4th-gen Apple TV with its 8GB RAM in order to support some games, though these ones run on the 3rd-gen box.

Another Redditor is working on porting Nintendo 64 games to Apple TV using an app called Nativecade. How long any of these types of projects will survive is anyone’s guess.

#3337. This Hidden Device Could Free Up Gigawatts of Grid Power

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

Variable frequency drives can slash motors’ power use

Zurich-based ABB is one of several manufacturers of variable frequency drives (VFDs), such as this ACH580. VFDs could help make the millions of electric motors running in industrial facilities more energy efficient.

This article was originally published by Canary Media.

America’s energy supply crunch is driving a surge of federal and private investment in new electricity generation—from polluting gas turbines to cleaner developments like solar farms and geothermal plants. But gigawatts of power are already available for the taking across the U.S. economy in the form of wasted energy from an unexpected source: motors.

Some 50 million electric motors drive the fans, pumps, and compressors found in virtually every factory and building. Together, they gobble enough electricity to equal nearly a third of total U.S. power demand. Often, the motors use far more energy than they actually need to keep America’s machines humming.

Companies can install devices known as variable frequency drives, or VFDs, to make motors run super efficiently. Yet adoption remains relatively low, in part because of the perceived hassle of retrofitting equipment and because they’re typically not required. On average, only 16 percent of motor systems at industrial facilities and 4 percent of commercial-sector motors use VFDs, according to a 2021 market report by Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory.

However, there are now more reasons than ever to equip the nation’s motors with power-saving devices, energy experts and device manufacturers say. They’re urging federal agencies, utilities, and deep-pocketed tech giants to spur a wider rollout of VFDs through financial incentives and efficiency standards.

For one, slashing motors’ power use would free up grid capacity for large electricity users like data centers and electric vehicles, they argue. It would help curb costs for factories that are switching from fossil-fueled heating systems to electrified, motor-based solutions like heat pumps—all at a time when industrial power prices are climbing fast. Plus, VFD technology has become far more sophisticated and less expensive to install than earlier iterations.

“This is low-hanging fruit that gives a lot [of energy] back and is reasonably simple,” Nik Sawe, a senior policy analyst at the nonpartisan think tank Energy Innovation, says of the technology.

Energy-wise, the main problem with electric motors is that they’re always running at full capacity. Consider an office building, which empties out in the evening. The heating, ventilation, and air-conditioning system can wind down in those hours, with dampers and valves restricting the flow of cold or hot air. But the motors and fans that drive the whole setup are still working in the background, wasting energy.

VFD technology, such as the Danfoss iC7 series, has gained some momentum in recent years among factories and buildings trying to combat rising electricity costs. Danfoss Drives

VFDs are electronic controllers with temperature sensors that continually adjust the speed of motors, automatically ramping up or down to match demand. The technology, which is also called adjustable speed drives, has the potential to curb a motor’s energy use by around 40 to 60 percent, says Neal Elliott, director emeritus of the American Council for an Energy-Efficient Economy.

All those energy reductions add up. Toyota, for example, installed VFDs on over 200 motors inside the HVAC system at its auto manufacturing plant in Georgetown, Kentucky, as part of a US $1.25 million pilot project in 2015. The automaker saved more than $700,000 in annual electricity costs thanks to the VFDs, and it continues to use the technology at other manufacturing facilities across the U.S., the company said by email.

“We’ve known for many, many years that there’s a huge opportunity for energy savings by varying the speed of the motor,” says Elliott, who noted that he literally wrote the book on energy-efficient motor systems in 2002.

Certain aspects of the technology have historically held the drives back since they debuted in the late 1960s. Measuring the flow of water, air, refrigerant—whatever is moving through the system that the motors are driving—was for decades an expensive engineering process. Accurately controlling motors to deliver the right amount of juice, at just the right time, faced similar issues.

But recent advances in sensors and machine-learning algorithms have significantly slashed the cost and complexity of using drives, Elliott says. Modern VFDs have also benefited from the increased production of advanced power chips that are used in high-voltage applications such as electric vehicles and solar power inverters.

Another long-standing challenge has been that commercial and industrial building developers often prioritize reducing upfront costs over netting long-term energy savings, and so they don’t always build to the highest efficiency levels, says Zack Valdez, senior director of regulatory and industry affairs at the National Electrical Manufacturers Association, whose members include drive and motor makers.

“If the facility that you’re putting it into doesn’t require it, then oftentimes people will overlook [VFDs], because they’re just trying to build to a minimum set of energy requirements,” he says. And if companies don’t install drives from the start, they’re likely less inclined to take time to retrofit an operating system.

The trade association recently launched a pilot program with manufacturers, utilities, and energy-efficiency groups to collect real-world data about how VFDs reduce motors’ electricity use and lower utility bills. The goal is to demonstrate how the technology can benefit not only individual facilities but also the wider grid—giving utilities a concrete reason to provide rebates for industrial customers.

Proponents say they hope the results will help the U.S. Department of Energy shape future efficiency measures and incentives that encourage adoption of the drives, including in federally owned buildings. Despite the Trump administration’s open hostility toward home appliance and equipment mandates, agency staff have apparently been receptive to discussing solutions that could meet the soaring power needs of data centers.

“If you added a drive to all the motors that are out there, you could provide [power for] up to five years of data center growth without having to build any new generation,” says Kirk Anderson, director of government relations and public affairs for ABB. The global manufacturing giant makes VFDs domestically near Milwaukee.

Anderson floated the idea of having tech companies help pay for factory owners to install VFDs to free up room on the grid. After all, hyperscalers are already spending many billions of dollars to revive shuttered nuclear plants, support next-generation geothermal projects, deploy fleets of grid-scale batteries, and supercharge the build-out of gas turbines and power plants.

“Instead of ‘bring your own power,’ it should be ‘offset your own power,’” he says, referring to a growing effort by states to get data centers to secure their own power resources and prevent rising costs for regular customers.

Michael Reckamp, the director of enterprise strategy for Danfoss Drives, North America, another VFD manufacturer, said that despite the traditionally low adoption rates, the technology has gained some momentum in recent years among factories and buildings as rising electricity costs and other grid-wide challenges make it harder to justify wasting energy.

Still, “it hasn’t permeated enough to get everyone utilizing it,” he says. “In the current situation, where we’re having so many issues with grids, brownouts, and now data centers wanting to take the load, I think there should be a renewed focus on putting drives out there to really reduce the stress on the grid and improve energy savings.”

Maria Gallucci is a clean-energy reporter with Canary Media.

I've been training my dad for roughly six years, and one element of his training I've been really ramping up lately? Core work. It's all well and good watching him get stronger, more mobile and better balanced, but a strong core reduces pain, minimizes risk of injury and helps you move well as you age.

There are essential strength exercises in his routine already, but we often work on his core strength at the end of sessions. We try to stay as low-impact as possible, supporting his back while focusing on building deep core stability. My dad has sciatica, so keeping his spine and glutes strong and active is crucial.

As you get better and stronger, you can adapt the load, reps and sets to suit your needs. If you’re ready to get started, check out the three exercises below.

A post shared by Tom's Guide Fitness | Workout Tips & Gear (@tomsguidefitness)

If you experience limited mobility in your hips, knees, ankles, or spine, go easy and take these exercises slowly. You could progress by adding weight or slowing the exercises down more.

Clamshells strengthen your glutes, which are powerful muscles that help stabilize your pelvis and protect your lower back. Overhead squats require plenty of core stability to help stabilize the weight overhead while you squat. Again, your core works hard to keep your torso upright and stable while carrying a heavy load during the farmer's carry. If you choose to carry one weight, this trains your core for anti-rotation, making you more robust.

If you experience pain, or you're unsure if this exercise is for you due to pregnancy, a health condition, illness, or injury, I recommend seeking medical advice first.

I have my dad hold a weight plate with both hands overhead during overhead squats, but we have been doing this exercise for a long time. You can also wrap a band above your knees and push against it with your legs as you squat. Try to sink your weight into your heels and spread weight to your little and big toes; lift your chest and lower your butt as far as you can.

During squats, I commonly notice heels rising (thoracic, hip, or ankle-related), knees caving in (often lower-joint-related), backs rounding, or a lack of squat depth. It's better to use your bodyweight first until you improve overall strength and mobility.

Try to keep your spine straight and your shoulders pulled back and down during all exercises, with your core switched and locked on. Imagine bracing for an impact and drawing your breath downward as you move.

#3335. There's a New Way to Automatically Back Up Your Android Photos for Free

In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.

If you're an Android user looking for a way to save your photos and videos without maxing out your cloud storage space, your device may soon be able to back up automatically to your PC. As spotted by Android Authority, Google included automatic backups from Android to Windows via Quick Share in its release notes for Google Play services v26.43.

Quick Share is a wireless file-sharing feature for Android that allows users to send photos, videos, and documents to nearby devices, including Windows computers and iPhones with AirDrop. The new automatic backup feature, which is likely to roll out gradually, uses Quick Share's functionality to transfer copies of photos and videos on your phone to your PC when nearby.

Since these backups happen locally, you don't need to rely solely on cloud storage in your Google account, nor do you need to remember to initiate transfers of photos and videos between devices. Plus, this is all free and doesn't require a separate cloud service subscription. While you can back up your media to Google Photos, as of earlier this year, more data from your Android backups count toward your Google Account storage cap unless you exclude specific types. Alternatively, you can also cobble together a decent amount of cloud storage from other providers at no extra cost, but automatic backups between Android and Windows minimize the likelihood that you'll forget to save data, and your PC provides plenty of space for free.

Once the feature is available on your device, you'll be able to initiate backups in the Quick Share for Windows app. Your Android and Windows devices must be in close proximity and signed into the same Google Account. You can toggle Automatic backups on and change the settings for what gets backed up and to where. The transfers will then occur wirelessly in the background.

As Android Authority reports, early hints at this feature suggested that Samsung phones and PCs would be excluded from automatic backups, but the release notes don't specify any further details.
