#3316. The Robot I Didn’t Expect to Build

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

Agility Robotics’ first practical robotic worker is nothing like I dreamed

Author and Agility Robotics co-founder Jonathan Hurst next to his new Digit 5 humanoid robot worker.

Agility Robotics, the company I cofounded out of my robotics lab at Oregon State University in 2015, has just launched Digit 5. It’s designed to be the first humanoid robot that can safely and economically do useful work at scale, allowing us to bring tens of thousands of humanoid workers into the real world. Engineered to lift 23-kilogram bins onto high shelves and with a battery that can run for 90 minutes on a 9-minute charge, Digit 5’s goal is to handle heavy warehouse tasks shift after shift, filling the need for labor in jobs that are too physically stressful or too dull for humans to want to do.

Digit 5 is what Agility has been working toward for over a decade. But the robot is heavy and bulky, lacking the graceful natural motion of its predecessors, and it’s farther than I thought possible from the robot I dreamed of building when I started this company. To deliver a useful commercial product, Agility has taken a path that is very different from what I first imagined.

My dream has always been to build robots that combine locomotion and manipulation to move through the world and interact with it as people do. I seek a mastery of motion, achieved through devices designed to navigate the constraints of physics with elegance. When I started the Dynamic Robotics Laboratory at Oregon State in 2008, we began with a theory derived from decades of work in biomechanics: that a simple “spring-mass” model (a body supported by legs that act like springs) should be able to reproduce every known walking and running gait found in animals.

We put theory into practice by building the bipedal robot ATRIAS—short for “Assume The Robot Is A Sphere,” a joke among physicists about reducing a complex system to its simplest possible form. ATRIAS looked like a large microwave on stilts because it was only intended to demonstrate the physics of human walking and running. This was the first glimmer of achieving my dream; even though ATRIAS wasn’t designed to look like us, it still seemed natural, and even somehow alive, when it settled into a walking gait.

With the success of ATRIAS, the barriers to progress shifted from scientific to engineering and organizational, and a startup company seemed like the way to bridge the gap from a one-off research concept to an actual robotic product. I felt confident of two things: that I would be able to build robots that could go where people go, and that this capability would be incredibly useful. This combination of ambition and naivete is necessary for anyone to found a new company—how hard could it be?

Good advice for starting a company is to understand a customer problem, and then find a way to solve it using your unique capabilities. My cofounders, Damion Shelton and Mikhail Jones, and I did not do this. We relied on our belief that this technology would enable new possibilities and trusted ourselves to figure out the business as we went. So we simply focused on building our first product: the bipedal robot Cassie.

Cassie was the first dynamic bipedal robot that researchers could buy, able to maintain its balance through active, fluid motion rather than careful, rigid steps. It had ostrichlike legs, not because we were imitating ground-running birds, but as a result of engineering strictly for performance. It was not intended to be commercially useful, and had no torso, arms, or head. We sold Cassie robots to Harvard, Caltech, the University of Michigan, the University of California, Berkeley, and a handful of other research institutions, ultimately saturating the market for US $250,000 bipedal research robots after having sold a total of 10 of them.

ATRIAS, Cassie, and Digit 4 EVT [left to right] are on display at Agility Robotics’ RoboFab in Salem, Ore. The 70,000-square-foot facility has the capacity to produce more than 10,000 Digit 5 robots per year.Agility Robotics

Because Cassie’s hardware enabled research into the physics of walking and running, the legged-robot research frontier shifted to control software. Traditionally, engineers controlled legged robots with detailed mathematical models that determined how the machines should move. With Cassie, researchers pioneered the new approach of reinforcement learning for bipedal legged locomotion: A simulated robot learns through trial and error, and the resulting neural network controls the physical machine. This approach is what enables virtually all of the dynamic behaviors that you see on legged robots today, and Cassie looked alive as it recovered from stumbles while climbing stairs, ran 5 kilometers across the Oregon State campus, and broke the robot world record for a 100-meter dash.

Cassie got us closer to being able to move through the world with confidence and grace, but to make it useful, we needed manipulation. After exhaustively exploring different configurations, we found that an upright torso helped the robot balance, while two arms mounted near the top of the torso allowed it to pick up large objects and to catch itself when it fell. Digit 1, which added a torso and arms to the Cassie legs, was our first mobile manipulation robot, and another step on the path toward a product that could do useful work for commercial customers.

As we explored the first applications for Digit, potential customers kept asking us: Why legs? And why a humanoid? These were tough questions for me to answer, because they exposed a core business reality: It didn’t matter to Agility Robotics if we solved a cool science problem in a beautiful way. What mattered to the business was solving real problems for customers.

After years of engagement with industry partners, we found one answer in warehouses and manufacturing facilities: moving bins. Bin handling is a clearly defined task where two arms are needed to lift large bins up high and legs are the best way to balance and move in narrow spaces. Because the task can vary widely from one deployment to another, it hasn’t been broadly addressed by single-purpose automation. Yet it was constrained enough to give Digit an economically viable first job while it developed a broader set of skills.

In 2019, Digit began demonstrating its capabilities to do real work. With Ford Motor Company, we showed how Digit 1 could carry packages from an autonomous vehicle to a front porch. We developed Digit 2 and 3 while working with a certain global package delivery company on moving and sorting cardboard boxes. Amazon tested Digit 4 on moving and stacking bins, and it became the world’s first commercially deployed humanoid at the logistics provider GXO. In 2024, Digit appeared on the cover of Time magazine.

Despite Digit’s apparent success, we began to run into conflicts between my dream and the needs of actual customers. We were no longer working with relatively patient university research labs. Agility has to sell robots to survive, and customers will only purchase robots that provide value. If bins weren’t moving, our customers were losing money. We spent a huge amount of time and effort keeping our first deployments operational, which arguably eliminated any profit we made. Yet this also kept our company learning and alive the way no lab demo ever could.

I had no idea how hard it would be, or that running a company would involve so many things that have nothing to do with solving technical problems: deployments across the country; shipping, service, and customer support; fundraising and investor relations; more fundraising; human resources and IT; developing fleet-management software; managing a supply chain; and even more fundraising. I had no experience with any of these things. My career had focused on solving the technical challenges of robots interacting with the world, and it turned out that was only a tiny piece of building a successful robotics company. But Agility was the only path I saw to continuing the technical work and having an impact.

I knew that Agility needed to focus more on robots as a product, but I didn’t know how to make that happen. Hiring the people we needed to run the company meant giving up an immense amount of control, but we had no other choice. We recruited a new executive team with the experience required to commercialize this new technology, and they quickly made changes that were both painful and necessary.

Digit versions 1, 2, and 3 [left to right] show the evolution of the robot from a dynamic walking platform into a useful mobile manipulator. Agility

We had intended the next revision of Digit, Digit 4 EVT (Engineering Validation and Test), to be a relatively minor upgrade. But Agility’s new leadership insisted that the robot was missing key features that were essential if Digit was going to become a real product. So Digit 4 EVT instead incorporated a series of major changes in a highly compressed timeline, such as larger batteries and system-wide upgrades for safety and regulatory compliance, which added enough mass to dramatically alter the robot’s appearance and capabilities.

While early Digits were headless, Agility Robotics was able to justify a head for Digit 4 to optimize antenna and camera placement, and it turned out to be surprisingly useful for human-robot interaction.Christie Hemm Klok

I could only watch as others brought their own talents to bear to make Digit into a successful product, in gut-wrenching ways that didn’t always align with my vision. There were some especially difficult times when I felt like there were compromises made that didn’t seem necessary, but making those decisions was no longer my sole responsibility. I had to accept that Digit had grown far beyond me, and look for ways of influencing decisions rather than directing them. In the moment, it was incredibly frustrating, as Digit 4 EVT took a few steps backward from my vision of how humanoids should look and move.

Agility is in our name because agility is core to the future of the company. I want Digit to be lithe and graceful. When people see Digit, I want them to like the robot, to understand what it can do at a glance, and to feel that it’s there to help. But with Digit 4 EVT, all of that was sacrificed to functionality, because of course it had to be—the customer just needs the robot to do the work. The design process became a ruthless triage, with aesthetics and elegance of movement being delayed over and over again in favor of brutal functionality. For an engineer whose mind lives more in the future than in the present, it has been hard for me to accept this trajectory. And yet, through Digit 4 EVT’s commercial deployments, we began to really understand specific applications and what they required. We mapped the first 10 use cases Digit would perform, and then began designing Digit 5 from scratch based on everything we had learned.

Digit 5 will be Agility’s first real step toward a general-purpose robot. It marks our transition from imagining what a future humanoid robot should be to designing a product around the realities of customer deployments. These realities include things like European CE regulatory compliance, North American UL electrical-safety certifications, and Federal Communications Commission limits for electromagnetic radiation—all of which felt tangential to my dream for Digit, but were absolute requirements.

Digit 5 is designed to be the first humanoid robot that can operate safely next to human coworkers while working 20 hours a day and lifting more than a human can.Christie Hemm Klok

Customer requirements helped us realize that safety in particular was one of the most critical barriers to scaling. In Digit 4’s commercial deployments, the robots had to work behind physical barriers, separated from humans at all times, to meet insurance and regulatory demands. This seemed silly to me, because I’ve never felt that our robots were dangerous, but we have to prove that they’re safe. And since keeping the robots in safety cages severely limited their usefulness, enabling Digit 5 to operate safely around people became a primary design goal. We spent two years on this challenge.

Digit 5 is designed to be the first humanoid robot that can operate safely next to human coworkers. It will rely on an array of sensors to locate nearby people in a manner that’s certifiably safe, and then take actions based on that information. As a person approaches, Digit 5 is programmed to stop what it’s doing, set down its payload, sit on the floor, and cut power to its motors before the person gets close enough to touch the robot. This conservative approach reduces the risk to nearby people in a verifiable way, and we believe it’s the only approach that makes sense as a first step toward working alongside humans.

Yet this strategy also feels like a massive slowdown on the path toward robots becoming part of everyday life. Enabling coexistence with humans has influenced almost every aspect of Digit 5’s design: the shape of the legs and the body, the safety-rated sensors within protective housings, the isolated computers dedicated to safety, and more. All of these features increase the robot’s complexity, power consumption, mass, and physical size.

Digit 5 is Agility’s largest, heaviest, strongest, and most capable humanoid robot worker.

The robot’s design was driven by safety, with integrated protection for the robot and for the humans it will work around.Agility Robotics

Weighing over 120 kg, Digit 5 is a huge robot. It needed to achieve the lifting limits recommended under the U.S. National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health guidelines for human workers, which include repeatedly lifting 23-kg bins and reaching shelves 1.75 meters high. Digit is designed to perform tasks like these for 20 hours a day—something no human can do. This requires motors with enough power and torque to lift the load, but also enough precision to delicately control the force Digit applies when it makes contact with the world. To power those motors, we needed a large battery and a dock for rapid autonomous charging. The dock will deliver 240 amperes at 48 volts, which is enough current to make its thick charging cables visibly wiggle under the induced magnetic forces, while powerful fans blow air through cooling channels in the robot’s torso to keep the battery from overheating. The battery and cooling system takes up about 75 percent of Digit’s torso, but it will allow the robot to operate for 90 minutes and fully recharge during a 9-minute break, enabling near-continuous work.

All of this extra bulk means that Digit 5 can no longer run or jump the way previous generations could, and the svelte form I imagined has become physically impossible. In some ways, Digit 5 feels more like a forklift than the graceful humanoid I set out to build. But looking at the situation rationally, I believe this trade-off is necessary for any company that claims its humanoid can do this kind of work today: If you see a robot that looks like a human working in a factory or warehouse, it either can’t lift the required weight or can’t make it through the whole shift. And if it’s not covered with sensors, it’s likely not safe to stand next to.

The most visible change with Digit 5 is that humanlike legs replace the ostrichlike legs of our earlier versions. While the “backward” leg configuration was optimized for walking and running, we discovered that it created problems with squatting because the ankle will strike the ground. Digit 5 will spend a lot of time lifting heavy objects from near the floor, so we used a humanoid leg configuration with knee and hip motors that both contribute torque to help the robot stand up again.

When Digit detects an approaching human, the robot will lower itself to the floor and cut power to its motors. Agility believes this is the only near-term approach to verifiably reduce risk when the robot is working near people.Agility Robotics

Other companies building humanoid robots have copied the human form without ever understanding its purpose. It’s very frustrating that, to an outside observer, it now looks like we discarded Agility’s distinctive leg design and simply did what everyone else was doing. Yet I know that we arrived at this shape based purely on functional engineering choices. Making a robot look like a human is the easy part—without the function to match, and the understanding of the physics underlying that function, the whole point of the human form may be lost.

With the power, battery life, and safety features that we are designing into Digit 5, we will have a truly useful robot. But it also compromises on some things that are core to my vision and mission. I understand why we made the choices we did and can justify them all, but together they leave me unsatisfied. It’s the curse of the engineer.

I believe Digit 5 will be the scaling moment for Agility Robotics, the inflection point where we can begin deploying robots in large numbers. While the robot will continue carrying bins, our road map includes many more tasks, from picking individual items and tending machines, to preparing parts for assembly and shipping, and eventually doing assembly work itself. Its interchangeable tool interfaces and modular design will enable us to gradually upgrade its subsystems. It will be a platform for improvement, a source of data for future behavior training, and a viable product all at the same time.

Hurst stands between the previous version of Digit, Digit 4 [left], and Digit 5.Christie Hemm Klok

But I cannot love Digit 5. It’s the largest, heaviest, most expensive robot Agility will ever build, full of design compromises that enable it to be exactly the robot it needs to be right now rather than the robot I dreamed of. In the beginning, I envisioned steady progress on agility and dexterity, with each version becoming more dynamically capable. Instead, developing Digit 5 has required large detours to incorporate requirements that seemed unrelated to my original vision. However, I now recognize that tackling these challenges was always necessary. Customers and product requirements didn’t ruin my vision; they revealed what my vision was missing. This is how robots will achieve commercial success and make a real-world impact, which will bring me closer to my scientific dream as well.

We won’t have a humanoid that matches the capabilities of humans until it achieves that mastery of motion that inspired me to found Agility over a decade ago. I saw glimmers of it with the spring-mass locomotion of ATRIAS, and more glimmers with Cassie’s running gait.

I know that such mastery is physically possible with the tools and hardware that we have right now, and despite all of its compromises, Digit 5 will give us a practical foundation for pursuing that dream. I want every future version of Digit to be lighter and more graceful, to interact more naturally with humans, and to be better at manipulating objects and moving through the world, enabling robots to enter aspects of our lives that they haven’t been able to help with before. By the time I’m old enough to need assistance at home, I expect Digit will be up to the task.

With Digit 5, Agility has built a robot that will be useful in our world. Now I’m getting back to work to make it beautiful, too.

This article appears in the November 2026 print issue.

Jonathan W. Hurst is the co-founder and chief robot officer of Agility Robotics and a robotics professor at Oregon State University.

This is the most honest account I've read from a robotics founder. While Tesla and Figure are still showing demos, Agility has actually deployed robots in real customer environments, moved over 100,000 totes at GXO, and hit 98% accuracy at Schaeffler. Digit 5's specs are driven entirely by what customers need: 20 hours of work per day, 9-minute charge, 23 kg lift to 1.75 m shelves. That's real engineering for real problems. The tension between engineering vision and commercial reality is something every robotics founder will face. Professor Hurst lays it out without spin.

Why humanoid though? In particular, why bi-pedal? Why use legs at all? Are wheels surely better and easier? Legs seem like unnecessary complexity. Wheels on 'legs" for suspension can be a great alternative. I don't understand the obsession with humanoid form?

It seems to me that even at scale production, the robot we employ in industry should do jobs people cannot. Highly radioactive, highly toxic, and factors where the atmosphere needs to be unsuitable for humans. i.e., oxygen-deprived environment or low pressure/vacuum. Or use them on the 3rd shift when people are less willing to work.

Robots should increase manufacturing that was impossible to do in the past. We should be exploring new types of manufacturing, not replacing people in manufacturing that humans can do. That's how you create growth.

#3315. iOS 27.3 gives Apple One’s high-end tier a compelling upgrade

iOS 27.3 is coming next month and is packed with new features, including some that make Apple One Premier more compelling than ever.

Apple One launched in 2019 with Individual, Family, and Premier plans. And in the seven years since, the service bundle has stayed remarkably consistent.

Every plan has always included Apple Music, Apple TV, Apple Arcade, and iCloud+. And the high-end Premier option adds Apple News+ and Fitness+ alongside more iCloud storage.

Apple News+ has gotten a lot better over the years. Following the New York Times playbook, Apple has added daily puzzle games, food-focused content like recipes, and audio stories, all while continuing to improve the basic news experience.

Apple Fitness+ keeps improving too, but there’s an upgrade in iOS 27.3 that makes it far more compelling in my view: Gym Strength.

Built-in video demonstrations accompany your personalized plan, making strength training accessible even for newcomers. And you can track your progress in the app, with key Apple Watch integration too.

I’ve used Fitness+ plenty and enjoyed it, but a comprehensive strength plan like this was a big gap in the service previously. With iOS 27.3 though, Fitness+ takes a big leap forward and makes Apple One Premier more compelling than ever.

Also relevant: with the new HomeView product and other Apple Home accessories almost here, Apple One Premier’s support for Apple Intelligence video summaries and clips with HomeKit Secure Video becomes more valuable. All of this together amounts to a stronger-than-ever Premier plan.

Apple One starts at $21.95/month and includes services like Apple TV, Apple Music, iCloud+, and more.

#3313. Gulfport Energy (GPOR) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Liquids output jumped 67% as a continuous Appalachia program takes shape.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Gulfport Energy Corporation (GPOR -2.53%) reported a transition toward continuous operational programs in Appalachia to improve capital efficiency and lower development costs. Management stated the company reached a production inflection point in the third quarter, driven by the completion of liquids-rich pads in the Utica shale. The company indicated it is reallocating capital from the SCOOP asset in Oklahoma to Appalachia while assessing alternative drilling horizons in the Anadarko Basin. Furthermore, Gulfport expanded its shareholder return framework through an increased share repurchase authorization and secured long-term supply agreements to capture premium pricing from growing regional power demand.

Operator: Greetings. Welcome to the Gulfport Energy Corporation Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Call. At this time, all participants are in a listen-only mode. A question-and-answer session will follow the formal presentation. And please note, this conference is being recorded. I will now turn the conference over to Jessica Antle, Vice President of Investor Relations. Jessica, you may begin.

Jessica R. Antle: Thank you, and good morning. Welcome to Gulfport Energy Corporation's Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Conference Call. I am Jessica, Vice President of Investor Relations. And with me on today's call are Nick Dell'Osso and Matthew H. Rucker. Nick will give a brief overview of our results and then we will open up the teleconference for Q&A. I would like to remind everybody that during this conference call, the participants may make certain forward-looking statements. Actual results and future events could differ materially from those that are indicated in these forward-looking statements due to a variety of factors. Information concerning these factors can be found in the company's filings with the SEC. In addition, we may reference non GAAP measures.

Please refer to our most recent earnings release and investor presentation for important disclosure regarding such measures, including reconciliations to the most comparable GAAP financial measures. An updated Gulfport presentation was posted yesterday evening to our website in conjunction with the earnings announcement. Please review at your leisure. At this time, I would like to turn the call over to Nick.

Domenic J. Dell'Osso Jr.: Good morning and thank you for joining our third quarter earnings call. Starting off, I would like to congratulate our team on our very strong third quarter results. Production, capital and operating costs all landed right in line with guidance. As you are aware, we forecasted total and importantly, liquids production to be up meaningfully from second quarter and we delivered on that planned ramp. In fact, liquids production represented 13% of total production in the quarter on the strength of our recent wet gas Utica TILs. That higher value mix, strong realized liquids pricing and our disciplined cost structure translated into strong EBITDA and adjusted free cash flow, both up meaningfully from the second quarter.

Similarly, the fourth quarter is off to a good start and we remain on track to execute within our original guidance ranges. Last quarter, I said our number 1 priority was delivering better and more consistent results for shareholders. And a clean, predictable quarter is evidence of that focus. We are pleased with the predictability of our business and remain focused on the next phase of business improvements to generate higher returns for shareholders. Our strategy will be built around 3 key value drivers. Improving our capital and operating efficiency, positioning our gas to respond effectively to growing in basin demand and growing our acreage position in areas with high return potential to Gulfport shareholders.

An important first step in maturing this strategy is our plan to move to continuous operations in Appalachia. We have included a slide in our presentation this morning to highlight the value of moving to a continuous 2-rig program in Appalachia and the expected improvement to our D&C cost per foot and the near term development of our highest return long lateral wet gas pads. Connected to this decision is the contracting of an electric frac fleet beginning in mid-2027, allowing us to reduce diesel exposure and total completion spend. All combined, we have line of sight to reduce our D&C cost per foot by more than 20% between now and 2028.

The reduced white space in our development plan lower costs and higher liquids content all point to improved returns on capital and a free cash flow inflection. In 2028. Just as important, a lower cost structure reduces the reinvestment rate required to hold the business flat. And that in turn raises free cash flow per share in every year that follows. Not just the next 1. Related to growing in basin demand, we are very pleased to have used our firm transport to access premium markets in the Upper Midwest to sign another supply agreement at attractive pricing beginning in Q4 2028, that supports growing demand in the region.

We are maintaining floating exposure to a basis location that has historically been a premium pricing point while locking in a higher spread to that location than we have received in the past. We like the structure of retaining strategic exposure to a dynamic we believe has further upside, while establishing ourselves as an important source of supply with an attractive spread. Combined with our 10-year agreement, delivering into Ohio beginning in mid-2027, this incremental contract secures advantageous pricing for about 10% of our forecasted Appalachia production over the life of the agreements. Contracted at a premium to what we have historically received for those same molecules all using firm transport we already hold.

We think this is strong evidence of the demand pull nature of Appalachia gas markets and how marketers and customers are looking to secure available supply. Of our peers recently described acreage along the Ohio River as beachfront real estate to this growing demand. If that is the beach, we have our toes in the water at Gulfport. Our core position sits in the heart of Ohio. Where new gas fired generation and data center load are just starting to show up. We have about 30% to 40% of our production sold in basin to benefit as it grows.

Third, from an acreage growth perspective, we closed $83 million of Ohio State land acquisitions this quarter, and are finishing out our $140 million 2026 discretionary program, $50 million to $55 million of remaining spend before year end. This will continue to add valuable life to our portfolio of attractive drilling opportunities and support our ability to run a more effective development program. This program will continue into 2027, and we expect to focus on areas that have great rock at attractive upfront bonus and royalty structures leading to opportunities for greater returns. Looking at our SCOOP asset in Oklahoma, we are seeing some really compelling development by our peer companies targeting different horizons.

We believe it is prudent to reduce our activity in the SCOOP during 2027 and reassess our development plan in consideration of these opportunities beyond our historical primary target. We will work through the year to reset our longer term development program to better capture the upside we believe exists in this acreage. While the reduction in SCOOP capital helps to fund the shift to capital in Appalachia. We will provide 2027 financial guidance concurrent with our Q4 earnings, as we typically do, but want to give investors a few things to consider today as laid out in our slide deck.

As we move to a more efficient continuous 2-rig program in Appalachia, realize the savings from the e fleet and incorporate recent high quality acreage in the wet gas window with long lateral units. Our wells drilled per year and liquids content will increase and cost per lateral foot will decrease. This in turn positions us to better serve our growing demand base in Appalachia and realize higher value per unit and further creates advantages in returns on expected acquired acreage. We believe this strategy will generate attractive returns for shareholders in a more sustainable fashion over the coming periods. We are not adding activity to grow volumes for their own sake.

We are doing it because every dollar we invest will generate more cash. A more efficient base of operations means more efficient cash flow generation, and our flexibility to allocate that cash to the highest return opportunities increases with a reduction in the reinvestment rate and allows us to clearly evaluate the merits of buybacks, balance sheet, acreage and drill bit. Every dollar competes on the same basis. What it adds to cash flow and value per share, For 2026, we expect adjusted free cash flow to grow more than 15% over 2025 at $3 gas. That discipline remains true in 2027.

Even with low projected gas prices and the repositioning of our capital, we expect free cash flow to remain strong. Still a double digit free cash flow yield at $3 gas. And we expect to be active across the full suite of investment opportunities. To that end, we announced today a 33% increase in our share repurchase authorization, to $2 billion, having repurchased approximately 1.2 billion of our stock since the program began. And we will do all of this while maintaining a strong balance sheet. To sum up, we are lowering our cost structure and our maintenance capital, increasing cash flow per share and allocating every dollar to what is most accretive per dollar invested.

Third quarter execution was on track. Continuous operations make that execution more efficient. 2027 is the investment that drives higher returns and free cash flow inflection from 2028 and beyond. Excited about where Gulfport is headed, and I look forward to updating you on our full 2027 plan in February. Operator, we will now open the call for questions.

Which gives you more financial flexibility in how you think about every decision from returning capital to shareholders, to reducing debt, to adding valuable assets to the portfolio. Tim Rezvan: Hi. Nick, I want to ask about the Marcellus Gulfport has done a pretty good job delineating the inventory in Eastern Ohio, and you have talked about 100 locations. I am not trying to pin you down to a number because I know you will not give 1. But is the opportunity set, do you feel like that $100 million level is that out there? Could you transact in that? Or could you transact more? Just trying to understand what the opportunity set is I know that the board has to decide on what that budget is. But what does that opportunity set look like, I guess, what I am trying to ask Thanks.

Domenic J. Dell'Osso Jr.: Good question, Timothy. And you are right that it is a little early for us to give you a specific number here because we are going to work through our budgeting process as we typically would. But, there is plenty of opportunity out there. We are excited about a lot of things we are seeing. Our team is super active. They keep in close contact with a number of different, you know, directly with landowners and with other brokers and really trying to assess the opportunities. And they exist across a number of different, I would call them, subparts of the play. And we will be active.

So I am pretty optimistic about this company's ability to continue to add great acreage to this portfolio at really attractive prices. And I think our governor will be we think about capital allocation, the competition for capital allocation from the balance sheet, from the value of our stock, from all of those things. So I think the governor will be what do we choose to do as opposed to are there enough opportunities.

Operator: Thank you. Our next question is from Gabe Daoud from Truist Securities. You may proceed with your question.

Gabe Daoud: Nick, you alluded to this in just your prior answer, but was curious how the buyback fits into the capital allocation framework in 2017. I know there is a lot of calls on capital as you run a continuous 2-rig program as you highlighted, but curious maybe where the buyback sits?

Domenic J. Dell'Osso Jr.: I mean, again, it is competitive. Right? We will have excess free cash flow in the year. And the way I think about that excess free cash flow is we will be looking hard at exactly how we implement this decision to go to 2 rigs, And the timing of that, we will be looking hard at reducing debt or strengthening our balance sheet. We will be looking hard at buybacks, and we will be looking hard at adding really valuable acreage. And all those things have tension against each other. And depending on market conditions and anticipated return of anything you are looking at, you have the opportunity to you know, make a call.

I think you know, I like that. I like the ability to have a number of options for where to allocate our capital in ways that generate the highest rate of return. that is what we are paid to do as management teams and I think we have a full suite of options in front of us, and we increased the authorization so that it was clear that option remained relevant and on the table. And it will continue to compete against everything else that we do.

Gabe Daoud: Okay. That makes sense. Appreciate that. And then just as a follow-up, going back to Slide 6, you gave us a D&C per foot, and with an e-fleet locked in. I would imagine you contracted the second rig for a longer period of time But just curious, like what type of inflationary pressures, if any, are kind of embedded in those D&C per foot numbers?

Matthew H. Rucker: Yeah. Good question. We have baked all that in for 2027 based on our service contracts. I think on a stand alone basis, we would have expected to see around 5% inflation for 2027. And our typical cadence of development. what is really attractive about this development plan is we have been able to, offset all of those inflationary costs with our efficiency gains that we planned both from what we are going to feel like we see on the drilling side and the frac side on being a little bit better at what we do.

But, the ability to go sign up and lock in an e-fleet, which is significant dollar savings, on an annualized basis versus us utilizing our dual fuel fleets that we have used historically. So all of that to us is really an offset and then the. You know, any increase in capital you would see next year would be all activity based, Gabe. Right. All right. Awesome. Thanks, Matthew.

Operator: Our next question is from Carlos Escalante of Wolfe Research.

Carlos Escalante: Hey, good morning, Nick and Matthew and team. That part of the question is actually a perfect segue to what we want to ask. So going back to Slide 6 on DNC rollout, but there is some clear savings that we can see on the middle chart. But I am trying to understand, parse through what is the breakdown of those savings how much does it come from the continuous operations versus the electric frac fleet starting in mid-2027. And then when you think about decision triggers into early 2027, are there any conditions under which you would stay at a lower cadence versus what you anticipate today?

Domenic J. Dell'Osso Jr.: I will answer the second 1 first. Look. We are clearly headed in this direction, and we are going to start the year with 2 rigs because that is the typical cadence that we have. And so, you know, I will never say never. there is always some market conditions that cause you to rethink your capital allocation. So that is clearly why we are not giving guidance today and why we want to get through winter, and we want to have the full setup of plan laid out in front of us and make sure that we are ready to commit to a full year of this. We want to have all of our vendors lined up.

We wanna have all of the pads ready to go, and there is just a lot of detail that you have fairly well baked in November, but not completely. So we will hold on giving a formal answer to that until we give guidance. But, you know, we are clearly looking at this hard and wanting to be moving in this direction. On the breakdown, it is really hard to separate. They are very connected. The contract for the e fleet really becomes a lot easier for us to have taken on when we know that we are going to be moving to a more active program in Appalachia. Those fleets require commitment.

That commitment, in this case, is 18 months. And so, you know, we wanted to be in a place where we felt like we had good line of sight to having this level of activity. Now that said, we can sublease that out if we need to or work with the vendor to allow others to use it at times if we have a pullback in activity. So feel really good about the way that commitment is structured. But, they are interlinked. Sure. Thank you. Appreciate that, Nick.

Carlos Escalante: And then perhaps just as a quick reminder to us on the North Marcellus and maybe how that relates to how you view the next 2 years. What is the underlying assumption of a successful appraisal where you see results you like on that well. That go into the 2028 target and goals. And whether that is that would pose upside case, or would it simply mean that you have more optionality in your capital allocation program moving forward.

Matthew H. Rucker: Yeah. Carlos, I think the latter, to your comment there, the way we are viewing that is we have got a plan for next year that is baked generally speaking, with our core Marcellus. We will delineate through, completions and turn in line the 2 northern Marcellus wells, early next year. We will evaluate the production results. We will go to market for our midstream and processing agreements, which takes some time. And then upon successful completion of that, I view it as more optionality in our development program.

Our expectation is that this area will be very similar to our core Marcellus, and so you can think about the successful delineation there being an extension of the well set that we have currently that we are developing. So just more flexibility and optionality and that would be something we would determine at a later date.

Carlos Escalante: Appreciate the color. Thank you, Nick and Matthew.

Operator: Our next question is from Peyton Doorn of UBS. You may proceed with your question.

Peyton Doorn: Hey, good morning everybody. Thank you for having me on. I thought the new gas supply agreement that you detailed was a positive. Is this something that you see Gulfport looking to expand in the future if possible? Maybe said in a different way, is there a certain upper bound longer term in terms of how much gas you would like to dedicate to these types of supply agreements?

Domenic J. Dell'Osso Jr.: it is a great question. I think about an agreement like this as essentially a hedge. We are taking gas that we have been selling at Rec Zone 3 in Chicago Citygate, and we are still gonna sell it at those locations. What we have done is we have agreed to a fixed spread for our gas to that location. So the only part of the hedge that is in place is the spread we receive to those 2 pricing points. We still float at that point and just get a spread to it. And that spread is pretty attractive relative to what we have received in the past. So it is an uplift. And we like that.

We did not have to take on any more cost to do it. Because this is with firm transport that we already had. So this is a really good trade for us. Again, these 2 contracts combined to be about 10%. So I think there is plenty more that we could do here. And we have had other inbounds from people trying to secure gas across Appalachia thinking about the role that Gulfport plays in that. We are going to continue to listen carefully. We are going to continue to study the market and understand how it is evolving and understand where our gas has the most value, understand where we believe the most upside is.

And make, you know, further hedge decisions with all of that information over time. So I do think there is more upside here. I think you know, Gulfport will be a beneficiary of this growing demand. And we talked last quarter about how some companies will do really long term agreements that maybe are not the right fit for a company like Gulfport, but an agreement like this, which is, 5 or 10 years on the long end, fits much better. And, you know, again, the pricing that we can realize here is a great premium to what we have had in the past, and we are really happy with it.

So open to doing more, but it has to be on the right economics.

Peyton Doorn: Yeah. Makes sense. And I appreciate all the detail there. And I just want to ask on the balance sheet. You know, debt crept up a bit this quarter. With free cash flow in the fourth quarter looking like it is going to be a nice jump up. I am curious if you are comfortable with where the current leverage stands or if it is kind of at a point where you might try to take it down a little into next year? Thank you.

Domenic J. Dell'Osso Jr.: It will be down at year end. It will be back more towards 1x at year end. Or right about 1x. Actually at year end. So, yeah, I think, you know, look, it is it is up this quarter. We closed on the big state lands acquisition during the quarter, and we had a lot of priorities this year. And, we are generating most of our cash in the second half of the year, so it will come back down. Still think about that 1 times as a good mid-cycle place to be. And so now that we have ticked above it here for a quarter, we would expect it to come down. Okay.

Peyton Doorn: that is helpful. Thanks for having me on.

Operator: Thank you. Our last question is from Michael Scialla of Pickering Energy Partners. You may proceed with your question.

Michael Furrow: Hi, good morning. Thanks for taking our questions. I would just like to start with a big picture question for you, Nick. So now that you have had more time in the seat and a chance to really look under the hood, where do you see the room for the most improvement? And are there certain opportunities that are clearer to you now than they were from the outside looking in?

Domenic J. Dell'Osso Jr.: Yeah. I think, you know, not to beat the dead horse here, Michael, but I would just point you to Slide 6. I mean, that is why we laid out all this detail in the deck. This is the biggest opportunity for the company, and Matthew and I are both really excited about how this positions us for the next several years of development in Ohio. We are going to be a lot more efficient. We are going to drive our cost structure lower by better vendor contracting, by better execution, by better planning.

And we think there is an opportunity to continue to add great acreage to the business because we have the efficiency that is showing up and turn that acreage into great returns for our shareholders. So we think all of this is connected, and I go back to those 3 priorities that we are gonna have, which is improve capital and operating efficiency, positioning our gas for the growing demand, and adding valuable acreage to the portfolio. And I think, you know, this move that we are making here is the real catalyst to unlock that. So that is what this is all about. And, yes, my confidence has grown as I have been here. on executing exactly this plan.

Michael Furrow: Understood. Appreciate the response, and, I agree. it is a great slide, and the benefits look pretty clear. Just as a follow-up, we could not help but notice the layering on of hedges for next year, particularly the additional swaps. Do you feel like the 2027 hedge book is in a good place at this stage? And additionally, does the hedge protection kind of change your decision to allocate capital towards buybacks or do you kind of view it as a separate decision?

Domenic J. Dell'Osso Jr.: Separate decision. Always. Hedges are. You know, they are a trade you can take on and off. But no, I am happy with our hedge position for 2027. I mean, given where the strip is, I would love to have more at the average hedge price that we have And if we were to get some cold this winter that were to pop gas prices up, to an attractive level again, then I think we would hedge more. I do not really see us hedging beyond 2027 at these levels. But we are always nimble around hedges. And if we like prices in a given period, we can add more.

So feel pretty good about the protection we have for 2027. We are continuing to monitor basis hedges, basis hedge opportunities as well as, think about 2028 and 2029. Appreciate the time. Alright. Okay. Thank you all. I appreciate everybody's time on the call this morning and all the questions. We really do have a great inflection in front of us at Gulfport. We are very excited about what is to come in 2027 and beyond I think the setup for this company is really fantastic. So look forward to seeing you all in between now and earnings as we will be out on the road a little bit, and then we will talk about 2027 on the next quarter.

#3312. IEEE Report Highlights How Members Are Engineering for Public Good

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

They include humanitarian initiatives and STEM education programs

Kathy Pretz is the editor in chief of The Institute, IEEE's member publication

IEEE MOVE, EPICS in IEEE, the IEEE Global Museum, and the TryEngineering Summer Institute, were some of the projects showcased in the 2025 Social Impact Report.

Advancing technology for the benefit of humanity isn’t just the tagline for IEEE’s mission as a public charity. It’s something that the organization’s more than 500,000 members strive to do all the time. IEEE’s recently released 2025 Social Impact Report showcases a variety of programs volunteers worked on to increase public awareness of technology’s impact on society, many of which The Institute covered.

Here is a selection of the programs from the report, with links to our related articles:

“The IEEE global community of more than 500,000 members and volunteers demonstrates what is possible when expertise is mobilized for the public good,” Sophia Muirhead, IEEE executive director and chief operating officer, said in a news release about the Social Impact Report. “Technology has the power to expand opportunity, strengthen communities and improve lives, and IEEE’s mission is to ensure that this power is used responsibly, ethically, and in service of humanity. The 2025 report shows how IEEE members and volunteers are advancing solutions that make a real difference in people’s lives around the world.”

Engagement research shows that members increasingly cited “giving back to my profession and the world community” as a reason for joining IEEE and renewing their membership, IEEE President Mary Ellen Randall said in her September column about the report.

“Humanitarian programs are not only meaningful,” she wrote. “They also are magnetic. They attract younger engineers, keep them engaged, and help them build a professional identity rooted in purpose and impact.

“IEEE has the opportunity to become the world’s leading convening force for developing interdisciplinary technology solutions to solve humanity’s most important challenges. Our future relevance will be defined not only by the technologies we advance but also by the problems we choose to help solve.”

Kathy Pretz is editor in chief for The Institute, which covers all aspects of IEEE, its members, and the technology they're involved in. She has a bachelor's degree in applied communication from Rider University, in Lawrenceville, N.J., and holds a master's degree in corporate and public communication from Monmouth University, in West Long Branch, N.J.

#3309. How Wikipedia’s Editors Keep the Online Encyclopedia Human-Written

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

AI-generated text is harder to spot, but that hasn’t deterred them

Eliza Strickland is IEEE Spectrum's features editor. She also covers AI and biomedical engineering.

Ellia Lebleu is a cofounder of the WikiProject AI Cleanup effort to keep Wikipedia human-written.

Ellia Lebleu is a founding member of the WikiProject AI Cleanup, a volunteer effort launched in 2023 to find and remove AI-generated material from Wikipedia that breaks the website’s guidelines. When the cleanup began, AI writing was often betrayed by conspicuous clichés. Today, the project’s volunteers are developing tools to detect subtler forms of machine-generated content and debating AI’s role in the world’s most widely used encyclopedia.

When did you realize Wikipedia had a problem with AI-generated material?

Ellia Lebleu: It was around December 2023. A few other editors and I were chatting on Wikipedia’s Discord server, and we had all seen very strange articles with the same odd characteristics. They repeated phrases like “stands as a testament” or “rich cultural heritage.” They sometimes had conclusion sections, or sections called “Why is this important?” That was very typical of ChatGPT in 2023 and early 2024 but very odd for Wikipedia articles—and very easy to spot. Then I decided, let’s create an official project on Wikipedia so more people can deal with this.

Ellia Lebleu Ellia Lebleu is a founding member of the WikiProject AI Cleanup. Lebleu is pursuing a Ph.D. in AI at the Inria Center of the University of Rennes, part of France’s national research institute for digital science and technology.

Ellia Lebleu is a founding member of the WikiProject AI Cleanup. Lebleu is pursuing a Ph.D. in AI at the Inria Center of the University of Rennes, part of France’s national research institute for digital science and technology.

How do editors spot AI-generated writing today?

Lebleu: By 2025, the signs of AI writing were becoming subtler and more structural. For example, AI loves the “rule of three,” negative parallelisms, and other structures of speech that aren’t conclusive by themselves but become meaningful as they accumulate. We also look beyond the article. If someone writes five articles of thousands of words each in 5 minutes, there is reason to suspect AI.

Does the AI problem just appear in the main text, or also in citations?

Lebleu: Fake or misleading citations have become a major worry. Sometimes an AI hallucinates a citation entirely, although that’s much rarer today because of retrieval-augmented generation that allows the AI to find sources. More often, it finds a real source but gets its content completely wrong. AI citations that don’t actually support what is being written are extremely commonplace.

English Wikipedia recently prohibited editors from using LLMs to generate articles. How much AI-generated content is still getting through?

Lebleu: I’ve been working with [AI-detection company] Pangram to estimate the proportion of AI-generated content. I tested it on Wikipedia content from before ChatGPT and found no false positives, so its results provide a very conservative lower bound. In late 2025, it flagged perhaps 20 percent of new articles and drafts as AI-generated. In early 2026, that went down to 15 or 16 percent. But we don’t yet know whether that’s because our recent policies have had an effect or because models are getting more powerful and Pangram hasn’t had time to adapt.

Lebleu: Another Wikipedia editor has made an AI source verifier, which goes through the sources on a page and checks whether they match the claims. Since it is itself an AI model, there is no guarantee that it will be correct every time. But if you want something that works at scale and filters out obvious cases, it’s a good first step. The Wikimedia Foundation is also working on a tool called Paste Check, which can flag text pasted directly from some AI chatbots.

And we’ve seen Claude sometimes say, “I can’t write a Wikipedia article; it would go against Wikipedia’s policies.” If all major AI companies implemented that kind of prompt refusal, it wouldn’t solve the problem entirely, because there are still open-weight models that can be tweaked to avoid restrictions. But it would help with people who use commercial models and aren’t especially familiar with the technology.

Can you tell if the rule prohibiting AI writing is working?

Lebleu: It’s still a little early to tell. We see possible effects, such as prompt refusal and the apparent slight drop in AI-generated content. But again, we don’t yet know if that is because models are getting better or because beginners are learning the rules. The vast majority of AI-generated content is submitted by beginner editors, so we’ve made many efforts to make the rule very visible in welcome messages, editing help, and advice.

What if AI becomes capable of writing truly reliable Wikipedia articles?

Lebleu: That’s one of the big questions we’re facing. When the guideline was passed, it was for very practical reasons: We were flooded with AI content, we didn’t have good tools, and we needed to put a stop to it. But since then, it has taken on a more philosophical dimension. Many people have called Wikipedia “the last good place on the internet.” Being a place that was, in theory, free from AI slop has become part of Wikipedia’s identity.

A lot of Wikipedia’s communication is now centered on the idea that we’re a human-written encyclopedia. Even AI companies find that interesting. It can be valuable to have a purely human-written corpus on which to [train] AI systems. The fact that Wikipedia is still that, and will remain that for at least the near future, makes it a precious resource that isn’t replicated anywhere else.

But will the people who read and contribute to Wikipedia want it to become partially AI-generated if that makes it more comprehensive? We could preserve Wikipedia’s identity as a human-written corpus while also offering an AI-assisted option.

Has Wikipedia reckoned with the idea of “Google Zero”—a possible future in which websites no longer get traffic from Google search?

Lebleu: If everything goes through AI search and websites plummet to zero visibility, how do we expose Wikipedia and show that it can be edited and that people can still contribute? Wikipedia is frequently cited in [Google’s] AI Overviews, but users may only see an AI answer citing Wikipedia. They may not realize that Wikipedia is a living project they can edit and contribute to.

The Wikimedia Foundation is working on an attribution framework that could give AI users more information about the article [being cited]: when it was last edited, how comprehensive it is, whether editors have flagged problems, and perhaps even a call to action. In the future, readers might even contribute through AI models: “The AI cited Wikipedia, but there seems to be an error. Can I make an edit request and add this other source I found?”

I can see a very strong symbiotic relationship between Wikipedia and AI models in the future. I don’t see Wikipedia disappearing, but I can see it taking a very different shape. Yesterday, AI was something to clean up. Today, it’s a tool to help us with the cleanup. Tomorrow, it will be the air we breathe.

A condensed version of this article appears in the November 2026 print issue as “Ellia Lebleu.”

Eliza Strickland is IEEE Spectrum's features editor, where she helps develop and shape the magazine’s longform stories. She also oversees Spectrum's coverage of artificial intelligence and biomedical engineering. She holds a master’s degree in journalism from Columbia University.

I feel like all of us human writers are going to have to grapple with AI-mediated readers, whether we use the AI to augment our content or our readers use AI to engage with our writing. Here's to figuring out together how to ensure our words still shine through the AI layer.

AI slop is a small problem for Wikipedia. The bigger problem is very biased editing on anything with even minimal political implication. And that's a human problem, not AI.

#3307. Manfred “Fred” J. Schindler Is 2027 IEEE President-Elect

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

He has been an active volunteer for more than 30 years

Joanna Goodrich is the associate editor of The Institute.

Manfred “Fred” J. Schindler is the 2027 IEEE president-elect.

IEEE Life Fellow Manfred “Fred” J. Schindler has been elected as the 2027 IEEE president-elect. He will begin serving as president on 1 January 2028.

Schindler, who was nominated by the IEEE Board of Directors, received 16,421 votes in the election. Senior Member David Alan Koehler received 13,874 votes.

Schindler’s Top 3 Goals as President-Elect Strengthen IEEE’s connection with industry by coordinating events across geography, industry, and technology to revitalize professional activities, especially ones for young professionals.Champion the improvement of IEEE’s digital infrastructure to eliminate manual processes and modernize interfaces.Prioritize the advancement of technology to benefit future generations by expanding and supporting IEEE initiatives and programs.

At press time, the results were unofficial until the IEEE Board of Directors accepts the IEEE Teller’s Committee report in November.

Schindler, an expert in microwave semiconductor technology, is an independent consultant supporting clients with technical expertise, due diligence, and project management.

Throughout his career, he led the development of microwave integrated-circuit technology, from lab demonstrations to high-volume commercial products. He has numerous technical publications and holds 11 patents.

Schindler served as CTO of Anlotek, and director of Qorvo and RFMD’s Boston design center. He was applications manager at IBM, engineering manager at ATN Microwave, and a lab manager at Raytheon.

An IEEE volunteer for more than 30 years, Schindler served as the 2024 vice president of IEEE Technical Activities and the 2021–2022 Division IV director. He was chair of the IEEE Conferences Committee from 2015 to 2018 and president of the IEEE Microwave Theory and Technology Society (MTTS) in 2003. He received the society’s 2018 Distinguished Service Award and its 2015 N. Walter Cox Award. His award-winning micro-business column has appeared in IEEE Microwave Magazine since 2011.

He also led the 2025 One IEEE to Enable Strategic Investments in Innovations and Public Imperative Activities adhoc committee.

Schindler is an IEEE–Eta Kappa Nu member and a MTTS honorary life member.

Joanna Goodrich is the associate editor of The Institute, covering the work and accomplishments of IEEE members and IEEE and technology-related events. She has a master's degree in health communications from Rutgers University, in New Brunswick, N.J.

#3306. tvOS 27.2 adds new Apple TV 4K setting that’s an instant favorite

tvOS 27.2 launched last week as the latest software update for Apple TV 4K, and it includes a new setting I’m a big fan of: Shuffle for screen savers.

Screen savers have been one of the best Apple TV features since tvOS first launched in 2015. Largely that’s due to the gorgeous aerials captured around the world (and even from space).

Aerials are still my favorite type of Apple TV screen saver, but tvOS has steadily added other categories worth checking out too.

Currently inside Settings ⇾ Screen Saver you’ll find four categories:

The second and third options tap into your Apple Photos library and introduce the joy of seeing your favorite memories pop up on the big screen. Snoopy screen savers feature the beloved Peanuts character in a variety of entertaining scenes.

All of these screen saver options are great. But until tvOS 27.2, you had to select just one category and that’s all you’d ever see.

Now with tvOS 27.2, Apple has introduced a ‘Shuffle’ option that randomly cycles through screen savers from across all four categories.

It’s a welcome new setting, long overdue but I’ve been enjoying it a lot. The ability to be surprised by more different screen savers may sound like a small thing, but it’s a meaningful improvement to the Apple TV 4K experience.

Have you tried the new Shuffle setting for screen savers in tvOS 27.2? Let us know in the comments.

Federal model update lifts dairy RNG credits and returns Aemetis to profit.

Aemetis, Inc. (AMTX +38.40%) reported a return to profitability driven by the recognition of federal production tax credits and operational growth across its fuel segments. Management stated that the update to the federal carbon intensity model significantly increased the value of credits generated by dairy renewable natural gas production. The company is advancing infrastructure projects intended to reduce fossil fuel consumption at its ethanol facility while expanding feedstock production for the renewable diesel market. Additionally, the company is pursuing international growth through biodiesel exports and a potential public offering of its subsidiary in India.

Operator: Hello, and welcome to the Aemetis Third Quarter 26 Earnings Conference Call. Joining us on today's call are Eric A. McAfee, the chairman and chief executive officer, Todd A. Waltz, chief financial officer and Andy Foster, president of Aemetis Advanced Fuels.

Todd A. Waltz: I will now turn the call over to Todd A. Waltz. Thank you, and welcome, everyone. Before we begin, I would like to remind you that during the call, we will be making forward-looking statements within the meaning of the Private Securities Litigation Reform Act of 2000. These statements involve risks and uncertainties that could cause actual results to differ materially from those expressed or implied. Please refer to our earnings release and SEC filings for a discussion of these risks. We will also refer to adjusted EBITDA, a non-GAAP measure, A reconciliation to the most recently comparable GAAP measure is included in our earnings release.

Before reviewing in detail, I want to highlight that the company posted net income of $5.2 million or $0.07 per basic share in the third quarter and adjusted EBITDA of $24.8 million For the third quarter of 26, revenues grew 49% to $88.2 million compared with $59.2 million in the third quarter of 25. With growth in both the California ethanol and dairy renewable natural gas operating segments, from both operations and 45Z clean fuel production tax credits. Section 45Z production tax credit revenue was 24.7 million in the quarter, comprised of $20.1 million from dairy renewable net-- Net-- dairy renewable natural gas and $4.6 million from California ethanol.

45Z revenue included an $11 million cumulative true up for the first and second quarter of 26 from the regulatory updates to the 45Z GREET model. Biodiesel sales in the third quarter were $7.3 million rebounding from $2.5 million in the second quarter as delivery to 3 India oil marketing companies resumed under a $17 million allocation to our India subsidiary. Operating income was $20.9 million in the third quarter, an improvement of $29.4 million compared to the third quarter of 2025 which had an operating loss of $8.5 million Net income was $5.2 million, equal to $0.07 per basic share. An improvement of $29 million compared to a $23.7 million loss in the third quarter of 25.

Adjusted EBITDA was $24.8 million in the third quarter, an increase of $29.8 million compared to the negative $5 million in the third quarter of 25. For the first 9 months of 26, adjusted EBITDA was $33.2 million compared with negative $21.5 million during the same period of 2025. Cash at quarter end was $3.4 million In September, we received $22.4 million from the sale of section 45C production tax credits. In August, Aemetis Biogas amended its series a preferred unit agreement to extend the redemption date to December 31, 2026 and to reduce the interest rate on the credit agreement that would apply if the units are not redeemed to the greater prime plus 5% or 12%.

Capital investments supporting our energy efficiency projects and investments in biogas production were $20.2 million in the third quarter, and $35.3 million for the first 9 months of 2026. With that overview, I will turn the call over to Eric A. McAfee.

Eric A. McAfee: Thanks, Todd. Let's highlight 3 key takeaways from the third quarter. First, Q3 continues the financial inflection points we noted during the Q2 earnings call with the posting of net income of $5.2 million and adjusted EBITDA of $24.8 million during the third quarter. We continue to grow with consolidated revenue up 49% year-over-year, and improvement in operating income of $29.4 million and increased adjusted EBITDA by $29.8 million compared to the third quarter of 25. Second, we now generate higher revenues due to the California Air Resources Board approval about a year ago, of 7 new low carbon fuel standard pathways for our renewable natural gas business.

At an average carbon intensity score of negative 380 compared with the negative 150 default carbon intensity score for these digesters, which was shown in Q2 25 revenue. The approval of 7 diget-- Biogas digesters has been providing additional revenue with a higher LCFS value each quarter since Q3 25. And additional biogas digester pathways are nearing approval These LCFS pathway approvals substantially expand the LCFS credit generation per MMBtu of RNG produced. And will continue to drive meaningful revenue increases as we scale production. And third, our capital projects are advancing with $20.2 million of investment during the quarter. Review these projects and how we continue to create value as federal and state laws are being implemented.

In our dairy renewable natural gas business, every MMBtu of dairy RNG generates 4 revenue streams, natural gas molecule, a California low carbon fuel standard credit that is sold to oil companies, a federal d 3 RIN that is also sold to oil companies, and a section 45Z production tax credit. The LCFS credit and the 45Z tax credit are calculated using the carbon intensity of our biofuel. So credits are generated in proportion to how far below the standard a biofuel is scored. An LCFS pathway at negative 380 generates substantially more credit per MMBtu than the negative 150 default score.

We have 7 approved California LCFS pathways, averaging negative 380 carbon intensity, with 6 more pathways nearing approval by CARB. For the 45Z production tax credit, the Department of Energy issued its updated 45Z CF GREET model on September 8th of this year, Which decreased the carbon intensity scores used to calculate 45Z credits for dairy RNG credits we sold in July were valued at $15.20 per MMBtu. The credits we sold in September generated from ethanol and RNG production during 2026. Represent a tax credit value of approximately $62 per MMBtu for dairy RNG, and $0.33 per gallon of ethanol. For 2026, before sales debt discounts and transaction costs.

We received $22.4 million from the September 45Z tax credit sale and our third quarter results included an approximately $11 million cumulative true up for RNG dispensed in the first half of the year. As dairy renewable natural gas volume grows, all 4 revenue streams grow. But the approval of LCFS pathways in California is expected to create significant increases in revenues from the renewable natural gas production. We operate 14 biogas digesters today, taking waste from 17 dairies and transporting biogas through a 36 mile pipeline to our RNG production facility that is connected to the utility gas pipeline. We have more than 50 dairies that have signed participation agreements. 2 new methane capture digesters were completed last month.

And we have received 13 additional cleanup and compression units that will be located at the next 13 digesters to come online. Regarding our California ethanol business, we have 2 projects that are slated to significantly improve our financial performance. In addition to further improvements in 45Z values, and expected increases in LCFS credit prices. Our mechanical vapor recompression system installation is an energy efficiency project that is expected to add approximately $32 million in annual cash flow from 3 positive impacts on our operations. We will reduce about 80% of the natural gas needed for our operations, and the 45Z credit and the LCFS credit generated by every gallon of ethanol. The MVR project is making excellent progress.

Key equipment arrived this summer, and we have completed major steps in construction of the system. Including placement of the 6 3.5 thousand-horsepower turbofans. Foundation concrete has been completed. And electricity transformers are scheduled to arrive in the next month. The MVR project has been awarded approximately $19.7 million in grants and section 48 c tax credits from the California Energy Commission, Pacific Gas and Electric Company, and the IRS. Second, in the past few months, we have installed 2 of the planned 3 corn oil separation units at the ethanol plant. With the third unit slated to be operating by the end of this year.

Distilled corn oil is recovered from the ethanol process and sold as a low carbon feedstock into the renewable diesel biodiesel, and sustainable aviation fuel markets. Where demand has strengthened this year with higher federal renewable volume obligations issued by the federal EPA. Combined, the units are expected to approximately double corn oil production compared to our first quarter production rate. And prices have been increased significantly this year. Our India biofuels business shipped biodiesel to oil marketing companies and commercial customers during Q3 2026.

Biodiesel sales rebounded to $7.3 million as we delivered biodiesel to the oil market companies under their new tender, also building our base of private commercial customers due to increases in the price of India petroleum diesel this year. And we have applied to the India and EU governments for approval to export biodiesel to Europe. India's stated goal is to raise biodiesel blending from less than 1% today to 5% by 2030, which would create about 1.2 billion gallons of additional biodiesel consumption. We continue to prepare documentation for a potential public offering of a minority stake in Universal Biofuels our subsidiary, subject to market conditions.

Of the milestones we outlined last quarter, the 2 new dairy digesters are now operating and the Department of Energy has issued the dairy RNG update to the 45Z CF GREET model. #3302. Anthropic upgrades Claude with new Personal Finance feature

Having the right context is what makes AI tools useful. Anthropic just launched the ability to securely use personal finance data with Claude. The company emphasizes that the feature is read-only and can’t take financial actions.

“Getting answers about your money no longer means opening every banking app and doing the math yourself,” Anthropic says. “With Personal Finance in Claude, you can securely connect your bank and card accounts and ask in your own words. Access is read-only, and Personal Finance can’t move, manage, or invest your money.”

Similar to ChatGPT’s finances feature, Claude’s new capabilities essentially give you a way to use chat as a way to make sense of your finance data. It can also present data in dashboards, calendars, and more.

Given the importance of security, here’s what Anthropic has to say regarding the new finance feature and Claude:

Claude’s access is read-only. Personal Finance helps you understand your money, and it isn’t designed to give investment advice. Claude can make mistakes in its answers, so ask which transactions are behind a number, and check important figures with your bank.

Your accounts are only connected once you sign in to your bank yourself through Plaid, a service that connects apps to banks. That’s where you agree to its terms and approve Claude’s read-only access, so Claude doesn’t ask for or see your bank password.
