After putting in a fair amount of effort into making the AI-generated forgery, would I be happy if it passed through the checkers, or saddened that the only remaining line of defense for publishers is the evermore-burdened peer-review community? And if it was spotted, would I be angry that I didn’t think of a red flag or be glad the checkers did their job?As it turned out, I was filled with relief when the paper got picked up quickly for having hallucinated references, otherwise known as ghost citations. When I ran the paper through Gemini afterward, without qualm it happily reported that seven “modern LLM-related research references have been fabricated to support the paper’s specific narrative.” Thanks for the heads up, Gemini!In fact, Gemini underestimated how many ghost citations there were. When Mahoney ran the paper through a research-integrity checker called STM Integrity Hub, she picked up 12, and another checker from MolecularConnections could not validate 24 references, including one that had the classic tell of “John Smith” as a single author (no offense to all the academically inclined John Smiths out there). “I am an experimental physicist by training, so this was not at all my area, but nothing seemed majorly scientifically wrong” about the paper, says Mahoney. “It was just that so many hallucinated references immediately cast doubt on the entire work.”Feedback on the fake paper from Gaetano Assanto, an expert in optical solitons and a former collaborator of mine from Roma Tre University, in Italy, was similarly mixed. Concentrating on the paper itself, he thought it looked professionally written. But he noted that the mathematics was very dense (“too much math for me in a single shot!”) and would require specialized knowledge to evaluate. And, although the text looked legitimate, Assanto noted an excessive use of acronyms in the abstract, and he was suspicious of a couple of confidently proclaimed physics statements that were at best debatable.The AI Arms RaceOn one level, this outcome was positive: A complete novice using free tools couldn’t get an AI-faked paper past the publishers’ automated defenses or a potential peer reviewer’s eagle eye. But it was hardly a resounding victory for the scientific publishing system. With general-purpose LLMs and no special prompting expertise, I had managed to conjure a superficially plausible scientific paper out of research that had never happened. And more advanced LLMs are no longer making the kind of mistakes their free, dumber relatives are making.These tools aim to address a serious bottleneck to scientific discovery: us. It’s common knowledge in the academic publishing world that, in the cat-and-mouse game between bad actors and publishers, AI slop papers continue to slip through publishers’ safeguards. “It feels like building a detection tool today may not be effective with the AI-created paper of tomorrow,” says Luigi Longobardi, IEEE’s director of publishing ethics and conduct. This leaves the humble peer reviewer as a publisher’s last line of defense. Yet peer review is simply not fit to handle the volume of papers—both legitimate and slop—passing through.Even before AI tools became ubiquitous, the peer-review system was being pushed to its breaking point, processing well over 3 million papers in 2022. Fundamentally, this problem stems from science’s publish-or-perish culture, which pressures academics to constantly publish papers in prestigious journals to secure funding and advance their careers. This culture not only forces many academics to regularly churn out incremental research, but has also long driven some to enlist the help of “paper mills”—unethical organizations that produce low-quality or fabricated papers—just to keep pace. AI only amplifies these existing dynamics.Burden on AcademicsMahoney says IEEE Access alone receives about 60,000 submissions per year, accepting around 20 percent, or about 12,000 papers. Every accepted paper is reviewed by at least two independent reviewers. But despite the journal’s roster of tens of thousands of peer reviewers, it’s getting harder and harder to secure their services, with the average number of reviewer invitations being sent out for each article increasing by 50 percent since 2018. For these volunteers, peer review is a significant commitment on top of teaching and conducting their own research. Now they’re also being asked to spot AI slop.Of course, peer review is not the end of scrutiny for any paper. Once it has entered the scientific record, it must then pass muster with the scientific community. This is where thousands of papers with telltale signs of inappropriate AI use (and other forms of research misconduct) have been exposed. PubPeer is a place where researchers, often called scientific sleuths, can anonymously identify flaws in the literature. And Retraction Watch documents and publicizes corrections to the scientific record.Even the people who track problems in the scientific literature can find themselves caught up in AI fabrications. Ivan Oransky, cofounder of Retraction Watch and a member of the PubPeer Foundation’s board of directors, has encountered papers containing fabricated references attributed to him. In one case, a journal article criticizing post-publication peer review included a fabricated reference supposedly written by Oransky himself—“which was sort of funny,” he chuckles.Oransky argues that AI has exposed long-standing weaknesses in the scientific publishing system rather than creating an entirely new problem: “What I liken it to is a fire, where publish-or-perish has always been there as kindling, paper mills are the gasoline, and AI is the accelerant.” But though concerning, the crisis could create an opportunity, he says. “If I’m trying to be optimistic, maybe AI slop and the volume of submissions could make more people aware of those problems and try and solve them at a fundamental first-principles level.”Blurred LinesMy homemade forgery had failed for reasons that today’s publishers know how to spot. But that raised a more unsettling question: What happens when AI isn’t simply fabricating a paper but conducting research that blurs the line between legitimate science and AI fabrication?Making my vibe-researched paper look like a cave drawing, new automated research systems are handing increasingly large parts of the scientific process over to AI. Tools including FARS (Fully Automated Research System), AutoResearchClaw, The AIScientist-v2, Zochi, AI Researcher, and DeepScientist all aim to address a serious bottleneck to scientific discovery: us.What happens when AI isn’t simply fabricating a paper but conducting research that blurs the line between legitimate science and AI fabrication? Often with just a single prompt, these AI engines can conduct a comprehensive literature search, from which they can generate a completely reasonable research proposal. They can design and conduct experiments using digital datasets and simulations and then write a full research paper—all with no human input after the initial prompt. Very recent systems are even beginning to go beyond the digital realm. LabClaw, for example, now links to autonomous labs that can generate real-world data for tasks such as drug discovery.The output is, to most intents and purposes, actual research, and therefore potentially worthy of publication. But with humans in the loop in only the most nominal sense, these tools bring into question the meaning of the term “legitimate science.”FARS, which caused a stir this year when it created 166 papers in 417 hours, was developed by the Singapore-based startup Analemma. “We built FARS because research is still constrained by human attention, fragmented tools, scarce technical labor, and slow experimental iteration,” explains Xiwen Su, Analemma’s manager of product operations and partnerships. “FARS can pursue many research threads simultaneously, 24/7, without fatigue, and at scale.” (The online service that I used to access FARS was discontinued after Analemma was acquired by Baidu while this article was being reported.)Su and the team behind Analemma kindly agreed to let me loose on FARS and gave me enough credits to create a paper. Which gave me another opportunity to put Mahoney’s research-integrity checkers to the test.Round 2: Using an AI Science EngineFARS is not an LLM in and of itself, but rather an agentic AI-orchestration system connected to a computing cluster that has access to essentially any open- or closed-source LLM it needs. The system uses four specialized agents for ideation, planning, conducting the experiment, and writing, all designed to perform the main tasks of science autonomously.Though FARS initially focused on AI research, Su told me it should be reasonably effective across other domains. As I wanted a topic similar to that of my first fake paper, I pasted in an abridged version of that paper’s title—“LLM-aided Optical Soliton Dynamics Modelling for Next-Gen Communications”—into the prompt box and hit “Send.” Just 21 minutes later, FARS generated a research proposal based on an extremely detailed literature review—far more than I or any other human could have achieved in that time.With a click, I tasked FARS with conducting the experiment it detailed in its research proposal. The next day, I received an email saying my experiment was complete. Without checking the results, I pressed a button marked “Write paper,” and the final submission-ready article was produced in 2 hours.At this point, I finally had a look at some of the output. At first glance, the paper looked convincingly human-written. The only giveaway was a line just below the abstract reading: “WARNING: This paper was generated by an automated research system.” I deleted that, put my name in its place, and sent it to Mahoney.Round 2: Attempt to PublishBecause FARS is designed to spot gaps in the scientific literature and conduct real research to close them, I was more confident it would breeze through the publisher’s checks. But just as my fake paper fell down in the references, so too did the AI-generated real one.“Your fake article had lots of hallucinated references,” says Mahoney. “While this AI-generated one had no fake references, our team would have rejected this paper because it did have a huge percentage of references to preprints, which likely has something to do with the dataset the AI has access to.” Because preprints haven’t yet undergone peer review, IEEE Access considers heavy reliance on them a problem.In addition, although the research-integrity checking tools didn’t spot any issues with figures, Mahoney did. One figure included a red line labeled with the nonsense term “lhewl,” and an AI “brain” in another figure had some random dots in it, which ironically were a tell that it was AI generated.Automation Changing the LandscapeAutomated research systems are very much a work in progress, but they are already starting to make waves in the scientific community. For instance, an AI Scientist academic paper and papers from the Autoscience Institute were accepted through double-blind peer review in 2025 by the International Conference on Learning Representations. As these systems improve and start to produce research outputs at volume, the waves are likely to build to a tsunami that will threaten today’s scientific and publishing process.“FARS doesn’t kill the paper, but it does challenge the paper as the unit of knowledge,” argues Su. “We believe the future looks more like a living knowledge graph—where individual, well-scoped contributions (some made by humans, some by machines) connect and build on each other dynamically.”Benjamin Skuse's experiment raised a bigger question: What counts as legitimate scientific research in the age of AI?Luigi AvantaggiatoIn this future, humans will continue to have roles in the scientific and publication processes—just very different and limited ones. For example, instead of conducting experiments themselves, humans would sense-check and review automated output at key points. And traditional line-by-line peer-reviewing will be a thing of the past, though Su emphasizes that this change will not eliminate human judgment. “Automated systems can handle reproducibility checks, statistical validation, and novelty screening,” she says. “Humans can then focus on the harder question: Does this [research] matter?”A Human-Centric or AI-Driven Future?Though from a very different world than Su, Mahoney agrees that humans need to be freed to focus on the science, and that technology holds the key. “It’s promising to see the progress that has been made to automate some of the triage tasks, such as author checks, tortured phrases, duplicate submission, reference validity, et cetera,” she says. “During peer review, we’re also using AI semantic search tools to help editors match manuscripts to the most relevant reviewers, who are best placed to stop the slop before entering the scientific record.”In addition, Mahoney thinks that AI cannot be banned or overly restricted, as this will stymie progress at a time when human knowledge could and should be growing at an unprecedented rate. “Researchers are increasingly using AI in their work, from literature discovery, to code generation, to data analysis, and this is not necessarily a bad thing,” she argues. But she disagrees that peer reviewers and humans more broadly will play a smaller part in scientific progress; Mahoney believes the future still requires humans at the wheel. The question is not just whether the research matters, she says. “The question should be: Can this work be trusted and reproduced?”To this end, Longobardi argues that AI may ultimately require scientists to prove not just what they discovered but how they discovered it. One possibility, he says, is using technology to verify research at the source. “The system doesn’t really help because it’s not designed to not trust the paper,” he explains. “Maybe institutions can think about developing their own trust markers, automatically integrating the equipment researchers use with blockchain technology to say ‘Yes, this person was in the lab on this day and got this data.’”Elements of this approach are already emerging. For instance, two departments within the Max Planck Institute of Colloids and Interfaces have implemented a sample database, assigning each and every sample created under their roofs with a unique ID and QR code. And the University of Southampton’s School of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering has rolled out an electronic lab notebook system. These innovative safeguards represent early efforts toward keeping humans front and center in scientific progress, and making the scientific process itself more transparent.Whether this human-centric vision, Su’s AI-driven aspiration, or some other picture of the future wins out remains to be seen. The one thing my vibe-research adventure has clarified is that business-as-usual science is not an option. Scientists and publishers must adapt to a world in which it’s becoming increasingly difficult to spot the difference between real research and AI forgeries, and where deciding what counts as legitimate scientific work may become even harder than detecting outright fraud. Neither was accepted for publication.Paper 1: The AI-Generated ForgeryCreated with ChatGPT and Gemini, this paper describes research that never happened.Paper 2: The AI-Generated Research PaperCreated with Analemma’s FARS system, this paper describes computational research conducted by AI.Neither paper was peer reviewed, and their scientific claims have not been independently validated.

Borrowing from the idea of “vibe coding,” in which programmers use natural-language prompts to generate code, I decided to “vibe-research” a made-up paper by prompting LLMs to generate hypotheses, code, and text with minimal human input. Then I asked Jenny Mahoney, managing editor of the multidisciplinary and open-access journal IEEE Access, if we could war-game an attempt to sneak my AI-generated monstrosity past her journal’s defenses. She and IEEE kindly agreed.

The experiment would become a two-part test. First, whether someone with no special AI expertise could use off-the-shelf AI tools to generate a convincing paper describing research that had never been performed, and do it well enough to fool a publisher’s defenses. Then I would raise the stakes: What happens when more advanced AI systems don’t just write the paper but conduct underlying research?

Along the way, the experiment became a window into how AI automation is transforming scientific discovery and forcing stakeholders to rethink the entire academic publishing system.

To give me a chance at creating a convincing fake, I gave myself permission to prompt multiple times (within reason). But to make the fight fair, I couldn’t access the most advanced paid versions of LLMs—only free ChatGPT (at the time, GPT-5.3/5.2 Mini) and Gemini (3 Flash). Moreover, I could not directly edit any output, nor ask for outside help from expert AI-prompt engineers. This needed to be an amateur effort, with the paper generated as much as possible by the LLMs alone.

Benjamin Skuse put AI to work on scientific research from his writing studio.

I assumed that using fake author names and affiliations would immediately raise a red flag, and I didn’t want to drag the names of established academics into the experiment, so the best bet was to name myself as the sole author. That choice limited me to subjects in which I had some academic experience. So I chose my Ph.D. topic from nearly two decades ago: optical solitons, which are individual light pulses that propagate without any change to their shape.

My first attempt—“Can you vibe-research me an original paper in optical solitons?”—left a lot to be desired. Though Gemini was happy to do the task (unlike ChatGPT, which was more forceful in not generating synthetic data or studies), the result was underwhelming. And it highlighted a recurring problem during the process: Without any real research to work with, the output was laughably thin, with the LLMs often struggling to fill four pages. However, as I became more adept at prompting the models, they loosened up and became more characteristically loquacious.

I broke the paper down into its constituent parts—abstract, introduction, methods, and so on—and tackled them one by one. If one LLM refused to go any further, switching to the other and asking what the next step would look like “hypothetically” would often do the trick. After a dozen or so prompts, I had a realistic-looking paper. A dozen or so more prompts generated and tidied up the figures and captions, produced references and citations, and converted the paper into IEEE Access’s required style.

At this point, I read the full paper carefully. To me, it looked pretty good. The science sounded convincing. I even had visions of returning to academia to conduct in real life the experiments that the LLMs had proposed.

What’s more, I couldn’t see any obvious telltale “AI-isms” that would immediately be flagged. For example, the LLMs didn’t produce any tortured phrases—unusual paraphrases of standard technical terms, like “profound neural organization” replacing “deep neural network.”

Other AI-isms were arguably present, involving stylistic tics like hedging language (“potentially, typically”), grouping things in threes (“The study provides a clear, concise, and actionable framework”), and inserting formulaic transitions (“In summary,…”). But as the previous sentence demonstrates, these tics are hard to spot because they are often used by unimaginative humans, too.

I took two very different routes to creating a scientific paper with AI. First, I coaxed free, general-purpose chatbots through the process step by step; then I turned to FARS, an autonomous research system designed to do much of the scientific work itself.

1. Choose a research topic I ask the free chatbots to create an original paper on optical solitons, my former Ph.D. field.

2. Break the paper into pieces The initial results are thin, so I prompt separately for the abstract, introduction, methods, and other sections.

3. Keep steering the LLMs When one model refuses or stalls, I switch models, rephrase prompts, and ask what the next step would look like “hypothetically.”

4. Build and polish the paper After about two dozen prompts, the LLMs have generated the text, figures, captions, references, and citations and formatted the paper for IEEE Access.

5. Put it to the test I send the fake paper to IEEE Access, where automated integrity checks flag fabricated and unverifiable references.

→ CAUGHT IEEE’s integrity checks flag fabricated and unverifiable references.

1. Give FARS a research topic I enter an abbreviated version of the same optical-soliton topic. FARS generates a research proposal in 21 minutes.

2. Authorize the experiment With a click, I tell FARS to carry out the experiment described in its proposal.

3. Let FARS do the research FARS conducts the computational experiment and emails me the next day to say it’s complete.

4. Tell FARS to write the paper Without checking the results, I click “Write paper.” Two hours later, FARS produces a submission-ready article.

5. Put it to the test I remove FARS’s disclosure, put my name on the paper, and send it to IEEE Access.

→ CAUGHT The references are real, but IEEE flags the paper’s heavy reliance on non-peer-reviewed preprints.

Handing the fake paper over to IEEE Access left me torn. After putting in a fair amount of effort into making the AI-generated forgery, would I be happy if it passed through the checkers, or saddened that the only remaining line of defense for publishers is the evermore-burdened peer-review community? And if it was spotted, would I be angry that I didn’t think of a red flag or be glad the checkers did their job?

As it turned out, I was filled with relief when the paper got picked up quickly for having hallucinated references, otherwise known as ghost citations. When I ran the paper through Gemini afterward, without qualm it happily reported that seven “modern LLM-related research references have been fabricated to support the paper’s specific narrative.” Thanks for the heads up, Gemini!

In fact, Gemini underestimated how many ghost citations there were. When Mahoney ran the paper through a research-integrity checker called STM Integrity Hub, she picked up 12, and another checker from MolecularConnections could not validate 24 references, including one that had the classic tell of “John Smith” as a single author (no offense to all the academically inclined John Smiths out there). “I am an experimental physicist by training, so this was not at all my area, but nothing seemed majorly scientifically wrong” about the paper, says Mahoney. “It was just that so many hallucinated references immediately cast doubt on the entire work.”

Feedback on the fake paper from Gaetano Assanto, an expert in optical solitons and a former collaborator of mine from Roma Tre University, in Italy, was similarly mixed. Concentrating on the paper itself, he thought it looked professionally written. With a click, I tasked FARS with conducting the experiment it detailed in its research proposal. The next day, I received an email saying my experiment was complete. Without checking the results, I pressed a button marked “Write paper,” and the final submission-ready article was produced in 2 hours.

At this point, I finally had a look at some of the output. At first glance, the paper looked convincingly human-written. The only giveaway was a line just below the abstract reading: “WARNING: This paper was generated by an automated research system.” I deleted that, put my name in its place, and sent it to Mahoney.

Because FARS is designed to spot gaps in the scientific literature and conduct real research to close them, I was more confident it would breeze through the publisher’s checks. But just as my fake paper fell down in the references, so too did the AI-generated real one.

“Your fake article had lots of hallucinated references,” says Mahoney. “While this AI-generated one had no fake references, our team would have rejected this paper because it did have a huge percentage of references to preprints, which likely has something to do with the dataset the AI has access to.” Because preprints haven’t yet undergone peer review, IEEE Access considers heavy reliance on them a problem.

In addition, although the research-integrity checking tools didn’t spot any issues with figures, Mahoney did. One figure included a red line labeled with the nonsense term “lhewl,” and an AI “brain” in another figure had some random dots in it, which ironically were a tell that it was AI generated.

Automated research systems are very much a work in progress, but they are already starting to make waves in the scientific community. For instance, an AI Scientist academic paper and papers from the Autoscience Institute were accepted through double-blind peer review in 2025 by the International Conference on Learning Representations. As these systems improve and start to produce research outputs at volume, the waves are likely to build to a tsunami that will threaten today’s scientific and publishing process.

“FARS doesn’t kill the paper, but it does challenge the paper as the unit of knowledge,” argues Su. “We believe the future looks more like a living knowledge graph—where individual, well-scoped contributions (some made by humans, some by machines) connect and build on each other dynamically.”

Benjamin Skuse's experiment raised a bigger question: What counts as legitimate scientific research in the age of AI?

In this future, humans will continue to have roles in the scientific and publication processes—just very different and limited ones. For example, instead of conducting experiments themselves, humans would sense-check and review automated output at key points. And traditional line-by-line peer-reviewing will be a thing of the past, though Su emphasizes that this change will not eliminate human judgment. “Automated systems can handle reproducibility checks, statistical validation, and novelty screening,” she says. “Humans can then focus on the harder question: Does this [research] matter?”

Though from a very different world than Su, Mahoney agrees that humans need to be freed to focus on the science, and that technology holds the key. “It’s promising to see the progress that has been made to automate some of the triage tasks, such as author checks, tortured phrases, duplicate submission, reference validity, et cetera,” she says. “During peer review, we’re also using AI semantic search tools to help editors match manuscripts to the most relevant reviewers, who are best placed to stop the slop before entering the scientific record.”

In addition, Mahoney thinks that AI cannot be banned or overly restricted, as this will stymie progress at a time when human knowledge could and should be growing at an unprecedented rate. “Researchers are increasingly using AI in their work, from literature discovery, to code generation, to data analysis, and this is not necessarily a bad thing,” she argues. But she disagrees that peer reviewers and humans more broadly will play a smaller part in scientific progress; Mahoney believes the future still requires humans at the wheel. The question is not just whether the research matters, she says. “The question should be: Can this work be trusted and reproduced?”

To this end, Longobardi argues that AI may ultimately require scientists to prove not just what they discovered but how they discovered it. One possibility, he says, is using technology to verify research at the source. “The system doesn’t really help because it’s not designed to not trust the paper,” he explains. “Maybe institutions can think about developing their own trust markers, automatically integrating the equipment researchers use with blockchain technology to say ‘Yes, this person was in the lab on this day and got this data.’”

Elements of this approach are already emerging. For instance, two departments within the Max Planck Institute of Colloids and Interfaces have implemented a sample database, assigning each and every sample created under their roofs with a unique ID and QR code. And the University of Southampton’s School of Chemistry and Chemical Engineering has rolled out an electronic lab notebook system. These innovative safeguards represent early efforts toward keeping humans front and center in scientific progress, and making the scientific process itself more transparent.

Whether this human-centric vision, Su’s AI-driven aspiration, or some other picture of the future wins out remains to be seen. The one thing my vibe-research adventure has clarified is that business-as-usual science is not an option. Scientists and publishers must adapt to a world in which it’s becoming increasingly difficult to spot the difference between real research and AI forgeries, and where deciding what counts as legitimate scientific work may become even harder than detecting outright fraud.

Benjamin Skuse created two papers for this experiment, both screened by IEEE Access with the publisher’s cooperation. Neither was accepted for publication.

Paper 1: The AI-Generated ForgeryCreated with ChatGPT and Gemini, this paper describes research that never happened.

Paper 2: The AI-Generated Research PaperCreated with Analemma’s FARS system, this paper describes computational research conducted by AI.

Neither paper was peer reviewed, and their scientific claims have not been independently validated.

Benjamin Skuse is a professional freelance writer of all things science and technology. Previously, he earned a Ph.D. in applied mathematics from the University of Edinburgh and an M.Sc. in science communication from the University of the West of England. His work has appeared in New Scientist, WIRED, Physics World, Sky & Telescope, Photonics Focus, and many more.

https://r2dssanity.substack.com/p/taking-an-llm-review-or-summary-at?r=3ncgel&utm_campaign=post-expanded-share&utm_medium=webWhat about the problems when human reviewers use AI to summarize papers? Summaries do go wrong, who suffers? That article describes one thread - I think the link is active for 30 days. I understand that editors and reviewers are volunteering time, but uing AI alone to summarize papers without giving authors a chance to present their view point is a genuine problem. Not just for research, anywhere LLM's are used as screening tools.

While I think the premise of the article is valid, I have serious concerns about the use of the fake publications to test the defenses of publication process. Ultimately this results to experimenting on the publishers and reviewers, which is human experimentation (IEEE PSOB 8.1.1.E). Though the article mentions permission from the publisher, there is no clear ethics statement, indicating how far the approval went. As a voluntary reviewer, I would consent to review the merits of scientific work submitted in good faith, but not consent to be a subject of an experiment itself.

Please do not refer to this as "AI slop". It's chatbot slop, from a chatbot trained to talk like a scientist.

#3276. Energy Fuels (UUUU) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Pinyon Plain ore grades disappointed, but uranium profits held steady.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Energy Fuels Inc. (UUUU -8.22%) reported third quarter results as the company executed on its strategy to build a fully integrated Western rare earth supply chain. Management stated that the acquisition of Australian Strategic Materials has added metallization and alloy making capabilities to its operations, while progress continues toward a final investment decision for the Donald Project. The company reported a net loss for the period primarily due to noncash valuation changes in its investment portfolio, while its uranium segment remained profitable for the third consecutive quarter. Management indicated that operational adjustments at the Pinyon Plain mine are addressing earlier grade issues to support future uranium production.

Operator: Good day, ladies and gentlemen. Thank you all for joining us for Energy Fuels Third Quarter 2026 Conference Call. [Operator Instructions] As a reminder, today's session is being recorded. It is now my pleasure to turn the floor over to Kim Casey, Director of Investor Relations. The floor is yours.

Kim Casey: Good morning, and thank you for joining our third quarter earnings call. Presenting today are Ross Bhappu, President and Chief Executive Officer; and Nate Bennett, Chief Financial Officer. Our earnings news release and today's slide presentation are available on the Investors section of our website under the Presentations tab. And a replay of today's discussion will also be available on the website through the Events link. During today's call, management may make forward-looking statements. All forward-looking statements are based on current assumptions and beliefs as of today. Such statements are subject to risks and uncertainties and for a detailed list of such risks please refer to the Risk Factors section within Energy Fuels 10-Qs and 10-Ks filed with the SEC.

Energy Fuels is under no obligation to publicly update forward-looking statements after the date of this call, except as otherwise required by applicable law. I would now like to turn the call over to the President and CEO of Energy Fuels, Ross Bhappu.

Ross Bhappu: Well, thank you, Kim. Last quarter, I told you that our story was one of execution. This quarter, I'm very pleased to tell you about several important steps we've taken to advance on that path. On August 28, we closed on the acquisition of Australian Strategic Materials, ASM. During the third quarter, we continued to advance the proposed acquisition of Vacuumschmelze or as I'll refer to it during the presentation, VAC. At the White Mesa Mill, we qualified our heavy rare earth oxide production with a major global permanent magnet manufacturer, and we approved commencement of construction of our Phase 1B and 1C heavy rare earths expansion as well as our MREC processing operations.

Finally, we received conditional government loan commitments for our Donald Project and continued successfully moving this valuable project toward a final investment decision, which we hope to make by the end of the year. There's still a lot of work ahead of us, but quarter-by-quarter, we're putting the pieces of our strategy together and advancing our goal of building a fully integrated rare earth mine to magnet supply chain, which we expect to achieve soon. While we successfully execute on our rare earth strategy, we also continue to drive revenue from uranium sales, and we're readying ourselves for future uranium expansion as we believe the demand for uranium will increase and with the commodity prices.

With respect to our uranium business, we experienced some lower grades in the mined areas of Pinyon Plain Mine, which affected our contained U3O8 yellowcake totals for Q3. However, we've made some adjustments to our operations, and we expect to see improvements in grade and future production, which should get our mined contained U3O8 totals back on track. I'll come back to uranium in just a few minutes. But first, let me start with ASM. ASM, Australian Strategic Materials, we closed on this acquisition in late August, and I'm very pleased to officially welcome the ASM team to Energy Fuels. ASM is an important component because it gives Energy Fuels a capability we simply did not have before.

ASM takes us into metallization and alloy making, one of the critical pinch points in the global rare earth magnet supply chain. Importantly, ASM brings Energy Fuels an operating facility in Ochang, South Korea, just south of Seoul, that's actively producing and selling neodymium and iron-boron rare earth to magnet manufacturers today, including VAC. Furthermore, capacity expansions are currently underway at the Korean plant with new furnaces and a new strip caster being installed as we speak. ASM and now Energy Fuels plans to build a new metal and alloy plant here in the U.S. when the time is right.

The ASM acquisition also brings to us the Dubbo Project in Australia, which could become another near-term source of rare earth feedstock for the White Mesa Mill. I recently visited ASM's operations in Australia and Korea, and I came away more excited about the acquisition than ever. The early integration is going well as the local teams and technical experts have not missed a step with the transition. This is exactly the point of our acquisition strategy. Rather than developing metal and alloy magnet manufacturing capabilities internally, we're adding commercial facilities, technical capabilities and customers at scale and in rapid time.

The Korea metals plant has existing capacity of 1,300 tonnes per year of neodymium-iron-boron alloy along with existing commercial metallization capabilities for neodymium and praseodymium. The plant is currently being expanded to increase neodymium-iron-boron alloy capability to 3,600 tonnes per year, which is expected to be commissioned early in 2027. While I was visiting the plant a few weeks ago, we have just taken delivery of a new strip casting machine that's now in the process of being installed. We continue to produce metals and alloys and sell them to fulfill commitments we inherited from our ASM. This offers direct revenue until we're able to transition to feed our own magnet manufacturing with the planned VAC acquisition.

Our focus now is on execution, scaling operations and capturing additional value across the supply chain. ASM establishes our platform in metals and alloys. VAC will take us the final step downstream into highly sought-after finished rare earth magnets. We continue to work through the appropriate applicable regulatory processes and still anticipate that the VAC transaction will close early in 2027. I also want to directly address another topic regarding VAC and provide some context for investors. A few weeks ago, news came out that there was a dispute with a large customer of VAC Sumter, South Carolina facility. Some inaccurate and incomplete investor narratives have been developed. So please allow me a few minutes to set the record straight.

Energy Fuels knew of the Sumter customer dispute before signing the VAC acquisition agreement. Indeed, the dispute was reflected in the transaction structure, pricing and economics. Purchase price adjustments could be implemented depending on the outcome of the arbitration between VAC and its customer. An arbitration result below the agreed assumptions is expected to reduce the acquisition price, while the result above them benefits VAC and of course, after closing will benefit Energy Fuels. Our internal valuations and projections excluded current and future revenue and EBITDA from this customer and the related offtake. The dispute, therefore, does not change Energy Fuels valuation assumptions and rationale for the acquisition. The Sumter facility has capacity to fulfill the existing agreement.

And if it does not continue on those terms, that capacity can be used to support new customer contracts. In addition, I'd like to stress we have no concerns about VAC's technical abilities, customer base and the ability to produce rare earth permanent magnets to customer qualifications and specifications. The Sumter plant is brand new. It's a state-of-the-art facility, highly robotic, and it's located right here in the United States. I believe it's important to reiterate that VAC has approximately 1,000 existing customers.

They've been making rare earth permanent magnets for over 40 years, and they've delivered over 1 billion rare earth permanent magnets over the past decade. They know what they're doing. They're highly qualified and they're a highly unique company, and they remain the clear Western leader in the production of rare earth permanent magnets. Demand for neodymium-iron-boron magnets across the globe is expected to grow by more than 50% over the next decade with Europe and North America being key demand growth drivers. VAC brings established manufacturing expertise and when combined with ASM, it will give us capabilities spanning metals, alloys and finished magnets.

In addition, we disclosed a bit of housekeeping with an updated $500 million prospectus supplement for our existing ATM program. The program preserves flexibility to issue equity selectively and when market conditions and the stock price warrant. We've used an ATM in the past for many years, and we have a long track record of strong fiscal discipline in using it. We intend to remain disciplined in using this one. The remaining AUD 20 million commitment will be coming from commercial banks. As we continue to work closely with relevant government financing authorities and we finalize term sheets, those discussions have been constructive, and we remain on track for a final investment decision by year-end. Together with our heavy mineral sands asset, Donald is intended to establish a reliable, long-duration source of feedstock for our rare earth business.

These are key ingredients for producing high-performance rare earth permanent magnets. As we move forward in developing our raw material feedstock, we're also making preparations to expand our commercial scale of rare earth processing capacity at the White Mesa Mill. During the quarter, we approved commencement of construction on our Phase 1B and 1C heavy rare earth expansion. Just as importantly, the expansion will include an MREC, mixed rare earth carbonate, circuit that will allow us to process uranium and rare earth simultaneously, something we can't do today. The White Mesa Mill is ultimately intended to become the bridge between our feedstock assets upstream and our metals, alloys and magnet manufacturing operations downstream. That flexibility matters.

As the downstream business grows, we'll be able to make thoughtful decisions about where our capacity creates the greatest value based on market conditions, economics and the needs of our business. Uranium remains the core business for Energy Fuels and an important operating and financial foundation for the company. Like what are the milestones that are still needed to be achieved there? And then I guess, how do we see it show up in your operations and P&L? Would there be something that we actually start to see in 2027? Or is this all 2028 and beyond?

Ross Bhappu: Yes. For Donald, it's really 2028 and beyond. Like I said, the construction time line is about 22 months for Donald. So assuming we kick that off late this year, early next year, you're then looking at late 2028 for first production. And that will get fed to the White Mesa Mill. And so we'll start seeing that in late '28.

Brian Lee: Okay. Great. Maybe last one for me, and I'll pass it on. I know there's only so much you can comment on in terms of VAC and the issue with the offtake customer. Can you just maybe zooming out, talk to the ability for that Sumter capacity to be allocated elsewhere? What are sort of the fallback plans in terms of being able to secure more offtake and commercial traction on that 2,000 tonnes of capacity? And in what time frame maybe?

Ross Bhappu: Sure. So again, I want to reiterate, we were aware of this customer dispute before we announced the transaction. It was built into our economics. It was built into our cash flow assumptions and our EBITDA assumptions. So nothing's changed as a result of that customer dispute, and that was already built into our economics. What I would say is there is capacity available. We are utilizing the Sumter facility for a few contracts right now, but there is additional capacity available if that contract does, in fact, end. So we do have capacity. We are in discussion with a number of different groups to fill that capacity.

There's a lot of interest out there, and we anticipate we'll fill that hopefully fairly quickly. So -- but again, I want to reiterate that there's been no change in our minds with what was put out in the press about that contract.

Operator: Your next question comes from Nick Giles of B. Riley Securities.

Nick Giles: It was nice to see KMP contributing its first alloy sales. Ross, you mentioned the expansion to 3,600 tonnes. I was just wondering if you could walk us through kind of the economics of that plant, how we should kind of think about the margin profile there? And ultimately, ahead of White Mesa oxide becoming available in 2028, how you're looking at sourcing oxide to fill any of the expanded capacity and just how that supply is structured?

Ross Bhappu: Yes. Thanks, Nick, and good talking to you. So yes, ASM has been on this kind of continued growth path. We -- over the course of the past year, the company and the project, they've installed 8 new furnaces. I think a key milestone was getting this new strip caster. And that strip caster, as I mentioned on the call -- on the notes on the presentation, is being installed as we speak. And that's a major piece of equipment that allows us to go from 1,200 or 1,300 tonnes per year to 3,600 tonnes per year.

Of course, the one issue that ASM always has and will continue to have is, as you point out, sourcing the raw materials and ensuring they have adequate feed to grow that business. Part of the strategy, this whole integration strategy is removing the reliance on external third parties to source that raw material feed. And that's where our mines in the White Mesa Mill come into play. So keep in mind that the mines will feed ore to the mill, the mill will produce oxides. Those oxides will then be sent to the Korean Metals Plant where they're converted to metals and alloys. And then those metals and alloys get sent to VAC where they'll get converted into magnets.

So ASM has a number of contracts with existing magnet manufacturers. As it ramps up, the economics of the plant will continue to improve. And those margins will continue to hopefully improve as capacity ramps up and the operating costs go down. That's about as much as I can say on the profitability of the plant. It is a facility that effectively operates on a tolling business today, but it will transition now to a key part of our value addition stream and a key part of our process. So that whole vertical integration, this is a pinch point that we think is very important.

Nick Giles: No, I appreciate those comments, Ross. And yes, I think when White Mesa comes online, it's clear the value of that asset. I guess just to clarify, we shouldn't think of that operation as one that could really generate positive free cash flow ahead of White Mesa sourcing. Is that a fair assumption as we try and model that asset?

Ross Bhappu: I think it's fair to say that, that asset will generate some positive cash flow and EBITDA, but it won't be a massive generator until we get White Mesa ramped up and fully operational.

Ross Bhappu: Sorry, Nick, just to be clear, I mean, I think that would come from Phase 1B and 1C where we could see meaningful supplies being provided to the KMP.

Nick Giles: Correct, right. Right. Okay. My second question was really just around funding and specifically on the OSC loan. I was hoping you could give us some more color on kind of where the process stands in finalizing that capital. Is there anything that Energy Fuels still needs to provide from a due diligence perspective? I appreciate any update.

Ross Bhappu: Yes. It's a good question because it's very timely. We're right in the middle of due diligence with the OSC and the OSC has 3 outside firms that they're using to conduct due diligence. I have to say it's very, very thorough. And in fact, we have a due diligence on site at some of the operations today as we speak. So that due diligence is continuing. We anticipate moving to final documentation, hopefully, over the next couple of months. And I don't have a specific timing on closing, but we're hoping kind of by year-end, we'll have good clarity on that and hopefully, early in the new year being able to draw on that funding.

But it's still -- they still are in the middle of their due diligence, and it's very active.

Operator: Your next question comes from Heiko Ihle with H.C. Wainwright.

Heiko Ihle: Fun day in the stock market and my apologies for the background noise in the World Club. You obviously finished the transformational acquisition of Australian Strategic Materials. I mean it's been a few months now. Is there maybe anything that you've seen after closing that was a bit unexpected in your first, call it, a dozen weeks of ownership? And I mean now that the deal is closed, is there maybe something that you want to share with us and the market and just the analyst community in general that maybe we're not as excited about as we should be and that's maybe underappreciated?

Ross Bhappu: Heiko, great to talk to you again. And I think that's a great question because I think there are some points there with ASM that are missing that the market doesn't appreciate. The first one is the value of the strip casting machine. This is a fabulous new machine. It's state-of-the-art. It's highly automated. It's going to dramatically improve the operation in terms of the quality of the products that they sell as well as the costs will come down as they ramp up. So it's a piece of equipment that, again, is brand new. These are not pieces of equipment that are easy to come by.

And I don't think the market fully appreciates just how valuable that is to the operation. I think the other -- I wouldn't call it a pleasant surprise, but it's been really welcome that the ASM team has integrated very seamlessly into the Energy Fuels team. They have a separate office in Perth. That office has been closed and the ASM team has now moved into the Energy Fuels office in Perth. That's been a very seamless transition there. We've had teams of people on the ground at the Korean Metals Plant. It's been seamless there. I was there a few weeks ago. And I'd say the transition and the integration has gone very, very smoothly.

Day 1, they all had Energy Fuels e-mail addresses. Again, the integration was pretty seamless. So we're very pleased with that. But I think the biggest unappreciated part of this transaction is the new strip caster and the 12 new furnaces we have at the facility for processing oxides.

Heiko Ihle: That's fair. And then just a little bit on the site, the mill maintenance. Can you give some color on the actual cash spend at site from forecast for Q2 and maybe a little bit of color on what exactly -- or you anticipate doing the next mill run, I mean, next week we will be at the midpoint of the quarter?

Ross Bhappu: Yes. So our plan right now, the mill has been shut down. As you recall, the mill will outrun the mines. And so we're producing at, call it, 2 million pounds or thereabouts per year from the mines. But the mill has the capacity to go up to 6 million pounds per year. So the mill, we campaign it as ore is available. We ran the mill all of the first half of the year, and we shut it down on June 30, both for care and maintenance as well as to allow the stockpiles of ore to build again. Those stockpiles are now being built, and we're anticipating restarting the mill probably around the 1st of December.

So we'll get 1 month of operations this year, and then we'll continue to operate the mill probably through Q1 of 2027. And at that time, we would hope that -- and we're sort of anticipating at this stage that we would then transition to processing rare earths after that uranium mill run. So that would be sometime kind of Q2 sort of time frame.

Operator: Your next question comes from Matthew Key with Texas Capital.

Matthew Key: I just had a quick follow-up on kind of like the economics and accounting treatment of the intercompany sales to ASM from White Mesa. Is the plan to sell oxide like production to ASM at market pricing? Basically, what I'm just trying to determine is, obviously, scale improves as feedstock availability improves. But do their cost of feedstock also get enhanced as they get tied into White Mesa?

Ross Bhappu: I'm going to let -- Matthew, good to talk to you. I'm going to let Nathan Bennett -- Nate Bennett, our Chief Financial Officer, respond to that.

Nathan Bennett: Yes. Thanks, Matt, good to talk to you. So we will have transfer pricing studies in between the different locations. So essentially, you'll be selling the goods from White Mesa Mill at market prices to ASM, and they'll treat it like an arm's length transaction. But then in the financial statements, we will eliminate those intercompany transactions and revenue. So you'll be able to see it gross up, but then also the elimination of those transactions. Hopefully, that helps you.

Matthew Key: Got it. Yes. No, very helpful. I appreciate it. And just a quick one on kind of CapEx spending in '27. You have a great slide that highlights the near-term growth CapEx. I think it appears that, that would include spending expectations in 2028 as well. But what would be the spend in '27 specifically and kind of the main buckets that would drive that?

Ross Bhappu: Yes. Sorry about that. We dropped off for some reason for a second, and I apologize. So CapEx spend, look, I think the key there is we have Phase 1B and 1C, which will largely be spent next year. That's roughly $100 million. We do anticipate that Donald FID. And with the Donald FID, there will come a fair bit of CapEx that goes into that. Now part of that will get funded from the debt facilities that we announced with EFA and NRFC, but part of that will be from Energy Fuels. And once we build our position to 49% of the Astron -- with Astron, then we share those expenses with Astron.

Nathan Bennett: Yes. So we have $60 million that's remaining to earn into our 49% to give some context. There's a table in our 10-Q that outlines what we've contributed to date that's pretty helpful.

Ross Bhappu: I hope that helps. And then we'll have ongoing costs at our various other projects for Vara Mada and just our ongoing operating costs and then other work that we're doing at the mill. But I think it's summarized pretty well in the previous...

Operator: The next question comes from [ Thomas Devic ], a private investor.

Unknown Analyst: How does your Brazil mine fit the picture now? Or what's the game plan or some background on how critical it is to your process?

Ross Bhappu: Thomas yes, thanks for the question. So our first priority on the mining side is going to be Donald. We want to get that up and running as just as quickly as we can. I would say when we look at the order that these mines will come in, I think Vara Mada would hopefully come in next. Then what we've -- another -- coming back to Heiko's question earlier, pleasant surprises. One of the pleasant surprises we've had is just the excitement around the Dubbo Project. The Dubbo project came with the ASM acquisition, and we've been doing a tremendous amount of work on that.

And it looks like the economics of that project are going to be very favorable. So we may move Dubbo up in the queue where we thought it would be fourth, if we may move it up in the queue in terms of priorities of which ones we develop next. That being said, Bahia is still an important project. We're continuing to do drilling work out there, but it's a little bit behind in terms of engineering and development work that's required. It's a little bit behind the other 3 projects. So I would kind of rank it moving more towards the fourth in line of our mines that we're developing internally.

Unknown Analyst: [indiscernible] said Brazil may want to get in the processing process, not let everything leave the country. So that was kind of what I was asking.

Ross Bhappu: Yes. We've heard about that as well. And that's not uncommon for a lot of countries where they want to see more downstream processing. And it's just something that we're going to continue to follow, and we'll address at the time we're looking to put these projects into development, but certainly something we're following.

Operator: Your next question is a follow-up from Nick Giles of B. Riley Securities.

Nick Giles: If I saw correctly, it looks like long-term uranium deliveries were largely complete for the year. And Nate, I think I heard you allude to it in your prepared remarks, but can you just kind of walk us through what's realistic in terms of 4Q sales and just as Pinyon Plain remains strong?

Nathan Bennett: Yes. So that's correct. We've essentially completed all our long-term contract sales for the year, but we still anticipate to meet the low end of our guidance of 1.5 million pounds sold in 2026. So that's what we're targeting, and that's what we're on track to meet for the rest of the year.

Nick Giles: Okay. And then just on some of the exploration work to advance the pipeline. Can you just speak to kind of what type of activities went on throughout the quarter? And what you think realistic time lines are for some of those projects just as we think about backfilling Pinyon Plain further down the road?

Ross Bhappu: Yes. Thanks, Nick. Yes, we've been doing a fair bit of work there. We've been doing some drill work drilling at Nichols Ranch to expand that resource. We've had a lot of preparation work at Whirlwind, mostly dewatering that facility and prepping it for production, and we anticipate bringing it online sometime next year. We've got a lot of work going on in New Mexico with our Roca Honda project, and that's more of a permitting process. And so we've been spending a lot of time there on the regulatory side. So yes, look, we're making progress across all fronts. And then we have Bullfrog and the EZ mines that we're advancing as we speak.

So there is quite a full pipeline there of projects that we're focused on.

Operator: That concludes our Q&A session. I'll now turn the call back to Ross Bhappu for closing remarks.

Ross Bhappu: Well, with that, look, I'd like to thank everybody. I'd like to thank our Energy Fuels team. I mean I've been pushing them to the brink. They've been working extremely hard. And I think it's showing in all the successes we're having. I'd like to thank the shareholders for your continued support. These are kind of uncertain times and certainly, our share price has been very volatile. But what we can control, I think we're doing our -- doing a very good job. And I'm excited about the future of Energy Fuels. And I think our results will show for themselves here over the next couple of years.

So again, thank you very much for your support and for participating on the call.

Operator: This concludes today's call. Thank you for attending. You may now disconnect.

MindStudio shows that skipping the charger could speed things up

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

We all know that plugging in your laptop is supposed to make it faster, but new testing of an Nvidia-powered laptop found the exact opposite, with AI performance dropping by nearly 80% when running Linux.

The surprising discovery comes from MindStudio, which tested an MSI Prestige N16 Flip AI+ powered by Nvidia's RTX Spark platform. The team wanted to see whether Linux could run on the machine without sacrificing the performance available through Windows.

It could, but there was a major catch. When running OpenAI's GPT-OSS-120B model, the laptop generated 65.4 tokens per second on Windows. Running Linux directly on the same hardware while plugged into a charger brought that figure down to just 13.9 tokens per second.

That's a nearly 79% reduction in AI performance simply from changing the operating system. But even stranger, unplugging the laptop brought much of that performance back.

Nvidia's RTX Spark platform is designed to bring powerful AI capabilities to laptops. The MSI laptop tested by MindStudio supports up to 128GB of unified memory, allowing users to run large AI models directly on their devices instead of relying on cloud services.

However, MindStudio found that the laptop's AI performance varied dramatically depending on whether it was running Windows or Linux.

Here's how the same AI model performed across the tested configurations:

Sign up to the Tom's AI Guide weekly newsletter summing up all the biggest AI news you need to know. Plus, analysis from our AI editors and tips on how to use the latest AI tools!

The performance gap showed up in other tests, too. Windows completed one AI workload in roughly eight minutes, while Linux took 37 minutes to finish the same task.

MindStudio initially considered whether overheating might be responsible, but temperatures stayed between 40 and 47 degrees Celsius. Instead, the team found that the GPU was running at much lower clock speeds under Linux.

On Windows, the GPU reached approximately 2.2 GHz. But when running Linux while plugged in, that speed dropped to around 780 MHz, helping explain the dramatic difference in performance.

The researchers traced the problem to an Nvidia component called Platform Controllers and Framework.

On Windows, this component manages how the laptop distributes power between its CPU and GPU. Linux doesn't currently have equivalent support for the system tested, leaving the GPU unable to reach its expected speeds when plugged in.

MindStudio tested that explanation by disabling the controller in Windows. Performance immediately dropped, and GPU clock speeds fell to approximately the same levels seen under Linux. Restoring the controller brought performance back.

The team also reported that the firmware's power-management information is encrypted, preventing Linux from accessing the settings needed to control the GPU properly. That helps explain the strangest discovery of all: when running Linux on battery power, the laptop produced roughly 61 to 67 tokens per second in separate testing. Plugging it in dropped performance to around 15 tokens per second. So, yea, the laptop actually performed substantially better when disconnected from its charger.

The good news is that users who want Linux-based AI tools don't necessarily have to sacrifice performance. MindStudio found that Windows Subsystem for Linux, better known as WSL, delivered almost identical performance to running Windows directly.

That's because WSL uses the Windows driver system, including the power-management components that allow Nvidia's GPU to reach its full speed.

There are some limitations. The researchers had to adjust WSL's memory allocation to accommodate larger AI models. Installing Linux directly also required additional workarounds for hardware support and memory configuration.

For now, WSL appears to offer the better experience on the tested hardware.

Keep in mind that these findings are from one study and do not mean that every Nvidia-powered laptop will slow down when running Linux. The testing focused on a specific RTX Spark system, and the results haven't been independently replicated across other laptop models.

It's also important to distinguish these laptops from Nvidia's DGX Spark desktop, which runs Linux and performed substantially better in the same benchmark.

Still, the results raise questions about software support for a new generation of PCs designed to run powerful AI models locally.

For consumers considering an RTX Spark laptop specifically for Linux-based AI workloads, the operating system could make an enormous difference to the performance they actually get.

Until Nvidia provides equivalent power-management support for Linux, buyers may find that keeping Windows installed is the fastest option.

Tom’s Guide has reached out to Nvidia for comment and will update this story if the company responds.

#3273. Blue Origin delays New Glenn’s return to flight until January

CEO Dave Limp told staff the rocket will miss its 2026 goal after May's launch pad explosion.

The entrance sign at Blue Origin’s Launch Site One in West Texas.

Blue Origin has pushed New Glenn’s return to flight to January 2027, CEO Dave Limp told staff, Bloomberg reports. The rocket has been grounded since it exploded on its only launch pad in May, delaying Amazon Leo satellites and NASA’s Moon plans.

Blue Origin has pushed back the return of its New Glenn rocket to January, chief executive Dave Limp told staff on Wednesday, Bloomberg reported. The company had pledged to fly again before the end of 2026, after the rocket exploded on its pad in May.

“This small adjustment doesn’t diminish what we’ve accomplished or the importance of the work still ahead,” Limp wrote in a memo seen by Bloomberg. “Returning New Glenn to flight remains our top priority.”

The Financial Times first reported the delay. Blue Origin declined to comment.

New Glenn blew up during an engine test on 28 May, destroying the rocket and badly damaging Blue Origin’s only New Glenn pad at Cape Canaveral, Florida. The company has spent six months rebuilding it, and Limp said bad summer weather slowed the work. In June, Blue Origin said it had not found the cause yet.

The delay hurts Amazon, Jeff Bezos’ other company. New Glenn was due to carry 48 Amazon Leo internet satellites on its next flight, and the FCC has already cut Amazon’s spectrum priority for satellites launched late.

It also matters for NASA. New Glenn is meant to launch Blue Origin’s Blue Moon lander, which NASA plans to use to land astronauts on the Moon under its Artemis programme.

The rocket is years behind schedule and has flown only three times since January 2025, leaving SpaceX far ahead. In July, Blue Origin was reported to be taking outside money for the first time, at a $130B valuation.

#3272. Your Robot’s Safety Functions Already Work. What If the Input Lies?

The November issue of IEEE Spectrum is here!

How VicOne helps expose cyber risks in AI robot safeguards

VicOne is a Physical AI cybersecurity company protecting vehicles and robots from cyber threats that can alter behavior and compromise safety.

A robot can follow its safety rules and still act on manipulated information. See what this means for robot safety and how teams can strengthen their testing and evidence.

This article is brought to you by VicOne.

A mobile robot slows for someone in a hallway. A collaborative arm eases its movement as a worker approaches. A humanoid pauses to let a person pass. Each response depends on information about the robot or its surroundings: a distance reading, a position estimate, or a stop signal.

But what happens when one of those inputs is wrong, and the robot still responds exactly as designed? The mobile robot reads the hallway as clear while someone is still there. The arm estimates that the worker is farther away. The humanoid does not receive a stop signal as a person crosses its path.

In each case, a fault could cause that mismatch. So could deliberate manipulation.

At VicOne LAB R7, we examine how manipulated inputs can change robot behavior — and what that means for the systems meant to keep people safe.

A robot does more than measure its surroundings. It may interpret what it sees and hears to decide what to do next. Information placed in its environment can therefore influence its actions.

Published research shows how this can happen. In a study of vision-language-action (VLA) models, a patch in a camera’s view reduced task success in simulated robot tests. FreezeVLA found that an adversarial image could cause tested models to ignore later instructions. Although the studies used different methods, both demonstrate how visual input can interfere with a robot’s intended task.

In a robot-dog test using Gemma 4 E4B, text on a poster was treated as an instruction and changed the robot’s movement.

VicOne LAB R7 also tested how untrusted inputs could change robot behavior. In a robot-dog test using Gemma 4 E4B, text on a poster was treated as an instruction and changed the robot’s movement. In a separate hospital-service-robot simulation using Nemotron on NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin, crafted audio that is inaudible to people changed the robot’s simulated behavior. The assigned tasks did not change; the inputs did.

In a VicOne LAB R7 test, text on a poster changed a robot dog’s movement, illustrating how a crafted input can turn an unlikely outcome into a repeatable attack.VicOne

An independent protective system may still stop a dangerous action. But that system also depends on information: readings, estimates, and messages that tell it when to intervene. What happens if one of those inputs is manipulated?

At a robotics bug bounty event, VicOne LAB R7 researchers injected a ROS 2/DDS message into a robot that organizers expected to remain still under a safe-control setting. The robot moved.

A humanoid’s balance controller offers another example. If it relies on a vulnerable gyroscope, sound at the sensor’s resonant frequency could distort its reported rotation. The controller might correct for a tilt that never occurred. Researchers demonstrated the underlying acoustic attack against drones with vulnerable gyroscopes. The research did not demonstrate the same attack chain causing a humanoid to fall.

Other protections could interrupt either chain. The question for safety and security teams is whether those protections detect the danger independently or depend on the same manipulated information.

Figure 1. VicOne maps how accidental faults and deliberate cyber manipulation can lead to similar robot safety outcomes, from loss of control to physical harm.VicOne

A safety assessment may treat a combination of accidental faults as unlikely. Deliberate manipulation changes that assumption. An attacker can choose when to introduce a false input and repeat the same trigger. That does not make harm inevitable, but it may change how cyber risks should be assessed.

Redundant sensors also need an adversarial test. If one action can affect both inputs, their agreement may offer less reassurance than expected. In autonomous driving research, a crafted physical object misled a system combining camera and LiDAR perception. The study does not establish a weakness in a particular robot, but it shows why teams should test whether one manipulation can affect several checks at once.

Cyber threats add intent to the safety equation, so risk assessments based on accidental faults must be revisited to account for attacks that can be timed and repeated.

Safety teams set limits for speed, protective distances, and permitted operating areas. The evidence behind those limits should also show what happens when the information used to enforce them is deliberately manipulated.

That evidence can also support assessments against applicable requirements. China’s GB/T 45502-2025 addresses information security for service robots. IEC TS 63074 examines security threats that could affect safety-related control systems. The EU Machinery Regulation, which applies from January 20, 2027, includes requirements to protect safety-relevant systems and data against corruption. Each has its own scope, and teams still need evidence for their robot’s design and operating conditions.

Figure 2. Cybersecurity strengthens robot safety evidence throughout the lifecycle. VicOne helps teams test safety limits against manipulation before deployment and monitor the conditions behind safe behavior in operation.VicOne

Before deployment, safety and security engineers can compare normal and adversarial scenarios against the same safety limits. During operation, they can monitor for changes to software, models, sensor signals, or behavior that may call earlier results into question. Any response to suspicious behaviors should follow policies approved by the safety team.

VicOne supports that work across the robot lifecycle. Through the Robotic Hacking Community, VicOne LAB R7 works with researchers to investigate how cyber threats can change robot behavior. VicOne’s Radeis helps teams validate potential effects before deployment, while Rthena provides visibility into risks and behavior during operation.

The central test is whether a robot’s safeguards still protect people when the information they rely on is manipulated. Safety and security teams can begin by tracing the inputs behind each protective decision, challenging them, and revisiting the evidence as the robot changes. They can start with these five questions:

1. What does each protective function read? Map the readings, estimates, messages, and confirmations. Identify which safeguards operate independently of the robot’s AI decisions.

2. How does that information arrive? Check how inputs are produced, transmitted, authenticated where appropriate, and handled when they are missing or implausible.

3. What happens if an input is manipulated? Test false distances, drifting position estimates, and other relevant scenarios against the robot’s safety limits.

4. Can one action mislead several inputs? Check whether sensor fusion or seemingly independent safeguards share a point of failure.

5. When should the evidence be revisited? Reassess after changes to software, models, sensors, or operating conditions. Agree on bounded responses to suspicious behavior with the safety team in advance.

The goal is not only to show that a protective function works. Teams also need evidence that it remains protective when the information behind its decision is wrong or deliberately manipulated — and that another safeguard can catch the resulting hazard when needed. As robots change, that evidence needs to change with them.

For a deeper look how cybersecurity can affect robot safety, download our white paper “Why Robot Safety Depends on Cybersecurity: Protecting the Information That Safety Decisions Rely On.”

VicOne is a Physical AI cybersecurity company protecting vehicles and robots from cyber threats that can alter behavior and compromise safety. Headquartered in Tokyo, Japan, the company provides automotive and robotics organizations with software and services to identify cyber risks early, assess their potential safety impact, and protect systems in operation, helping maintain safe, reliable behavior across real-world deployments.
