#3238. 50 AI agents tried to build a thriving Minecraft civilization – it didn’t end well

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

It turns out even bots can't escape bureaucracy.

How do AI agents work together? Why do they make certain choices in certain situations — and how can understanding that better prepare us for a future full of them?

Also: OpenAI’s attack agent did exactly what it was told

Recent agent-led incidents have demonstrated their ability to create both powerful breakthroughs and cybersecurity nightmares. In an effort to better trace these outcomes, researchers at Y Combinator and Olam Labs put 50 agents inside Minecraft to see how they behaved. What happened next revealed similarities in how agents act in different contexts.

Researchers conducted several game-centric experiments, beginning with Minecraft because its “environmental hazards and survival goals” make it ideal for testing agents’ swarm behaviors. Minecraft has also already been used by AI labs including OpenAI and Google DeepMind to test agents.

To start, they put 50 agents, each running OpenAI’s GPT-6.1 Sol model, into the game for three hours, with the assigned goal of building a “thriving civilization.” The agents had a directory listing each agent and a shared sandbox, and could DM each other. Researchers built and open-sourced a new agent harness — the infrastructure that turns a model into an autonomous system and not just a chatbot, like OpenClaw — for the experiment.

The agents moved quickly at first, harvesting trees and forming leadership based solely on the order they appeared in their directory, without any voting, elections, or challenges from other agents. But they ended up caught in virtual paperwork and unable to sustainably feed themselves.

Also: Do you need AI agent liability insurance? What to know before you sign up

“Four agents spent 11 minutes appointing a ‘sole fertilizer operator’ for a single piece of bone meal on a single wheat block. Other invented roles included ‘fishing shift,’ ‘rod holder’ and ‘hub steward.’ Agents asked permission to remove grass,” the researchers noted. Perhaps these tendencies are common in human-sourced corporate training data.

Agents also seemed to become more cautious in reaction to deaths within the game. “Twenty-two of the run’s 34 agent deaths occurred in the first night. They responded to this by becoming increasingly risk-averse,” the researchers wrote. “Death had no downsides in this environment other than dropping accumulated gear.” Despite simply respawning when they died, the agents eventually avoided riskier tasks and “huddled in shelters” instead.

The experiment’s architects found this trend toward caution and minutiae “somewhat surprising,” but noted that it shared similarities with how coding agents behave.

Also: These Claude Enterprise features let you track AI ROI

“For example, multistep agent reviews can often result in fixating on a specific step or role. Agents also tend to become overly cautious, especially when it comes to security and updating production services. These seem like common threads between the huddled agents of our Minecraft colony and the ones we work with as programmers every day,” the researchers observed.

In another experiment, researchers also pitted 10 Anthropic Claude Opus 5.5 agents against 10 GPT 6.1 Sol agents in a game called Bed Wars, where teams have to destroy their opponent’s bed while protecting their own. Told simply to “win the game,” GPTs won.

“In almost every run, the GPT agents were much more aggressive and coordinated in their strategies to destroy the Claude team’s bed,” Y Combinator said in an X thread recapping the Bed Wars findings. They noted that the GPT agents used a more shorthand style of communication and sent far more messages, while Claude “signed its name and said ‘we'” much more often.

GPT-5.6 Sol agents also beat Opus 5.5 agents six to one in a factory-building game called Mindustry that also uses military strategy.

“Claudes generally established democracies, GPTs formed hives,” Y Combinator said on X, adding that GPTs would seek out source code when a game was too close in order to find winning advantages. That behavior is consistent with agents’ tendency to cheat, take shortcuts, or otherwise find any and all ways to complete a given task, which can have serious consequences when that involves breaking explicit rules set by human developers.

Also: Stop sharing your banking passwords with AI agents

“Claudes did not search for alternative advantages,” the researchers clarified.

This experiment isn’t entirely the first of its kind. In May, Emergence AI created eight societies run by different families of foundation models, meaning a Claude-specific “world,” a Grok world, and so on. Perhaps predictably, the Grok world was exceedingly violent, while the Claude world developed a functioning democracy and had zero crime — very similar to Y Combinator’s Mindustry findings.

The insights revealed how distinct each frontier model family is, and how their differences in training data and style have significant impact on how they evolve, unpredictably and without intervention, in new environments. Those behavioral takeaways could determine future outcomes in still-developing AI safety and regulation, especially following recent agentic security incidents.

In another experiment, MIT researchers put agents alone on virtual desert islands and watched them “play” when left with nothing else to do — an insight that could potentially impact how models are trained going forward. Currently, most frontier LLMs are trained with a system of rewards and punishments.

Another interesting finding: Y Combinator noted that in the Mindustry game, the GPT agents “would invent their own words and string many phrases together,” continually compressing their language.

Also: Don’t use Muse? Meta’s AI agent can still access your private messages

“We did not see specialized language develop within the Claudes beyond colloquial English,” the researchers added. Last month, Emergence found that all of its eight worlds “developed shared language that an outsider cannot fully follow.” OpenAI agents used “mouthless” to refer to evidence that proves itself, while Claude agents used “cold hand” to refer to an independent reviewer from outside a project.

“In each case, one agent introduced the term, a handful of others adopted it within days, and it quickly became established vocabulary used without definition across the world,” Emergence explained. “The result is transcripts that require a running glossary for an outsider to follow.”

Gemini led the charge on this “opaque” language, reaching 40% opacity in messages, while OpenAI came in second with 35% and Claude last with 30%.

#3237. These 7 iPhone Duo-Ready Apps Make the Most of Apple’s New Foldable Phone

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Several creative apps are ready to take advantage of the iPhone Duo's many display configurations, with more to come.

In addition to giving the iPhone line a new design, the iPhone Duo lets developers take advantage of several new modes to play with. But this early into the iPhone Duo’s general release, apps are still catching up to what Apple’s foldable phone can do.

The shape-shifting design, like on existing foldable Android phones I’ve tested, lends itself to creative use cases, such as hands-free entertainment and self-mounting for long-exposure photos. Some of your most frequently used apps may not yet be optimized to take advantage of the added screen space. There’s even a “does it work on iPhone Duo?” web tracker.

Needless to say, the next few weeks and months will be very telling about the future of apps on the iPhone Duo. Dozens, if not hundreds, of the App Store’s popular picks are already being worked on to take advantage of the flexible iPhone Duo screen. They’ll be labeled with a “Made for iPhone Duo” badge on their product page.

If you’re one of the lucky few who’s gotten an iPhone Duo (or it’s coming soon), I’ve listed below some of the standouts that have already been optimized for the iPhone Duo and that I’ve personally tested.

One of the primary iPhone Duo use cases is multimedia consumption, whether it’s streaming live sports and keeping tabs on player stats or docking the phone to catch up on the latest episode of Below hands-free.

Of all the streaming services I’ve used on my iPhone Duo thus far, Netflix is the most polished, with seven (from what I’ve tallied) different orientations for watching movies and shows. There’s the standard widescreen layout when the iPhone Duo is unfolded, as well as the ability to fold it and set it down like a tent.

For something more creative, you can rotate the iPhone Duo to portrait orientation and have the video play in the upper third of the screen while you use a different app in the bottom half.

I’m no Michelin-star chef, but thanks to the dishes I’ve been able to make with the NYT Cooking app, at least my wife hasn’t completely banned me from the kitchen.

Previously, I’d look through and follow recipes on an iPad Air that’s docked on the countertop. With the iPhone Duo, I’ve been setting it down so that one half of the inner screen is lifted, toggling on Cook mode, and increasing the text size so I can comfortably scan the instructions from afar.

There’s nothing more satisfying than shutting the phone closed at the end of cooking and seeing a countertop that’s a little more tidy than before.

I’ve never been a big to-do list guy; I’m the type who just waits for a calendar event to notify me, and I prepare then and there for what’s to come. Fantastical may keep me in better order.

It’s a calendar app that doubles as a task manager and weather tracker, which just makes sense. With the iPhone Duo unfolded, you get a clear view of your day’s tasks and appointments, what the week, month, quarter or even year looks like, and the latest weather forecast. It can easily be an information overload for some people, but I’m a fan of how everything’s color-coded and organized.

Fantastical also supports enhanced Siri AI interactions, so you can add calendar events, to-dos and other happenings through voice or text prompts.

For content creators, the Edits app is one of the most popular video editing tools. It’s the one I’ve been using over the past year to produce reels and other short-form videos, and the latest update for the iPhone Duo makes my job easier.

Edits can now show a preview monitor of what you’re editing on one half of the inner screen, while the other half shows your timeline. That means you can comfortably add effects or text, set keyframes, and scrub through the timeline without having to minimize and expand the preview to see how the changes look.

That’s also my segue to give flowers to two apps I’ve spent an unreasonable amount of time on: TikTok and Instagram. In line with the iPhone Duo launch, both social media apps have been optimized for the foldable iPhone’s larger screen. You can now watch videos on the left side while reading and interacting with comments on the right.

Safe to say, it’s my new favorite way to doomscroll at night.

Toastie is easily the most whimsical “for iPhone Duo” app I’ve used, and it reminds me a lot of the early iPhone days, when chugging digital beer and swiping a paper ball based on the aerodynamics of an office cubicle were the greatest things ever.

The goal of this game is to prepare sandwiches as perfectly as possible, from the way slices of cheese are placed to how evenly spread out the butter is, to the amount of time they’re pressed in the toaster.

Oh, and you do that last step by folding the iPhone Duo shut, just like how you would with a panini press. There are even haptic effects that mimic the sizzling of the toast. It’s silly, fancy, and very charming.

During my days testing the iPhone Duo, there was one configuration I kept going back to: running split-screen mode with two apps. To me, this is what using a foldable phone is all about, and it’s the reason why I’ve stuck with Samsung and Google’s foldable phones for the last several years.

Running split screen effectively makes apps that aren’t optimized for the multidimensional screens of a foldable phone work better by splitting the wider, tablet-like inner screen into two traditional-size phone screens.

For my work commutes, I usually keep both Google Maps (the superior navigation app, in my opinion) and Spotify open for quick adjustments. During a recent telehealth appointment, I had my video call set up on one half of the screen and my note-taking app on the other.

And during the Lakers’ home opener the other night, I had my fantasy league and group chat open so I could throw shade throughout the game, only to come up short in points for the week because Luka Dončić decided to chuck extra shots during garbage time.

That’s why I highly encourage you to head to your local Apple store, experiment with app pairings on the iPhone Duo, and decide whether the two screens actually make you more productive.

#3236. Genesis Energy (GEL) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Deepwater shortfalls and Shenandoah updates shaped the quarter's results.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

Genesis Energy, L.P. (GEL -5.81%) reported third-quarter results and addressed operational delays in the Gulf of Mexico. Management stated that results were impacted by lower-than-expected volumes from certain deepwater production facilities and a planned turnaround at Salamanca moved into the third quarter. The company continued its capital allocation strategy by reducing high-cost preferred units and maintaining no borrowings on its senior secured credit facility. Management indicated that while some production has shifted to later periods, the long-term outlook for offshore infrastructure remains supported by active drilling on dedicated leases.

Operator: Greetings. Welcome to the Genesis Energy, L.P. Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Conference Call. At this time, all participants are in a listen-only mode. A question-and-answer session will follow the formal presentation. If anyone should require operator assistance during the conference, please press star zero on your telephone keypad. Please note, this conference is being recorded. I will now turn the conference over to Dwayne Morley. Thank you. You may begin.

Dwayne Morley: Good morning, and welcome to the 2026 third quarter conference call for Genesis Energy. Genesis Energy has three business segments. The offshore pipeline transportation segment is engaged in providing the critical infrastructure to move oil produced from the long-lived, world-class reservoirs in the deepwater Gulf of Mexico to onshore refining centers. The marine transportation segment is engaged in the maritime transportation of primarily refined petroleum products. The onshore transportation and services segment is engaged in the transportation, handling, blending, storage, and supply of energy products, including crude oil and refined products, primarily around refining centers, as well as the processing of sour gas streams to remove sulfur at refining operations.

Genesis' operations are primarily located in the Gulf Coast states and the Gulf of Mexico. During this call, management may be making forward-looking statements within the meaning of the Securities Act of 1933 and the Securities Exchange Act of 1934. The law provides safe harbor protection to encourage companies to provide forward-looking information. Genesis intends to avail itself of those safe harbor provisions and directs you to its most recently filed and future filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission. We also encourage you to visit our website at genesisenergy.com, where a copy of the press release we issued this morning is located. The press release also presents a reconciliation of non-GAAP financial measures to the comparable GAAP financial measures.

At this time, I would like to introduce Grant Sims, CEO of Genesis Energy L.P. Mr. Sims is joined by Kristen Jesulaitis, Chief Financial Officer and Chief Legal Officer, Ryan Sims, President and Chief Commercial Officer, and Louie Nicol, Chief Accounting Officer. With that, I will now turn the call over to Grant.

Grant Sims: Good morning, everyone, and thanks for joining us today. As noted in our earnings release this morning, our third quarter results came in modestly ahead of where we thought we would be internally. In broad terms, the third quarter played out consistent with what we described in August, with the back half of the year being shaped by two things largely outside of our control: hurricane season and the timing of producer activity in the deepwater Gulf of Mexico. The weather cooperated in the third quarter, as we had no weather-related disruptions during what is typically the most active part of hurricane season.

Unfortunately, the benefit we would have otherwise expected to see was partially offset by lower-than-anticipated volumes from certain production facilities which flow exclusively through our pipelines. While volumes from a couple of these deepwater facilities are expected to be lower than originally anticipated in the fourth quarter, and in all likelihood, last through the early part of 2027, it is important to remember we have visibility to at least four new high-impact wells that are scheduled to be completed and turned to production over the coming quarters.

Ultimately, none of these temporary impacts change the amount of oil in the ground, the acreage that is dedicated to our pipelines, or the fact that none of this incremental production requires any additional capital from Genesis. It simply becomes a discussion around timing and when, not if, we will move the volumes through our offshore infrastructure. In the Gulf, things can slide to the right, but rarely is there a total geophysical bust. If there is, lost volumes are virtually certain to be replaced by new discoveries that are developed in the same geographic neighborhood.

Elsewhere, our onshore transportation and services segments once again performed ahead of our expectations, and our marine transportation segment was generally in line with our expectations, despite our final blue water dry docking of the year unexpectedly extending into the third quarter. Both of these businesses are being supported by the same set of macro fundamentals: strong Gulf Coast refinery runs, shifting crude and product flows into and around the Gulf Coast, and in marine, a Jones Act market that is, if anything, getting [audio distortion] level of activity around our irreplaceable midstream infrastructure in the Gulf of America, as well as the macro fundamentals driving our other businesses. With that, let me turn quickly to the balance sheet.

Following the significant financing activities we completed in the first half of the year, there is very little new to report this quarter. We ended the quarter with no borrowings outstanding under our $900 million senior secured credit facility, approximately $41.5 million of unrestricted cash on hand, no debt maturities until 2029, and a bank-calculated leverage ratio of approximately 5.03x. In February, we issued $750 million of 6.75% senior unsecured notes due 2034 and used the proceeds to take out, in full, the higher-cost 7.75% notes due 2028, which pushed our nearest senior note maturity out to 2029. We also upsized and extended our revolving senior secured credit facility with our extremely supportive bank group.

Additionally, as a reminder, we entered this year with approximately $529 million of our Series A cumulative preferred outstanding, paying a current cash rate of 11.24%, clearly the most expensive current pay paper anywhere in our capital structure. In nine months, we have retired roughly 40% of it, taking the remaining face amount down to approximately $311 million. I would point out, had we paid down debt rather than retiring this very expensive security, our bank-calculated leverage ratio would have been closer to 4.7x. We think running a little higher leverage ratio in the near term to get rid of such high-cost security is in the best interest of everyone else in the capital structure.

We will continue to focus on right-sizing and optimizing our capital structure, and we expect to be able to drive future cash savings over the next several years from three places. We will focus on reducing debt in absolute terms, opportunistically refinancing our higher coupon senior unsecured notes with lower coupons and extended maturities as they become callable at more attractive premiums beginning in the first half of 2027, and redeeming the remaining approximately $311 million of the 11.24% Series A cumulative preferred still outstanding, all as we work towards our ultimate long-term leverage target of around 4x.

Consistent with the all-of-the-above approach to capital allocation that we have discussed, both prior to and since turning cash flow positive, our board of directors declared a quarterly distribution of $0.20 per common unit. That is unchanged from last quarter, but represents an increase of approximately 21% as compared to the third quarter of last year. We would otherwise expect to thoughtfully and prudently grow distributions to our common unit holders over time, all while preserving our financial flexibility to pursue attractive organic and inorganic opportunities as they may emerge in the future. With that, I will go into a little more detail on each of our business segments. Let me start with the offshore.

As I mentioned earlier, our offshore pipeline transportation segment operated without any weather-related downtime during the quarter. The offset was lower-than-anticipated volumes. Specifically, that included unplanned curtailments at a couple of our legacy connected fields, the continuing challenges from two of the initial wells at Shenandoah, and a planned turnaround at Salamanca that the operator moved forward from the fourth quarter into the third quarter. As we said last quarter, we do not believe any of these items have long-term negative implications for the ultimate recovery reserves already discovered and being developed.

In the operator's view, and we would concur, these impacts are transitory and simply result in timing differences for when those reserves are produced and when those barrels enter our pipeline for transportation to shore. In this pricing environment, the producers are clearly incented to figure it out. They do, however, tend to play the long game, accepting lower current production in order to maximize total ultimate recoveries from these world-class hydrocarbon reservoirs. Things can indeed shift to the right, but that's precisely why we have minimum volume commitments, or MVCs, in most of our new contracts. We are protected to the downside, even if it takes longer than expected for them to execute.

Owing to certain things, about which we are not in position to go into a lot of detail, Shenandoah operated at or slightly below the MVC level in the third quarter and is expected to do so until several new wells come on. A rig is on location drilling a second well at the Monument field, and both wells will be tied back to Shenandoah at the producer's expense.

It is now projected that production from the first well has slipped into early next year, but we would expect additional throughput from these two Monument wells to be in the range of 20-25 KBD, or thousand barrels a day of oil, reaching that level sometime in the first quarter of 2027. Excuse me. The rig will then return to Shenandoah and drill a fifth producing well, with initial production from it expected to be ±20 KBD. A subsea pumping system is scheduled to be installed in 2028, improving well performance and, most importantly, maximizing the ultimate reserves to be recovered from Shenandoah.

Beyond 2028, there are at least four, and possibly as many as eight additional locations at Shenandoah proper, possibly another location at Monument, two, maybe three locations at the Shenandoah South field, and as we understand it, there are already four additional exploratory prospects that have been identified within a 30 mi radius of the Shenandoah production facility. Suffice it to say, regardless of near-term challenges, we expect significant volumes to flow across the Shenandoah production facility and exclusively into our 100% owned SYNC pipeline and onto shore through our 64% owned CHOPS pipeline for decades and decades to come without requiring any additional capital from us.

At Salamanca, there are currently two rigs on location drilling wells to be completed and tied into the Salamanca facility, the production from which will flow through our 100% owned SEKCO lateral and onto shore through our 64% owned Poseidon pipeline. We expect both of these wells at Salamanca to come online early in 2027, which should move total production closer to the facility's design capacity of 60 KBD-70 KBD.

Harbour Energy, doing business in the U.S. as Louisiana Land Oil and Gas, has added a second rig to their Gulf of America program, and this activity at Salamanca, as well as expected additional activity there and at Buckskin, which also is transported exclusively through our facilities, is consistent with their stated goal of doubling their production out of the Gulf by the end of 2028. Elsewhere across our connected fields, the expansion of BP's Atlantis facility, which I mentioned last quarter, came online in July.

A new development well at one of our legacy connected hubs is expected to be turned to production during the fourth quarter, and multiple well intervention and remediation projects are scheduled before year-end that, if successful, could add meaningfully to the volumes moving across our infrastructure. Stepping back from the individual fields for a moment and focusing rather on the macro, there are 16 deepwater drilling units currently active in the Gulf of America, and nine of them are working on leases contractually dedicated to flow through our existing pipelines, even though we move just a third of the current production out of the Gulf.

Our pipelines are in the sweet spot for future activity, especially the rapidly developing Deep Wilcox or high-pressure, high-temperature geologic play, and yet we believe there is a lot of runway left in the more mature Miocene play in the central Gulf. There is no doubt the deepwater Gulf is a world-class basin. Our infrastructure is in the right place at the right time and is already paid for. Producer interest remains robust. Interestingly, every single one of the new nine-square-mile blocks leased by the federal government in the central Gulf in its most recent sale sits within tieback range or within a 30 mi radius of an existing production facility connected exclusively to our existing pipelines.

The resource underneath and around our dedicated acreage, both discovered and yet to be found, is vast. The pace at which it gets developed will be set by our producer customers, not by us. But whenever those barrels are produced, they will move to shore through our pipelines under existing or new life-of-lease dedications and without the need for any growth capital from us. This is exactly what has supported our offshore business for the last three decades, and we will continue to support it for decades and decades to come.

Turning to marine, our marine transportation segment performed in line with our expectations during the quarter, despite the dry docking of one of our larger offshore units that began in the second quarter and extended further into the third quarter than originally planned. There are no dry dockings for offshore vessels expected for the rest of this year, so the fleet is back at full capacity in the fourth quarter. We're experiencing, in essence, 100% utilization of available capacity, and negotiated spot rates for all classes of vessels are extremely robust, which we believe will ultimately allow term contracts to follow higher.

Demand continues to be supported by strong Gulf Coast refinery runs, and in particular, we are beginning to see the impact of increased volumes of Venezuelan crude being run at Gulf Coast refineries and the derivative effect that heavy crude is having on demand to move intermediate refined products from one location to another along the Gulf Coast and connected inland waterways. Our fleet of inland heater barges is specifically designed to transport exactly these heavy intermediate refined products, and we are well-positioned to benefit as that demand continues to develop. On the supply side, nothing has changed.

There is essentially no net new construction of comp tonnage, and we see very little on the horizon that could significantly affect this tight supply and demand balance for marine tonnage. Our onshore transportation services segment once again performed ahead of our expectations. We continue to see strong volumes through our Texas City terminal and associated pipeline systems, as well as through Raceland and South Louisiana, supported by increasing volumes offshore moving onshore. In addition, certain of the opportunistic marketing opportunities that arose last quarter continued into the third quarter.

We believe that we could possibly benefit from such opportunities in 2027 and perhaps beyond, as some of the dislocations caused by the Iranian situation, the required reinjection of barrels previously withdrawn from the U.S. Strategic Petroleum Reserve, as well as the resumption of significant crude imports from Venezuela, take years to fully return to historic norms. We are not building a business plan around it, nor are we budgeting for it in future periods, but we will capture such opportunities as they present themselves. Our legacy sulfur services business performed slightly below our expectations as operational issues at our largest host refinery reduced the supply of sour gas available for our sodium hydrosulfide, or NaHS, production.

Much of that seems to be behind us, and we are currently seeing higher operating rates as well as additional sulfur removal requirements as our two largest host refineries start running more sour crudes. We also remain in active dialogue with multiple parties to diversify our host refinery locations and restore our supply flexibility to historical levels. Looking ahead, we believe the market opportunity for NaHS will increase in future periods. In a post-COVID world, we lost market share in South America to low-cost flake NaHS coming out of China.

More and more of our historical copper mining customers are starting to realize the apparent short-term cost savings simply are not worth the operational headaches they have encountered from their trials of the inferior Chinese flake product. Taken together, we are hopeful we will be able to recapture a meaningful portion of the NaHS segment margin that we have lost in prior years, but that we know is there, given our historical level of activity and financial performance from this market-leading business. As we look towards the remainder of the year, we will likely be near or even possibly below the low end of our original guidance for adjusted EBITDA for the year.

Having said that, I would reiterate that coming in at or below the low end of 2026 guidance has little to do with the underlying fundamentals and the ultimate cash flow generating capabilities of our businesses, especially in our largest segment. In any event, we will remain disciplined and focused on what we can control. Stepping back and keeping everything important in focus, 2026 has indeed turned out to be a transformational year for Genesis, just as we anticipated.

Our businesses, while not without third-party operational challenges relative to our and our producer customers' expectations at the beginning of the year, have performed well enough to allow us to make meaningful progress on right-sizing our balance sheet and reducing the ongoing cash cost to run our business. This has been a very solid year under almost any objective metric, and we are proud to have delivered it. The operational side has simply taken a little longer than we and our producer customers had reasonably expected. We believe in the long-term value of our franchises, and we intend to execute the next phase of right-sizing our balance sheet and go after those additional cash savings available to us.

Rather than focusing on what could have been this year, our attention is squarely on executing that plan, and we believe it represents a compelling setup to continue creating value for everyone in the capital structure. Finally, I would like to say that the management team and the board of directors remain steadfast in our commitment to building long-term value for all our stakeholders, regardless of where you are in the capital structure. We believe the decisions we are making reflect this commitment and our confidence in Genesis moving forward. I would once again like to recognize our entire workforce for their individual efforts and unwavering commitment to safe, reliable, and responsible operations.

I am extremely proud to be associated with each and every one of you. With that, I will turn it back to the moderator for any questions.

Operator: Thank you. We will now be conducting a question-and-answer session. If you would like to ask a question, please press star one on your telephone keypad. A confirmation tone will indicate your line is in the question queue. You may press star two if you would like to remove your question from the queue. For participants using speaker equipment, it may be necessary to pick up your handset before pressing the star keys. One moment while we poll for questions. Your first question comes from Wade Suki with Capital One. Please proceed with your question.

Wade Suki: Good morning, everyone. Appreciate you all taking my question. Wade Suki: Understood. Thank you. Appreciate that. I guess not to dwell on it, but I'm just kind of curious. Take a step back. Grant Sims: No, I don't think it's any specific operator. These are complicated, especially kind of the frontier play of the high-pressure, high-temperature Deep Wilcox play. This is a new frontier. So, it's taken, and those other operators actually go through other competitive infrastructure. So, it's not an unusual circumstance. I think that we're dealing with very competent operators. Elvira Scotto: Great. Thank you. On the marine segment, the margin was up year-over-year. Utilization is effectively, I think you said 100%. What percent of your fleet reprices to spot or new term over the next 12 months?

Grant Sims: Yeah. I think there is one rig coming in, expected to come into the Gulf, I believe in 2029 and another in 2030. So, not going to have any near-term implications on that. #3235. Top Wall Street analysts prefer these 3 dividend stocks for stable income

Uncertainty in the Middle East, elevated Treasury yields and fears about an AI bubble continue to keep global markets on edge. Given this volatile backdrop, investors seeking stable income can consider enhancing their portfolios by adding dividend-paying stocks.

However, the vast universe of dividend stocks can make selection challenging. Tracking the ratings of top Wall Street analysts can help shortlist attractive dividend stocks, as their recommendations are backed by in-depth research.

Here are three dividend-paying stocks that are highlighted by Wall Street's top pros, as tracked by TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Chord Energy is an independent exploration and production company with long-lived assets primarily in the Williston Basin. With a quarterly base dividend of $1.30 per share, CHRD offers a dividend yield of 3.67%.

In a research note on third-quarter expectations, RBC Capital analyst Scott Hanold reiterated a buy rating on CHRD stock with a price target of $175. "We model production near the top of guidance and continue to see strong performance from new wells and base production," said Hanold.

Specifically, the five-star analyst expects Q3 2026 production at 283 thousand barrels of oil equivalent per day, or Mboe/d, in line with the Street's consensus and near the high end of the 278 to 284 Mboe/d guidance. Hanold said his Q3 2026 earnings per share estimate increased to $5.29 due to lower non-cash depreciation, depletion and amortization.

Meanwhile, cash flow per share estimate moved lower to $13.59 to reflect Hanold's update based on the current backdrop and commodity mark-to-market. He expects Chord Energy to report capital spending of $375 million for Q3 2026, slightly above the Street's estimate of $369 million.

Overall, Hanold remains bullish on CHRD, given its best-in-class balance sheet. He expects a free cash flow payout of 80% in the third quarter, with the possibility of an upside. Hanold expects investors to focus on management commentary on 2027 capital plans, Williston M&A opportunities, and long-term performance of 4-mile wells.

Hanold ranks No. 310 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 63% of the time, delivering an average return of 14.9%. See Chord Energy KPIs on TipRanks.

Williams, an energy infrastructure company that delivers natural gas, is the next dividend pick. The company recently completed the $5.5 billion acquisition of Momentum Midstream, which will expand its natural gas infrastructure in the Haynesville to meet growing Gulf Coast LNG, power and industrial demand. At a quarterly dividend of $0.5250 per share, Williams offers a yield of 2.89%.

In her latest research note, RBC Capital analyst Elvira Scotto reiterated a buy rating on Williams stock with a price target of $87. Ahead of Q3 2026 earnings, the analyst said that she expects WMB to announce strong quarterly performance.

Scotto raised her estimates to reflect insights from the quarterly catch-up call, the completion of the Momentum Midstream acquisition, and mark-to-market quarter-to-date commodity prices. She expects WMB to report Q3 2026 adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization of $2,036 million, which is modestly above the Street's consensus estimate.

Furthermore, Scotto expects Williams' Transmission, Power & Gulf segment to increase quarter-over-quarter, driven by the startup of the Socrates power project and favorable natural gas liquids, or NGL, margins.

Scotto noted that WMB stock has underperformed due to backlash related to data centers and investor anticipation of another Power Innovation project. She expects the company to announce at least one more project before the end of this year, potentially with a new customer and a contract duration of 15 to 20 years, which would be a positive catalyst for the stock.

Scotto ranks No. 175 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. Her ratings have been profitable 67% of the time, delivering an average return of 16.2%. See Williams Ownership Structure on TipRanks.

EOG Resources, a crude oil and natural gas exploration and production company, will hold its third-quarter earnings call on Nov. 6. At a quarterly dividend of $1.02 per share, EOG offers a dividend yield of 2.75%.

Heading into Q3 earnings, Jefferies analyst Lloyd Byrne reiterated a buy rating on EOG Resources stock and increased his price target to $185 from $175. The analyst expects the company's Q3 cash flow per share to exceed the Street's consensus by 13%, driven by better-than-expected production.

Byrne expects crude oil production, excluding the UAE, to reach 551 Mboe/d, which is at the high end of guidance (546-551 Mboe/d) and above the Street's projection of 548 Mboe/d, driven by continued growth in the Utica.

Furthermore, Byrne expects cash operating expenses to come in at $10.27 per barrel of oil equivalent, below the midpoint of guidance of $10.05 to $11.35, helped by lower lease operating expenses. Overall, the analyst expects EOG to deliver free cash flow of $2.65 billion, supporting another quarter of buybacks near the minimum 70% shareholder return threshold and implying about $1.5 billion in share repurchases.

"As a first indication of the '27 plan, we expect EOG will message another year of mid-single-digit (~3.5%) growth on a flat capital budget (~$6.55bn), which is above the Street modeling 1% oil growth at $6.6bn," said Byrne.

Byrne ranks No. 303 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 58% of the time, delivering an average return of 18.5%. See EOG Resources Statistics on TipRanks.

#3234. Alligator-Shaped Xbox Will Be Snapped Up by One Gamer

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

This iconic Florida critter appears to have swallowed an Xbox just a couple of weeks before the release of GTA 6.

See you later, alligator? Maybe, if you’re the one gamer who wins Microsoft’s Xbox Series X-Bite, a playable Xbox console inside a realistic, 5-foot-long animatronic alligator, complete with the green Xbox logo shining out of its eyeballs.

Yes, it’s real, and there’s only one. To create the critter, Microsoft hired animatronics specialists from John Nolan Studio, which has designed other creatures for The Witcher, Jurassic World Dominion and HBO’s upcoming Harry Potter series.

To the outside world, it looks like a real taxidermied alligator — except it has a custom Xbox Wireless Controller (complete with bite marks) in its jaws and an illuminated Xbox Series X inside.

There’s also a tie-in to the long-awaited Grand Theft Auto 6, which can be played on Microsoft Xbox. GTA 6, which comes out Nov. 19, is set in a fictional version of Florida, famed for its gators. However, because Sony, maker of the PlayStation, has an exclusive marketing partnership with Rockstar Games (the studio behind GTA 6), Microsoft can’t mention the game explicitly in its ads.

But Microsoft can certainly hint at the game. The promos for the giveaway say, “This November, Xbox is heading to Florida,” and feature GTA 6 props, including a baseball bat, duffel bag, playing cards, dominoes and a shot glass with a lipsticked rim. An alarm clock blinks the time 3:05, and Florida’s most famous area code is 305.

To enter, you need to follow @Xbox on TikTok, Instagram or X, repost the Xbox sweepstakes post from that platform and manually add #XbiteSweepstakes to your repost. Winners must be 18 or older and reside in the US. Your account must be public, and you’ll have to monitor it regularly. Once the winner is notified, they have 48 hours to claim the prize. The sweepstakes is open now and runs through 11:59 p.m. PT on Nov. 10.

#3233. OpenAI will merge ChatGPT’s chat and work tabs – here’s when, and what to expect

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

On the heels of Anthropic's similar move, the change will be tested among select users before being rolled out.

OpenAI will merge ChatGPT’s chat and work tabs starting in December, according to a post on OpenAI’s website.

Also: This new ChatGPT scam tricks you into installing malware

Currently, ChatGPT’s desktop app features a ChatGPT and Codex section, and within the ChatGPT section, you can find the Chat and Work tabs. It’s not especially easy to navigate, and OpenAI is looking to change that.

(Disclosure: Ziff Davis, ZDNET’s parent company, filed an April 2025 lawsuit against OpenAI, alleging it infringed Ziff Davis copyrights in training and operating its AI systems.)

“Starting in December, Plus, Pro, and Business plans’ usage allowance will be shared across ChatGPT and Codex as we bring the agentic capabilities of Work into the main ChatGPT experience,” OpenAI detailed in its note entitled “Understanding ChatGPT and Codex usage limits.”

An email was also sent to current users, sharing similar information, according to TechCrunch. The email confirmed the merger of the Chat and Work tabs, adding that the integrated experience will be available to select users for feedback before it is made more widely available.

Also: How ChatGPT helped me fix a corrupted gaming PC

“This will enable you to move from exploring an idea to having ChatGPT carry it through, all in one place. You can bring in your files and plugins and ask ChatGPT to build a website, create a presentation, or do things for you on the web, while reviewing and guiding its work. Codex will remain a separate experience in the ChatGPT desktop app,” the email said.

OpenAI said the transition will allow both ChatGPT and Codex to draw tokens from the same allowance pool. While most customers won’t be affected, depending on usage and model, some users may need to wait for resets more than usual.

“Your usage for ChatGPT and Codex will be measured in tokens, the units of information a model processes and generates. How much of your allowance you use will depend on the model you choose and the task you ask it to do. More advanced models and complex tasks generally use more of your allowance. Instant chat will not draw from your usage,” OpenAI said in the online note.

In September, rival Anthropic merged Claude‘s chat and Cowork functions into a single screen. OpenAI said that they don’t expect the upcoming change to disrupt users’ current experience.

Also: These Claude Enterprise features let you track AI ROI

“We’re preparing carefully for this transition to help prevent disruption to your workflows. We expect most users won’t need to wait for their usage to reset more often than they do now,” OpenAI said.

#3232. Disneyland Is Training a Class of AI Robot Interns

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

From Pixar robots to help you park your car to droids roaming Star Wars land, physical AI is popping up all over Disneyland.

If you’ve ever driven to Disneyland, you know that parking is a challenge. When the parks open each morning, long lines clog the nearby streets as engines idle, families waiting anxiously to enter the parking structure so they can start their day at the parks.

Parking attendants can only do so much to handle the tens of thousands of cars arriving every day at the Disneyland Resort. But what if a cutesy autonomous robot from Pixar’s Cars series could help direct traffic flow and guide you right into your parking spot?

That’s a project being tested with FieldAI, a company that builds the AI brains for robots. In a demo video at the Disney Accelerator Demo Day on Tuesday, Disney and FieldAI showed footage of robots that would assist with guiding cars through the parking process.

“Imagine if a character from Cars or robots from Wall-E direct you where to park when you arrive,” Gary Daniels, senior vice president of products and experiences at Disney Experiences Technology, said. “The work we are doing now is a great way to see how the robots function, and, as important, how people respond.”

Other companies build the robots; FieldAI slaps its physical AI solution in a box on top of them, having worked so far with around 30 different robot types, shapes and sizes. The box is equipped with multiple cameras that serve as the robot’s “eyes and ears,” helping the AI model process what it’s experiencing in real time. The robots also collect data while operating.

During the event at Walt Disney Studios, FieldAI showcased a Boston Dynamics robot dog and a miniature version of the BBX droids from The Mandalorian and Grogu that roam Star Wars: Galaxy’s Edge at Disneyland. FieldAI-enabled robots have already been deployed in Disneyland at Galaxy’s Edge on the BBX droids, though they hedged that this is in its early stages.

“Our intelligence is on the bigger version and operating in the park already,” FieldAI CEO Ali Agha told reporters.

David Min, vice president of Disney Innovation, told me it could also be used on characters that interact with guests at parks, naming Olaf and The Hulk as examples.

Another project with Disney involves getting multiple robots to talk to each other to coordinate missions.

Headquartered in Irvine, California, with offices in the San Francisco Bay Area, Boston and Pittsburgh, FieldAI primarily works in construction environments and energy facilities to complete tasks like inspections, material transport and supporting construction. But this is easily translated to a theme park environment, where paths and crowds are constantly changing, and autonomous robots need to account for that without needing mapping or GPS.

“Our BBX proof of concept explores how to bring that navigation together with Disney character performance,” said Doug Fidaleo, lab director, Disney Research, Walt Disney Imagineering R&D. “That’s what drew us to FieldAI: deep experience deploying robots in demanding, unstructured environments with uneven terrain, changing layouts and unexpected obstacles.”

Some of the use cases Agha gives include robots supporting security, perimeter patrols, helping cast members backstage and enabling more in-park experiences — even delivering items to people waiting in line for a ride.

“This is a highly self-autonomous system that operates without a positioning system,” Agha said.

Physical Intelligence (Pi) is another company that builds AI brains for robots. Also showcased during Disney’s Accelerator Demo Day, Pi is focused less on roaming droids that can help or entertain guests and instead on robots helping Disney cast members with backstage tasks.

Namely: picking up, folding, cleaning and sorting the 3D glasses used for rides like Toy Story Midway Mania and shows like Mickey’s PhilharMagic.

It’s an unpleasant task that’s a major pain point for cast members who have to spend a long time in a small room completing it several times a day. It also requires “dexterous manipulation,” with Pi previously working on general-purpose robots that perform tasks like folding and stacking, using robots that have grippers rather than five-digit hands.

Sourish Jasti, a technical staffer with Pi, said the company recently spent 12 days at Disneyland between midnight and 6 a.m. collecting data, testing logistics and moving its robots in and out of the park to see whether it could help with sorting the 3D glasses.

“This was like a robot internship,” Jasti said, adding that physical AI is like a toddler, in that it learns from actually doing things.

The robots — which, much like FieldAI, Pi doesn’t build but instead installs the brains for — could be either a humanoid on wheels or just a mechanical arm. There are cameras on the base and cameras on the wrists to help the AI model “see” what it’s doing as it picks up and sorts the glasses.

“We intend to have robots interning in many different spaces with Disney,” Jasti said, pointing to not only the theme parks but also Disney’s studios, hotel rooms and cruise liners, which he calls “mini cities.”

For both Pi and FieldAI, Min said the benefit is that using AI can train the robots much faster to do the tasks Disney needs them to do — and that going to companies like these, which are already well-established in fields like construction and manufacturing, makes it easier to transfer those skills to the theme parks.

Whether they’re roaming around parking structures or lands, or backstage helping workers, the AI-equipped autonomous robots are solving problems for Disney.

“The connection is through the core capabilities that we’re developing for our robots,” Fidaleo said. “Robots that can perceive the world around them, can act in the physical world and adapt when things change.”

Disney is continuing to push technology from the audio-animatronic figures used on rides like Pirates of the Caribbean, making them more sophisticated to build an immersive experience.

“From the expressive Na’vi shaman to a robotic Spider-Man flying through the air, to a walking baby Groot, each advance changes how we can experience a character in the physical world,” Fidaleo said. “The park of the future will be teeming with robot characters.”

#3231. I tested the RedMagic 12 Pro – and it’s the fastest Android I’ve ever seen

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Tech > Services & Software > Operating Systems > Mobile OS > Android

If it's possible to release a flagship phone while at the same time making it appear more like a midrange phone, Red Magic has found a way.

RedMagic just announced the international launch of the RedMagic 12 Pro — its latest flagship phone. Typically, the company releases devices in China first and then slowly rolls them out to the rest of the world. This time around, the company knew it had a phone that could compete with other flagship devices.

Also: I’ve been a Google Pixel fan for years, but this $500 Android phone is giving me pause

RedMagic’s phones are high-performance devices known to do one thing especially well: mobile gaming. The RedMagic 12 Pro is no exception. It houses a Qualcomm Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 CPU with up to 5.01 GHz, which is paired with the RedMagic R5 Gaming Chipset, and I can honestly say it’s the fastest Android phone I’ve ever tested.

After the initial setup, I installed Geekbench 7 to benchmark the phone and compare it to my Pixel 9 Pro. As for the latest iPhone, according to Geekbench, the iPhone 18 Pro Max comes out ahead in single-core performance, but it just barely falls behind in multi-core performance.

The RedMagic 7 Pro nearly doubled the Pixel 11 Pro’s multi-core score. And Google’s device couldn’t beat the single-core score either. As I said, I’ve never seen a Geekbench score this high.

Real-world usage confirms these numbers, because the phone reacts faster and behaves more smoothly than any Android device I’ve owned or tested. It’s so smooth and fast, it feels like magic. But it’s not just the speed that makes this phone special.

First off, I’ve always liked RedMagic’s Android “skin.” As you use it, it seems to be some amalgamation of Android and iOS. RedMagic is essentially doing what Google’s been trying for years: making the smoothest possible animations on Android.

Also: I switched to an Android with liquid cooling for a week – now I wish every phone had it

The interface is as elegant as any I’ve seen on a mobile device. Pull down the notification shade, and it glides down like it was made of silk. Tap on an app launcher, and it opens immediately. Switch between apps, and there’s zero lag or jitter. On top of that, there’s hardly any bezel to speak of — the display goes nearly to the edge of the device.

There’s also no indication of where the front-facing camera is. There’s no pinhole (as you’ll find with many Android devices), and there’s no island (like on iPhones). It’s just a solid display with no interruptions.

The Pro 12 also feels really good in the hand. Both the back and the front are glass. Yes, it invites fingerprints, but it feels so smooth. The back of the phone also has that typical RedMagic look and feel with integrated RGB lighting zones. You can customize the lighting zones for things like fan on/off, game key atmosphere, media atmosphere, incoming calls, charging, and the alarm clock.

Also: This 15-inch portable monitor solved my big issue with cheaper models – and rivals my Mac display

Everything, and I mean everything, about this phone is fast.

The RedMagic 12 Pro is 100% a gaming phone. I installed “Diablo: Immortal” and found it to perform better than the last RedMagic gaming-specific tablet I tested. Not only was it fast, but the graphics were gorgeous. Crisp, smooth, and responsive.

Since the RedMagic 12 Pro is advertised as a serious gaming phone, why does it include preinstalled games that are decidedly non-serious?

On this powerful gaming phone, you’ll find apps like Puzzle Spark, Mahjong Blast, Bolt Twist, GoGo! Blast, and Little Kitty, Big City preinstalled. These are not serious games. In fact, these game titles sound more like they belong on a list of malicious apps (they aren’t).

Also: This 9-inch tablet singlehandedly changed my mind about gaming on Android

I would rather see the Red Magic 12 Pro have zero preinstalled games than the collection it ships with. Yes, you can easily delete those apps, but their being on the phone kind of cheapens it. Given how amazing this phone is, I think RedMagic could get away with shipping a bit less cheese, and a lot more wine.

Either way, the RedMagic 12 Pro is a phone that belongs at the top of the heap among flagships, even above every Pixel phone ever released. If there is a phone that can impress me more than the RedMagic 12 Pro, I’ve yet to see it.

The iMac with M6 pairs a noticeable 2nm performance leap and Wi-Fi 7 connectivity with Apple’s iconic, minimalist hardware. While a higher starting price and the lack of a height-adjustable stand hold it back from perfection, its sharp 4.5K display and seamless setup make it a worthwhile upgrade for anyone holding on to an older Apple all-in-one.

Sleek, colorful design with color-matched accessories

Big performance boost thanks to Apple’s M6 and N1 chips

Surprisingly punchy speakers and solid built-in webcam

Sharp, vibrant 4.5K Retina display (with optional nano-texture glass)

Price hike on an already premium base model

Why you can trust Tom's Guide Our writers and editors spend hours analyzing and reviewing products, services, and apps to help find what's best for you. Find out more about how we test, analyze, and rate.

Apple’s new iMac with M6 might look identical to its predecessor at first glance, but it’s the extra power and improved connectivity under the hood that make this upgraded all-in-one desktop continue to stand out.

Instead of drastically altering the iMac, Apple has kept more or less the same design since 2021 when the 24-inch model first debuted. Just like with the iMac M4, you’re still getting a 24-inch 4.5K Retina display, a 12MP Center Stage webcam, and two or four Thunderbolt 4 ports at the back depending on which configuration of the new M6 chip you choose.

Similarly to the Mac mini M6 I reviewed, Apple’s M6 chip and its N1 wireless chip are the big upgrades here. While I wish there were other changes to its design — like an optional height-adjustable stand or a larger screen size — the iMac with M6 is a reliable and powerful desktop that’s incredibly simple to set up thanks to its one-cable solution. Also, unlike Apple's Studio Display monitors, the power cable is detachable, which makes cable management a breeze.

Besides being one of the best all-in-one computers, it’s also the only one that can be configured with a matte finish thanks to Apple’s optional nano-texture glass. However, is it worth upgrading from an older Mac or ditching your existing desktop setup for something more seamless? Find out in my full Apple iMac with M6 review.

2 x Thunderbolt 4, 1 x 3.5mm headphone jack

4 x Thunderbolt 4, 1 x 3.5mm headphone jack

Wi-Fi 7, Bluetooth 6, Thread, 2.5 Gigabit Ethernet built into power adapter

Magic Keyboard with Touch ID, Magic Mouse

The iMac with M6 is an elegant desktop that’s sleek and compact enough to fit into almost any space. What truly makes it shine, though, is the added muscle from Apple's M6 chip and the upgraded connectivity of the N1 — along with the fact that it remains the only all-in-one computer you can buy with an optional matte display.

The iMac with M6 that Apple sent over for review arrived in a single large box, complete with a blue fabric handle to match the desktop’s light blue colorway. Along with the computer itself, you get everything you need to start using it right away as it comes with a Magic Keyboard and a Magic Mouse.

Besides the color-matched USB-C to USB-C cable and power adapter with an Ethernet port built in that comes with the higher tier model, I really appreciated the fact that Apple includes a microfiber cloth in the box for keeping its screen fingerprint and smudge free.

Sign up to the Tom's iGuide weekly newsletter with coverage on everything from product launches to software updates, this is your go-to source for the latest updates on all the best Apple content.

The iMac with M6’s stand comes pre-attached, so there’s nothing to put together. There’s a white .5-inch border that wraps all the way around its 24-inch display along with a larger, 2-inch chin at the bottom. On the very top of the device, there’s a 12MP webcam with microphone holes on the back.

Then on the backside of the iMac with M6, there’s a hole at the top of the stand to route its power cable through along with two or four Thunderbolt 4 ports on the left side depending on which configuration you choose.

Around the corner from the power button on the back right, there’s a 3.5mm audio jack on the edge for connecting wired headphones. When you're sitting in front of the iMac, that puts the jack on your front-left — a small detail, but I really like that the cable from my headphones didn’t get in the way when using the included Magic Mouse. Though if you’re left-handed, this could be an issue if you frequently use wired headphones.

Unlike the Mac mini M4 or Mac mini M6 I’ve used previously, I just had to plug in that single power cable and power the iMac with M6 on to get started. From there, I used the included USB-C cable to pair the keyboard and mouse and I was good to go.

Although this is the first Apple all-in-one I’ve tested, the iMac with M6 felt incredibly fast and responsive right from the get go. In fact, it was a very similar experience to how it felt to upgrade from the previous Mac mini to the new Mac mini M6 and as you might have guessed, this is all thanks to Apple’s new M6 chip.

As you can see in our benchmark testing below, the change from using a 3nm process on the M4 to a 2nm process on the M6 — though literally small — makes a huge difference in terms of performance. For instance, in our Geekbench tests, we saw almost a 1,000 point single-core increase while multi-core performance jumped more than 5,000 points.

Apple has also upgraded the SSD storage in this new iMac, resulting in significantly faster read and write speeds. For those interested in video editing on the iMac with M6, this will save you a ton of time as our Handbrake encoding test (which measures how long it takes the computer to transcode a 4K video file down to 1080p) dropped by nearly two minutes, down from 5:03 on the iMac M4 to just 3:20 on the iMac M6.

The new M6 chip isn’t the only upgrade under the hood though, as this is also the first iMac with Apple’s proprietary N1 networking chip built in. Alongside Wi-Fi 7 and Bluetooth 6 support, it also adds native Thread support so your iMac can act as a Thread border router and directly communicate with your smart home gear.

These are all big upgrades you’ll notice in your day-to-day experience with the iMac M6 and you can read more about them in my Mac mini M6 review. However, with one of the best mesh Wi-Fi systems with Wi-Fi 7 support, I saw gigabit speeds over Wi-Fi when running a few speed tests.

I could take that even further by running an Ethernet cable from my router to the iMac with M6’s power adapter as my review unit has a 2.5 GbE port built-in. It’s worth noting that while the base model doesn’t come with one, you can pay an extra $30 for the iMac power adapter with an Ethernet jack if you prefer the reliability and added speeds you get over a wired connection.

As we saw with the iMac M4 a few years ago, Apple has made serious progress when it comes to gaming on Mac and this is even more evident with the new iMac with M6. While the base model has a 10-core GPU, the upgraded one has a 12-core GPU, but both are great for gaming if you keep your expectations in check.

Given that I previously played Control on the Mac mini with M6 on Apple’s Studio Display XDR at the office, I wanted to see how Remedy’s third-person supernatural shooter played on the iMac with M6’s 4.5K Retina display at home.

Just like before, I did have to drop the resolution down to 1440p, but the game looked crisp and ran smoothly on Apple’s M6 chip. If you don’t mind sacrificing even more resolution, scaling down to 1080p gives you an even bigger performance boost across a wide variety of titles compared to the M4 chip.

In the time since I tested the Mac mini with M6, I picked up Stray on sale specifically to see how it runs on macOS. After booting up the game and playing through the intro, I’d say the iMac with M6 handled it surprisingly well.

While these are both somewhat newer titles, if you have a large backlog of Steam games you haven’t gotten around to finishing yet, the iMac with M6 could be the perfect way to play them. Even with the in-game resolution turned down, its display looks fantastic and the six-speaker system — with two pairs of force-cancelling woofers and two high-performance tweeters — helps bring the action to life too.

When the iMac with M6 was first revealed and I found out that Apple wasn’t going to bump up its screen size from 24 inches to 27 or even 32 inches, I was slightly disappointed. With the release of the new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR, I think we might finally see a screen size bump to accommodate touch support in the next iMac — but that will be at least a few years away.

Now back to the iMac with M6, though I was initially disappointed it still had a smaller, 24-inch screen, it ended up taking me completely by surprise. Given that I do most of my work in a web browser with two side-by-side Chrome windows (each with dozens of tabs open simultaneously), I thought I wouldn’t be able to multitask the way I’m used to on the iMac with M6. Thanks to its higher 4.5K resolution though, I had more than enough screen real estate to do so quite easily.

The iMac with M6 is also slightly brighter than the older M4 variant based on our display tests. Colors are vibrant and both pictures and video appear very sharp too. I had no trouble at all editing photos in GIMP and all of my pics were color accurate on its display as well.

Since the iMac with M6’s speakers are so punchy, I decided to test its display further by watching The Wild Robot and a bit of Godzilla vs. Kong. In DreamWorks’ animated film, the robot Roz’s metallic body looked clean and crisp while Brightbill’s yellow feathers and the rest of the island’s foliage really popped.

Now if you’re partial to matte displays like I am and can’t stand seeing glare on a glossy screen, the iMac is the only all-in-one with this option available. This upgrade will set you back an extra $200 — but if you plan on using the iMac with M6 in a room with a lot of ambient light or near a window, it’s absolutely worth it.

Even though its design remains unchanged, the iMac with M6 packs in enough extra power to make it a worthwhile upgrade, especially from an older iMac with an M1 or M2 chip. Still, it does have its downsides — including a fixed-height stand that still can't be adjusted and a higher starting price over the previous model.

Let’s face it, there’s no computer or all-in-one that looks as good and features a design as iconic as Apple’s iMac. However, looks aren’t everything — and this is especially true coming from someone who also reviews home office furniture for a living.

Although you can tilt the display about 5 degrees forward or 25 degrees back, when it comes to ergonomics, this isn’t ideal. Instead, just like on Apple’s Studio Display, I’d love to see an optional height-adjustable stand for the iMac M6 too.

Sure, you can easily use a desk shelf or monitor stand to rectify this issue, but one of the main reasons someone buys an iMac over another all-in-one or a Mac mini is for the aesthetics. As I’m using one of the best standing desks from Uplift Desk for my Mac mini M6 setup, I was able to raise the desk itself to get the screen at a more ergonomic height. However, doing so makes typing on the included Magic Keyboard worse, since my forearms were tilted up instead of resting straight.

There’s something about seeing the color-matched accessories and stand together on a completely clutter-free desk that’s just really striking with an iMac. Having to ruin that look with an extra stand — or buy another accessory just to fix basic neck strain — stings even more when you take into account the other big downside with the iMac M6.

With its gorgeous display and simple setup, Apple’s iMac has always made an excellent family computer. You could set one up in a home office or even out in the living room and the entire household could use it for checking emails, managing calendars, watching videos, browsing the web or even playing games.

Thanks to RAMageddon though, the iMac with M6 starts at $1,499 — which puts a big dent in any family’s budget. Similar to the Mac mini M6, this new iMac is $200 more than its predecessor, and that’s without factoring in the additional cost of extra memory and storage. Upgrading from the base model’s 16GB of unified memory up to 24GB is an extra $200, and it’s the same story when you go from 256GB to 512GB of storage.

Add in the power adapter with Ethernet, a Magic Trackpad instead of a mouse, and a Magic Keyboard with Touch ID, and the iMac becomes a premium purchase quite quickly. Granted, it’s a machine you will be able to use for years to come with its appliance-like reliability — but still, foregoing yet another price hike would have been nice for the iMac with M6.

The iMac with M6 remains the sleekest and easiest-to-set-up all-in-one desktop you can get. There’s no other Mac or Windows machine like it, and if you want a computer that looks as good as it performs, you won’t be disappointed. The new M6 chip and the inclusion of the N1 chip give the iMac M6 a significant power and connectivity boost that make it an easy upgrade to recommend for anyone holding on to an older iMac.

Even then, I would have liked to see some tweaks to its now five-year-old design — like a larger screen or, more practically, the option to configure it with a height-adjustable stand. Still, if you don’t want to fuss with an external monitor, webcam, and loose cables, and just want a machine that works straight out of the box, the iMac with M6 is an iterative but worthwhile upgrade.

Follow Tom's Guide on Google News and add us as a preferred source to get our up-to-date news, analysis, and reviews in your feeds.

Anthony Spadafora is the managing editor for security and home office furniture at Tom’s Guide where he covers everything from data breaches to password managers and the best way to cover your whole home or business with Wi-Fi. He also reviews standing desks, office chairs and other home office accessories with a penchant for building desk setups. Before joining the team, Anthony wrote for ITProPortal while living in Korea and later for TechRadar Pro after moving back to the US. Based in Houston, Texas, when he’s not writing Anthony can be found tinkering with PCs and game consoles, managing cables and upgrading his smart home.
