#3201. GEO Group (GEO) Q3 2026 Earnings Call Transcript

Adelanto sale proceeds funded a major debt cut and a bigger buyback program.

Need a quote from a Motley Fool analyst? Email [email protected]

The GEO Group, Inc. (GEO -8.57%) reported record-breaking quarterly financial performance, achieving its highest-ever levels of quarterly revenue and Adjusted EBITDA. Management stated that the results were driven by the activation of new facility contracts signed in 2025 and an expanded scope of services for federal agencies. The company completed the $950 million sale of the Adelanto complex to the federal government while retaining a multiyear contract to provide support services at the site. This divestiture enabled the redemption of $650 million in senior secured notes, significantly reducing corporate debt and lowering net leverage to approximately 1.0 times Adjusted EBITDA. Management also increased its share repurchase authorization to $1.25 billion, signaling a shift in capital allocation toward shareholder returns as the company transitions toward a support services-focused business model.

Operator: Good day, and welcome to the GEO Group Third Quarter 26 Earnings Conference Call. All participants will be in a listen-only mode. After today's presentation, there will be an opportunity to ask questions. To ask a question, you may press star then 1 on a touch tone phone. To withdraw your question, please press star then 2. Please note this event is being recorded. I would now like to turn the conference over to Pablo Paez, Executive Vice President of Corporate Relations. Please go ahead.

Pablo Paez: Thank you, operator. Good afternoon, everyone, and thank you for joining us for today's discussion of The GEO Group's Third Quarter 2026 Earnings Results With us today are George C. Zoley, Chairman, Chief Executive Officer and Founder and Shayn March, senior vice president and chief financial officer. This afternoon, we will discuss our third quarter results as well as our outlook. We will conclude the call with a question-and-answer session. This conference call is also being webcast live on our Investor website at investors.geogroup.com. Today, we will discuss non GAAP basis information. A reconciliation from non GAAP basis information to GAAP basis results is included in the press release and the supplemental disclosure we issued this morning.

Additionally, much of the information we will discuss today including the answers we give in response to your questions, may include forward looking statements. Regarding our beliefs and current expectations with respect to various matters. These forward looking statements are intended to fall within the safe harbor provisions of the securities laws. Our actual results may differ materially from those in the forward looking statements, as a result of various factors, contained in our Securities and Exchange Commission filings including the Form 10-Ks, 10-Q, and 8-K reports. With that, please allow me to turn this call over to our Chairman, CEO and Founder, George C. Zoley. George?

George C. Zoley: Thank you, Pablo, and good afternoon, everyone, and thank you for joining us. Our diversified business units have continued to deliver strong financial and operational performance through 2026. And our third quarter 2026 results marked a record breaking quarter for GEO. Compared to the same period in 2026, our third quarter 2020 revenues increased 12% to approximately $761.1 million. While our third quarter 2026 net income attributable to GEO operations was approximately $49.2 million. Compared to the same period in 2025 our third quarter 2026 adjusted EBITDA increased 21% to approximately $145.3 million. And our adjusted net income increased 48% to approximately $51.8 million.

These results represent the highest level of quarterly revenues and adjusted EBITDA ever reported in our company's history. Even better than expected performance in 2026 has been driven by the significant revenue growth from the new contracts that we entered into throughout 2025. They included the activation of 4 facilities to house ICE detainees totaling 6 thousand beds. Valued at approximately $280 million in annual revenues. So far in 2026, we have had an even more successful year for the new expanded services entering into new contracts for the activation of 4 additional facilities to house ICE detainees totaling approximately 4.8 thousand beds.

These contracts, along with the expanded scope of services at existing facilities created an overall value of approximately $500 million in incremental annual revenues. First, we entered into a 5 year support services contract with ICE for the activation of a federal immigration processing center at the 1.19 thousand-bed Bighorn facility in Hudson, Colorado while also entering into a lease agreement with the facility owner. The Bighorn support services contract is expected to generate approximately $85 million in annual revenues in the first full year of operations. Starting in the first quarter of 2027.

We then entered into a 5 year support services contract with ICE for the activation of a federal immigration processing center in the geo owned 1.32 thousand-bed Rivers facility in Winton North Carolina. The Rivers support services contract is expected to generate approximately $80 million in annual revenues in the first full year of operations, also starting in the first quarter of 2027. More recently, we announced earlier this week the city of Big Spring in Texas has entered into a 10 year intergovernmental service agreement with ICE for the activation of a federal immigration processing center at the 2.33 thousand-bed Big Spring complex comprised of 1.4 thousand-bed flight line facility and the 925-bed Cedar Hills facility.

GEO will provide support services at the Big Spring complex which is expected to generate approximately $200 million in annual revenues for GEO in the first full year of operations. Starting in the second quarter of 2027. Under all 3 of these contracts, ICE will reimburse GEO for the capital expenditures needed to reactivate these 4 facilities as well as providing funding for start up expenses during the activation period. Following the activation of these 4 facilities, our total ICE beds under contract will increase to approximately 33 thousand beds at 29 facilities. The current census across our active ICE facilities is approximately 24 thousand representing approximately 1/3 of the current national ICE population of approximately 73 thousand.

Over the past 2 quarters, we have also entered into new or modified contracts for the continued provision of support services at existing ICE processing centers. First, during the third quarter, we entered into a contract modification to increase staffing levels at the 1.94 thousand-bed Adelanto ICE processing center to support the increase in the scope of services at the facility adding $60 million in incremental annual revenues. More recently, last week, we announced that we have entered into a new 10 year management contract with expanded support services at incremental annual revenue value of $50 million at the GEO owned 1.64 thousand-bed Northwest ICE Processing Center in Tacoma, Washington.

The new 10-year contract is expected to generate approximately $140 million in total annual revenues for GEO and continue through 10/27/2036, making it the first contract we have entered into ICE with a full base term of 10 years. This new contract was awarded under ongoing procurement that involves 3 other geo owned facilities, the Aurora facility, the Moshannon Valley facility, and Broward ICE Processing Center. Which are also expected to receive new 10-year contract awards. ICE enforcement initiatives nationwide are supported by significant funding that has already been approved by the United States Congress. ICE was allocated $45 billion for the detention under the 1 big beautiful bill which is available through 9/30/2029.

We believe that less than $10 billion of $45 billion has been spent so far. Under the Secure America Act, ICE also received $38.5 billion in baseline appropriations funding as well as an additional $30 billion for other priorities under the 1 Big Beautiful bill all of which is also available through 9/30/2029. As ICE continues to pursue these enforcement initiatives, we expect GEO to continue to be part of the solution as a 40-year partner to the agency. Following our recent contract announcements, we now have approximately 2.9 thousand idle beds that remain available at 4 company owned facilities, which are well suited for the needs of the federal government.

At full capacity, these 2.9 thousand idle beds could generate approximately $170 million in combined incremental revenues. Additionally, we have expansion capacity of several thousands of beds at existing geo managed ICE facilities. Our third quarter 2026 results also reflect a significant expansion in our secure transportation services on behalf of ICE, and the US Marshals Service. As a result of new or amended contracts we entered into in 2025. The support services that we provide under ICE Air transportation subcontract have continued To Steadily Grow Driven By The Increase In The Number Of Removable Flights.

Additionally, Our New Bighorn Rivers and Big Spring contracts with ICE are expected to generate approximately $28 million in combined additional annual transportation services revenues once normalized in 2027. Importantly, during the third quarter of 2 thousand 26, our ISAP contract continued to experience a steady technology shift to more intensive and higher price monitoring devices such as ankle monitors. ISAP is the only ICE program currently in place to provide electronic monitoring and case management services for individuals on the non-detained docket.

The program relies on several forms of monitoring including GPS ankle bracelets, or wrist worn devices that provide real time tracking as well as the SmartLink phone app, which relies on facial recognition voice ID, and GPS to confirm a person's location during the predetermined check-in. The current overall ISAP count is approximately 190 thousand participants up from 184 thousand participants 3 months ago. The number is 58 thousand currently, from 17 thousand early in 2025. We also continue to experience a steady increase in the number of ISAP participants assigned to case management services, which involves staff interaction and monitoring for approximately 121 thousand individuals currently.

As a result of these trends, revenue and net operating income for our electronic monitoring and supervision services increased during the third quarter of 2026 compared to the same period a year ago, reversing a multiyear trend of revenue and net operating income declines. Additionally, during the third quarter of 2 thousand 26, we generated revenues of approximately $3 million from our skip tracing contract. Moving to our outlook, we have increased our net income and adjusted EBITDA guidance for 2026 to reflect the strength of our results in the first 3 quarters of the year. Our fourth quarter 2020 revenue and adjusted EBITDA guidance exceeds our third quarter 2 thousand and 26 results.

Positioning GEO to set another record breaking quarter. Looking forward to 2027, there are several sources of future upside compared to our 2026 guidance. They include the expected activation of 4 new ICE facilities at Bighorn, Rivers, and the Big Spring Complex. Comprised of 2 facilities. Additional growth in our additional secure services segment from the reactivation of additional idle facilities and or higher overall populations across our active facilities. The expected transition of our previously announced managed only contracts for the 1.88 thousand-bed Graceville facility and the 985-bed Bay facility in the state of Florida, which are expected to occur on 07/01/2027.

Additional volume increases and/or accelerated technology service mix in our ISAP contract, additional growth in our secured transportation services business, and additional revenue from higher utilization of our skip tracing contracts. Before I turn the call over to our CFO, Shayn March for a more detailed review of our third quarter results and guidance I would like to provide you with an update regarding the plan by ICE and DHS to purchase existing privately owned turnkey ICE processing centers. As we announced last month, we completed the sales of our 1.28 thousand-bed Adelanto West ICE processing center 660-bed Adelanto East, 704-bed Desert View Annex to DHS.

For an aggregate gross sales price of $950 million and net proceeds after taxes and transaction fees and expenses of approximately $705 million. We expect to continue providing support services at the Adelanto complex under our existing contract with ICE, which has a full effective term through 12/19/2034. We used proceeds from the sales of the Adelanto complex for the redemption of our $650 million 2029 senior secured notes and we also entered into an amended and restated credit agreement extending the maturity of our $550 million revolving credit facility to July 2031. And also increasing our restricted pay payment capacity, including share repurchases.

Following the redemption of the 2029 senior secured notes, our total outstanding corporate debt consists of our 2031 senior unsecured notes totaling $625 million. As we previously announced, our Board of Directors has increased our share repurchase authorization, which is effective through 12/31/2029 by $750 million to $1.25 billion. Based on our current leverage and so long as we remain below specified leverage levels, GEO is permitted to make unlimited restricted payments, including share repurchases under both the amended credit facility agreement and the senior unsecured note indenture.

Given the intrinsic value of our assets including 48 thousand owned beds, our strong financial performance in providing diversified secured support services and our expected future growth we believe that our stock continues to be significantly undervalued and offers a very attractive investment opportunity. Therefore, in addition to further debt reduction and other general corporate purposes, we intend to allocate a substantial portion of future facility sales proceeds and recurring free cash flow toward our expanded share repurchase authorization, which may include structured share repurchases on an accelerated basis. Following the recently completed asset sales, ICE now uses approximately 34 existing detention sites nationwide that are owned and operated by private contractors.

CoreCivic now owns and operates approximately 12 ICE detention facilities. While GEO owns and operates 20 ICE detention facilities. In addition to the facility sales we completed last month, we remain engaged in active processes for the sale of multiple other company owned facilities to ICE subject to mutual agreement on price and GEO's continued management of those facilities under long term support services contract. We believe we have 2 types of assets, the building and the businesses of providing support services. We are pursuing additional potential sales of the buildings but we want to retain the business of providing support services.

We continue to consider ourselves primarily a support services operator and will place particular importance on our ability to continue our support services at any additional facilities sold to ICE. Specifically, we believe that our current active negotiations could result in additional sales before the end of 2026 for up to 4 additional facilities. We believe that the future sales are likely to have similar valuations to the transactions that have already been completed by ICE. With standard adjustments with respect to geography, facility size, and age. And it is possible that the number of facilities targeted for acquisition by ICE could continue to grow in the future.

At this time, there is no definitive agreement in place and no precise timeline for the closing of any additional transactions. And GEO can provide no assurance that any additional transactions will in fact occur. While the exact timing of government actions is always difficult to estimate, we remain focused on pursuing new growth opportunities and allocating capital to enhance long term value for our shareholders. At this time, I will turn the call over to Shayn to review our quarterly results and increase guidance.

Shayn March: Thank you, George. Good afternoon, everyone. The third quarter of 2026 set all time highs for GEO in quarterly revenues and adjusted EBITDA, and also an all time high in quarterly adjusted net income under a non REIT corporate structure. Revenues for the third quarter of 2026 increased by approximately $761.1 million up from approximately $682.3 million for the prior year's third quarter. Reflecting a 12% increase. For the third quarter of 2026, we reported net income attributable to GEO operations of approximately $49.2 million or $0.37 per diluted share. This compares to net income attributable to GEO operations of approximately $173.9 million or $1.24 per diluted share in the third quarter of 2025.

Which included the $228 million gain on the sale of the Lund, Oklahoma facility. Adjusting for unusual and nonrecurring items, third quarter 2026 adjusted net income increased to approximately $51.8 million or $0.39 per diluted share up from approximately $35 million or $0.25 per diluted share in the prior year's third quarter. Our adjusted EBITDA for the third quarter of 2026 increased to approximately $145 million up from approximately $120.1 million in the prior year's third quarter reflecting a 21% increase. Driving this historical quarterly performance, our owned and leased secured services revenues increased by approximately $46 million or 13% compared to prior year's third quarter.

This increase was driven by the activation of 3 company owned facilities under new contracts with ICE, which was partly offset by revenue lost from the sale of the Lawton Oklahoma facility. Quarterly revenues for our managed only contracts increased by approximately $31 million or 19% from the prior year's third quarter. This increase was primarily driven by the joint venture agreement for the management of the North Florida detention facility, as well as certain transportation revenue increases that are reported in this segment. Quarterly revenues for our owned and leased reentry services increased by approximately $3.5 million partly offset by a $3 million decline in nonresidential services revenues compared to the prior year's third quarter.

Finally, third quarter 26 revenues for our electronic monitoring and supervision services increased by approximately 1.6% compared to the third quarter of 25, reversing a multiyear trend of quarterly revenue declines for this important segment and demonstrating the strength of the continued favorable technology and case management mix shift in our ISAP contract, which more than offset some price reductions previously reported. Turning to expenses. During the third quarter of 2026, our operating expenses increased by approximately 8.5% as a result of the activation of our ICE facility contracts and increased occupancy compared to prior year's third quarter. Our general and administrative expenses for the third quarter of 2026 increased modestly to approximately 9.5% of revenue.

Approximately 9.1% of the prior year's third quarter revenue the result of additional business development expenses. Our third quarter 26 net interest expense remained steady at approximately $36 million compared to the prior year's third quarter. Our effective tax rate for the third quarter of 2026 was approximately 27%. Moving to our outlook. We have updated our guidance for the fourth quarter and the full year 2026. For the fourth quarter of 2026, we have increased our GAAP net income guidance to a range of $591 million to $595.5 million which includes the gain on the sale of the Adelanto, California ICE complex.

We have also increased fourth quarter 2026 adjusted net income guidance to a range of $46 million to $51 million or a range of $0.35 to $0.39 per diluted share on a quarterly revenue of $777 million to $827 million We have increased our fourth quarter 2026 adjusted EBITDA guidance to a range of $149 million to $154 million If this guidance is achieved, the fourth quarter of 2026 would set another record breaking quarter for GEO. While also positioning our company for a strong 2027 outlook.

For the full year 2026, we have increased GAAP net income guidance to a range of $726.3 million to $730.5 million which includes the gain on sale of the Adelanto, California, ICE complex in the fourth quarter of 2026. We have also increased full year 2027 adjusted net income guidance to a range of $185 million to $190 million a range of $1.40 to $1.44 per diluted share on annual revenues of $2.975 billion to $3.025 billion and based on an effective tax rate of approximately 28% inclusive of known discrete items.

This represents a 56% increase over 2025 adjusted net income at the midpoint of $187.5 million We have increased our full year 2026 adjusted EBITDA guidance to a range of $568 million to $573 million representing a 23% increase at the midpoint of $570.5 million We expect total unreimbursed capital expenditures for the full year 2026 to be between $140 million and $150 million and expect normal unreimbursed CapEx to decline to approximately $100 million in 2027. Moving to our balance sheet.

Following the sale of the Adelanto complex in October, we completed the redemption of our $650 million senior secured notes and executed an amendment to our $550 million revolving credit facility extending its maturity and increasing our restricted payments capacity including share repurchases. Our total outstanding corporate debt consists of our 2031 senior unsecured notes totaling $625 million. Our available liquidity is approximately $600 million including cash on hand and revolver availability. Net of cash, our current leverage is approximately 1x adjusted EBITDA, And based on our current outlook, we have reset our capital strategy to remain at or below this net leverage level going forward.

Based on our current leverage and so long as we remain below specified leverage levels, GEO is permitted to make unlimited restricted payments including share repurchases under both the amended credit facility agreement and the senior unsecured note indenture. Given what I believe is a significant discount in our stock valuation, our Board of Directors previously reported, increased our share repurchase authorization which is effective through 12/31/2029, by $750 million to $1.25 billion We plan to remain active under this program regardless of future asset sales. At this time, will turn the call back to George.

George C. Zoley: Thank you, Shayn. To recap our third quarter 2026 was a historic quarter for our company, setting new all time highs for GEO for quarterly revenues and adjusted EBITDA. And based on our increased guidance, we expect the fourth quarter of 2026 to be another record setting quarter. This historic financial performance in 2006 will position GEO for a very strong outlook in 2027 with several sources of potential further upside heading into next year. Including the expected activation of 4 new ICE facilities at Bighorn, Rivers, and the Big Spring Complex, additional growth in our secured services segment from the reactivation of additional idle facilities, and overall higher populations across our active facilities.

The expected transition of our previously announced managed only contracts for the 1.88 thousand-bed Graceville facility. And the 985-bed Bay facility in the state of Florida. Which are expected to transition on 07/01/2027. The additional volume increases and or accelerated technology and service mix in our ISAP contract. Additional growth in our secured transportation services business, and additional revenue from higher utilization of our skip tracing contracts. In addition to our strong financial performance and significant expected future growth, we believe that additional asset sales could be completed before the end of 2026.

Having already completed the sale of the Adelanto complex for $950 million, we believe it is possible that up to 4 additional facilities owned by GEO could be sold in the fourth quarter of 2026. These potential asset sales would represent another significant liquidity and shareholder value creation event for our company. Given the intrinsic value of our assets, 48 thousand owned beds, our strong financial performance in providing diversified secure support services and our expected future growth. We believe that our stock continues to be significantly undervalued and share repurchases are therefore a paramount capital allocation priority for our company. That completes our remarks, and we will be glad to take any questions.

Operator: Thank you. We will now begin the question-and-answer session. To ask a question, you may press star then 1 on your touch tone phone. If you are using a speaker phone, please pick up your handset before pressing the keys. If you would like to withdraw your question, please press star then 2. At this time, we will pause momentarily to assemble our roster. The first question today comes from Joe Gomes with Noble Capital. Please go ahead.

Joe Gomes: Good afternoon. Thanks for taking my questions.

George C. Zoley: Good afternoon. So I wanted to start out, George. Looking at 93% occupancy at the end of the quarter, you know, how much additional utilization upside remains in your view? At existing facilities mathematically, it would be 7%. But we are now transitioning 4 new facilities as I discussed. 2 of which will open by January 1, representing about 2.5 thousand beds and 2 more facilities by March 1, representing about 2.3 thousand beds. Those are major increases in our capacity.

Joe Gomes: Okay. Thanks for that. And then maybe you could talk a little bit more about the ISAP contract. Obviously, it has not gone as the government had said, looking at numbers significantly higher than where we are today. I think there is about 1 year left on that contract. You know, obviously, you guys have been have won that contract on multiple occasions, but just want to get your view or your thoughts on, ISAP and, is ICE going to eventually start to use that contract and your expectations when it comes up for renewal.

George C. Zoley: Okay. Well, remember, the ISAP contract is under a program called alternatives to detention. The focus has obviously been under this administration to increase detention capacity, and we have participated in that initiative in increasing our contracted bed space at this point to 33 thousand beds, which is almost the entirety of the number of beds that was under the Biden administration. So it is been very significant. The ISAP contract did not develop as we expected 2 years ago, but we are very pleased that the technology mix has shifted towards these more intensive electronic devices, but in including increasing case management.

So we do think that contract will continue to grow and expand as the capacity or the detention capacity is achieved by this administration in this country. So once that is achieved, we think ISAP will continue to grow as it has, and particularly with regard to the technology mix.

Joe Gomes: Okay. Great. Thanks for that. I will pass it on.

Operator: The next question comes from Greg Gibas with Northland Securities. Please go ahead.

Greg Gibas: Hey. Good afternoon, George and Shayn. Thanks for taking the questions. Wondering how you are thinking about ICE's timeframe for additional facility sales if they were to occur? And maybe if you could discuss kind of how you expect the split incremental proceeds for debt pay down versus repurchases? And would you consider an ASR like we have seen from your public peer?

George C. Zoley: Well, I will take the first part of that question. We do think there is a reasonable chance of multiple sales occurring before the end of this year involving our company And it is a complicated process because, you know, these facilities are located in different states. There are different designs, different cost of replacement construction for each facility. And we have required that the facilities contracts continue for a significant period of time which further complicates and lengthens the process. But we are reasonably optimistic as I say that 1 or multiple facilities could be purchased by ICE from our company before the end of this quarter.

With regards to the use of proceeds, I will defer to Shayn March.

Shayn March: Regarding proceed application, we really do not have that much debt left. So it is a $625 million of unsecured notes. So any significant asset sale, we would definitely use to reduce our indebtedness, and we would absolutely consider any type of return of capital back to shareholders, including accelerated type structure transaction. So we are evaluating all the different options and we will act accordingly once those sales were to occur.

Greg Gibas: Got it. that is very helpful. And to follow-up on the previous question as it relates to ISAP, and I know ICE is very detention focused, but wondering if you could touch on how populations have trended with respect to the ISAP contract?

George C. Zoley: Well, the population is slightly trended up. it is gone from, I think, 185 thousand to approximately 190 thousand. But importantly, within that mix, are the changes as I have been discussing in the electronic devices that are used. They have gone to the more costly and more secure ankle monitors rather than phones. And the other part is the increase in case management, which involves our staff being involved on an interactive basis with people in the program to make sure we know who they are, where they are, and that they are going to be attending their meetings on-site with our company as well as the court hearings that will adjudicate their cases.

Greg Gibas: Got it. Thanks very much. I will pass it on.

Operator: The next question comes from Brendan McCarthy with Sidoti. Please go ahead.

Brendan McCarthy: Greg. Good afternoon. Appreciate you taking my questions. Just wanted to start off on the new Adelanto management contract. I think you mentioned there was a contract modification there that added roughly $60 million in annual revenue. I believe it was due to staffing level increases. Is that baked into the guidance at this point for this year?

Shayn March: Yes, sir. Yep, that is baked in for the rest of this year.

Brendan McCarthy: Got it. Okay. that is helpful. And could you remind us of the contract economics there and talk about the margin profile of that management contract and compare it to the margin profile of how it looked under ownership?

George C. Zoley: Well, it was an owned facility. it is now an acquired facility. Normally, you would expect that there will be a price reduction on the ownership cost issues that are still to be negotiated. They have not occurred yet. But concurrently, we have had as a as the process of renegotiation of that facility and expanded scope of services that was desired by ICE to add several more staff for several more purposes. And that will offset any decrease in the ownership funding of the facility.

Brendan McCarthy: Understood. I appreciate the detail. Last question. It looks like there is a large implied step up for capital expenditures for Q4 of this year. I hesitate to assume that is mostly reactivation spending that will be reimbursed by ICE.

Shayn March: Yeah. that is correct. it is that plus, obviously, just we have pushed some CapEx scheduled for earlier in the year to the fourth quarter. So it is a combination of both, but it is predominantly going to be tied to activations of the ICE facilities.

Brendan McCarthy: Understood. that is all for me. Congrats on a good quarter.

Operator: Thank you. This concludes our question-and-answer session. I would like to turn the conference back over to George C. Zoley, Chairman, CEO and Founder of The GEO Group for any closing remarks.

George C. Zoley: Okay. Thank you, everyone, for joining us today. We look forward to our next call.

#3200. I Took the iPhone 18 Pro Max to Japan and Its New Camera System Brought Out My Creative Side

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

The iPhone 18 Pro got fun new camera features and they made my bucketlist travel destination more memorable.

Apple gave its pro iPhones a crucial camera and battery boost this year. As a frequent traveler, these upgrades had me stoked for the iPhone 18 Pro Max, so I took it with me to Japan. Going vintage watch hunting through the streets of Tokyo to 6 a.m. hikes in Kyoto’s Fushimi Inari and the Shinto shrines, I used the new phone as my main camera. It made me rethink my shots, pushed me to experiment more with my perspective and surprised me in the most unexpected ways.

The variable aperture, manual camera controls and new Photographic Styles make the iPhone 18 Pro the most fun camera system from Apple, even if they are just minor upgrades from the 16 Pro and 17 Pro. The starburst effect in f4, grain in Photographic Styles and adjustable shutter speeds add drama, depth and more personality to even the most mundane shots.

From my time landing in Osaka to landing back in Delhi, the iPhone 18 Pro Max had me experimenting for two weeks. Here’s what I shot and how the new upgrades made an impact on my first trip to Japan.

The iPhone 18 Pro has manual controls baked into the Camera app. I can adjust the focus, choose the lens aperture from four stops, pick a shutter speed and select the white balance without needing to install a third-party app. The variable aperture is the main attraction here, letting me experiment with lighting as I visited various shrines.

You can go from f/1.48 to f/4 on iPhone 18 Pro’s main camera to adjust the amount of light hitting the sensor. Apple has programmed the f/4 (its narrowest) setting to give you a starburst effect with bright light sources, which showed up as light blobs on older iPhones. I used f/4 to get starbursts from the reflections of sunlight hitting a shrine:

Not every photo needs this effect, but starbursts add a unique style that you won’t find on any other phone. I was busy framing my shots to get the most reflections and the cameras didn’t disappoint.

Combine this with adjustable shutter speeds (takes a bit getting used to) and it leads to endless new possibilities. On the night I landed in Osaka, I went out for a stroll near my hotel, and took about 250 shots at a red light. I only got a few decent light trails, but it forced me to get more creative with my photography

After a few days I finally got the shot of a moving car stabilized with a blurred background. The trick? Finding the right shutter speed (1/15 in this case) through trial and error and moving my iPhone at the same speed as the car. At night, I stuck to 1/2s for moving vehicles with handheld stabilization. I’m happy with the results.

From light trails at night to a speeding car in daylight, the iPhone 18 Pro Max cameras create an effect that was previously only possible through third-party apps. This is different from simply taking a live photo and tapping Long Exposure in edits. You can track a subject to focus and the rest of the movement creates visual effects like the ones in my photos.

Apple’s manual controls are all about getting creative with your frames. You can then personalize these with the new film look and grain in Photographic Styles. These are like simulations that you’d find on the Fujifilm X100 series or Ricoh GR cameras.

For example, I edited this cyclist shot in the Photos app. I used the Dramatic + Film Style because I liked the blue tint in the sky and background, while keeping the skin tone intact. It gave my shot a moody look without editing the colors on my subject, like a regular filter would.

For these two nature shots, I brought all three aspects: adjustable shutter speed, f4 aperture and new Photographic Styles into a single frame. I love the grain, film and glow effects on the iPhone 18 Pro this year. They make the iPhone cameras exciting again.

However, there are a few things I’d like to change about this software.

The grain and film look are nice additions but I’d have loved to adjust the intensity of grain, much like my Vivo X300 Ultra. The current look is good for photos shot in bright light, but anything dim starts looking too artificial. The grain is too aggressive for most situations.

As much as I appreciate the new manual controls, I’m not fond of their placement in the Camera app. I missed a slow shutter shot of the Shinkansen because I was busy finding the manual control. These bullet trains are just too fast!

The new manual controls can be added to the top of the viewfinder or accessed through the six-dot settings menu at the bottom-right corner. In both positions, they aren’t made for one-handed use. It’d also be nice if I could adjust the position of certain toggles in the six-dot menu on the viewfinder. I need the aperture and shutter speed on the rightmost side, but I can’t edit it. The two icons aren’t instantly recognizable up on top. I believe that if I could change their positions in the bottom menu, I’d recognize them faster and remember their positions for a more reliable shooting experience.

Then comes the Camera Control. It doesn’t support any of the new manual controls. So, you can’t adjust the shutter speed or choose an aperture. If I have an extra button dedicated to the camera, I’d ideally like to use it for manual controls. It’d allow faster access to the new features.

In my opinion, Apple should also let us assign two separate Photographic Styles on the front and back cameras. On my trip, I had set a Fuji-like look for street photography, which seemed great for my surroundings but not for my selfies. You can always edit these photos in post, but if I’m out with new friends and sharing these photos with them, it’d be easier if I could set two different Photographic Styles for the front and back cameras.

During my trip, I didn’t have to top up my iPhone 18 Pro Max more than once a day. I left it on charge overnight as my mornings were reserved for breakfast and figuring out the train connectivity through Google Maps. (Seriously, I don’t know how I’d travel without this app.)

Japan is a unique mix of next-gen technology and decades-old systems. While it has a Suica card for public transport, I couldn’t add it to my Apple Wallet. Most stations don’t accept Visa contactless payments. I had to run to the nearest 7/11 to get cash and purchase train tickets. Some markets are also cash-only, so my iPhone was constantly running Maps, Music and Camera for a healthy 6 hours a day.

It lasted me through long photography sessions and constant navigation without any issues. In my experience, this is a huge upgrade over my iPhone 17 Pro Max, which required two charging instances if I was pushing it with Camera and Maps usage. The new model also doesn’t get as warm as its predecessor. I noticed the heat dissipates quicker when using the iPhone 18 Pro Max without a case. I’ve tried three cases so far and each one traps heat, making it warm to touch. If you can, going caseless is a good idea on the new pro iPhones.

The added battery life is a fantastic addition to this year’s model, and will be appreciated by anyone who travels regularly. This is in line with CNET’s tests, where the iPhone 18 Pro Max emerged as the longest-lasting battery life of any iPhone Apple has ever made. I just wish it was lighter. At 248 grams, it is one of the heaviest phones on the market and if you put a case on it, the iPhone 18 Pro Max becomes bulky and hard to use with one hand. I hope Apple finds a way to give us an even better battery life in a lighter form next year.

On the front, you also get a smaller Dynamic Island, which can expand to show up to three live activities (up from two) simultaneously. However, some apps aren’t yet fine-tuned to accommodate the change. On one occasion, when I ordered food through Uber, while running Spotify and Maps navigation, the Live Activity cut the “2” in 27-minute ETA for the order. So I had the next direction, music and an incorrect ETA as glanceable info on top of my screen.

Japan was one of my bucket-list locations and I’m glad I took the iPhone 18 Pro Max with me. This is the most fun I’ve had with an Apple camera system in a long time. From the shrines in Kyoto to the riverside walk along the Sumida River in Tokyo, these cameras invited me to get more experimental. The film-like Photographic Styles, new manual controls and variable aperture helped me get more creative with my perspectives.

It took me more than 250 shots at a crossing in Osaka before I figured out which shutter speed was ideal for what occasion. Similarly, I experimented with my frames to find the best angles for the starburst effect in f/4. Then came the film simulations in Photographic Styles to stylize my shots within the Photos app. All of these new iPhone camera features give me a more analog feel, and I’m here for it.

The iPhone 18 Pro Max, thankfully, has the battery life to support my curiosity and slow learning pace. Through my trips last year, I had to carry a power bank with me, but the iPhone 18 Pro Max changed that. I’m more confident it will last through the day. While none of those camera features would appeal to casual users, the battery life enhancements and improved heat dissipation are tangible upgrades that would benefit everyone.

#3199. Don't let inflation bite — how to hedge with TIPS, commodities and infrastructure funds

The Consumer Price Index hit 3.7% in September – the latest sign that inflation remains a problem that isn't going away.

It's a tough situation for investors looking for protection, but there are some good ways to hedge.

Long-term Treasury Inflation-Protected securities (TIPS) yield 2.9%, near multi-decade highs. Beyond TIPS, analysts suggest commodities, infrastructure, and other assets that can hedge against rising prices.

While inflation is down sharply from its 9.1% peak in 2022, it's still well above the Federal Reserve's 2% target. Headline CPI's 3.7% rate in September topped estimates for 3.6%. Core CPI, excluding food and energy, reached 2.6%, also higher than expected. Rising energy prices drove much of the increase. But the Personal Consumption Expenditures index, the Fed's preferred gauge, also remains elevated at a core 3% rate.

Americans' inflation concerns are also rising. The New York Fed's Survey of Consumer Expectations showed the one-year inflation outlook in September climbed to 3.9%, its highest level since May 2023.

Despite their name, TIPS haven't provided much inflation protection this year. The iShares TIPS Bond ETF, which tracks the ICE U.S. Treasury Inflation Linked Bond Index, has a total return of -1.16% year-to-date.

Like most other bonds, TIPS have been hit hard by rising rates. The 10-year Treasury note is up sharply this year and spiked Wednesday to 5.29%, near the highest levels since 2002. Bond prices and yields move inversely, and as rates climbed many TIPS funds suffered.

But higher yields have made TIPS more attractive. The 10-year TIPS' 2.9% yield is up from roughly 1.9% early in the year.

"Given where rates are, it's getting interesting," says Jason Draho, head of asset allocation Americas at UBS Global Wealth Management.

TIPS pay a fixed coupon, or interest rate, but as inflation moves higher, the principal value of the bond increases. The adjustments reflect changes in inflation, based on the non-seasonally adjusted CPI for All Urban Consumers, with a three-month lag.

The upshot is that TIPS investors earn interest on a higher principal value over time. That's the essence of the protection compared to traditional Treasuries.

TIPS' poor performance this year isn't because of a surge in inflation expectations. Almost all the increase has been due to rising real yields — the nominal yield minus expected inflation. Real yields are up because of factors like robust economic growth and a U.S. fiscal deficit around 6% of gross domestic product (requiring far more government borrowing).

If nominal rates were rising just due to inflation, then TIPS total return — a mix of yield and price — would be fine, said R.J. Gallo, chief investment officer of global fixed income at Federated Hermes. But that isn't the case.

"TIPS have produced losses in total return because their income accruals have been insufficient to offset the price decline produced by the rising underlying real yields," Gallo explained.

TIPS maturing in 10 years or more are highly sensitive to duration risk, Draho notes. "You're making a big call on rates not rising any further if you buy TIPS, especially longer maturities of 10-year plus," he said.

The bull case is that inflation comes down quicker than expected. That's not the market's expectation, based on short-term Treasury yields, notes Draho. But if inflation does ease next year, which he expects, the yield curve would adjust lower.

One way to manage duration risk is to own individual TIPS rather than a fund that has to maintain duration consistent with a benchmark index. Investors could create a TIPS bond ladder with varying maturities, pegged to their income needs over the next decade, for instance.

If you hold a TIPS to maturity you may experience price volatility, but you'll get the original principal or inflation-adjusted price, whichever is greater, when the bond matures.

Short-term TIPS provide more protection against rate increases and they look attractive, said PIMCO portfolio manager Greg Sharenow.

"While as a firm, our view is that inflation will ultimately come down, that view keeps on being pushed out as real world events unfold," he said. "We've seen over and over again the last five to seven years — where we're now in our third supply shock — that you end up actually underpricing versus realized inflation," he added.

Funds focusing on short-term TIPS include Vanguard Short-Term Inflation-Protected Securities ETF, iShares 0-5 Year TIPS Bond ETF and PIMCO 1-5 Year US TIPS Index ETF.

TIPS, of course, aren't the only way to go. Rick Rieder, BlackRock's chief investment officer for global fixed income, suggests a multi-pronged strategy, including equities, commodities, and alternative assets.

"I'd start layering in more income, keep interest-rate exposure moderate, and then what a lot of people are doing is use things like alternatives to to create more balance in a portfolio," he said. "That makes a lot of sense to me."

Broad inflation-protection funds include State Street Multi-Asset Real Return ETF, Fidelity Strategic Real Return Fund and PIMCO Inflation Response Multi-Asset Fund.

The PIMCO fund's holdings include TIPS, commodities, gold and real estate investment trusts.

"The idea is to have a number of different exposures so that we can have a more balanced return and not try to be so specific in getting the exact right asset class at any one moment," said Sharenow, a manager on the fund.

He adds that he sees "significant value" in TIPS, which have the heaviest weighting in the portfolio. Commodities are the next largest holding. They have price "pass-throughs," which is how much companies can shift costs to customers through price increases. That is beneficial to investors, he noted.

Separately, the fund holds about 10% each in gold and REITs.

Draho recommends commodities, based partly on long-term asset-allocation studies that include the 1970s when inflation was far higher. "Over a long period they can help reduce risk and improve diversification," he said. "Their benefits have been most pronounced when inflation was overshooting expectations."

Rather than picking individual commodities, he suggests owning a basket that's consistently rebalanced. Gold and oil, for instance, perform well in different economic and monetary policy scenarios, and it can be tricky to get the timing right.

Commodity ETFs to consider include the Invesco Optimum Yield Diversified Commodity Strategy ETF (PDBC) and the iShares S&P GSCI Commodity-Indexed Trust (GSG).

Another asset class Draho suggests is infrastructure — operators of roads, ports, bridges, and other hard assets. Companies in the space tend to be toll takers, collecting long-term revenue under contracts that include inflation riders or built-in price adjustments.

Investors can get exposure to infrastructure through ETFs such as the iShares Global Infrastructure ETF (IGF) and ProShares DJ Brookfield Global Infrastructure ETF (TOLZ).

Draho isn't sounding alarms on inflation but says it makes sense to add protection against another move higher.

"The risk now is there will be supply side shocks that could push up inflation again," he said.

— CNBC's Daren Fonda contributed reporting.

#3198. Your Apple Watch has 2 new controversial listening features – but you have to opt in

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Siri Recap and Live Rewind are finally here, two months after Apple unveiled the always-listening Apple Watch features. Here's how they work.

Siri Recap and Live Rewind, Apple’s two controversial, always-listening Audio Intelligence features, are now available on the Apple Watch Series 12 and Apple Watch Ultra 4 with the iOS 27.3 developer beta. Both features are opt-in.

Apple unveiled Siri Recap and Live Rewind in September alongside its Series 12 and Ultra 4 smartwatches, but it waited to release the features until after the smartwatches launched. Siri Recap provides a high-level summary of meetings, while Live Rewind continuously buffers audio so the watch wearer can pull up a transcript of the last 15 seconds.

Also: Apple’s Audio Intelligence is priming us for its real AI wearable future

To try both features today, update your iPhone to the iOS 27.3 developer beta, and then update your Apple Watch.

Within the Siri app, users will find a new section called “Recaps,” where both the Siri Recaps and Live Rewinds live.

Siri Recap isn’t listening for nitty-gritty details within a meeting or recording a transcript’s worth of text. It’s more geared toward a conversation’s key takeaways, like important dates, times, prices, and action items. A demo of the feature showed an off-the-cuff conversation between a parent and a child discussing college application strategies. Siri Recap took notes on the high school activities the student could pursue to include in their application, the topics they could write about in their essay, and the colleges they could consider applying to.

After a conversation, a user can save the meeting notes in the Siri app or export them to Notes or Journal. If they don’t save the conversation, it’s automatically deleted after seven days.

Apple designed the feature to exclude certain information from the Siri Recap. It includes a person’s name only if they introduce themselves or if their name is regularly brought up in conversation. Otherwise, it avoids identifying speakers. It also scrubs the audio of language that promotes self-harm, financial and authentication data, and personal identifiers.

You can enable or disable Recaps at any time through Control Center. You can create something akin to a Focus mode to automatically enable the feature once your Apple Watch detects you’ve reached your office or college lecture. Each morning, Siri Recap sends a notification to alert you that the feature is on. At the end of each day, you get a reminder to check your daily recaps in the Siri app.

The feature constantly assesses whether a conversation is relevant, optimizing its detection based on the conversation’s context, proximity, and length. It pauses summarization when a user is on a phone or FaceTime call, plays music, or uses earbuds. It won’t work when Bluetooth devices like AirPods are in use.

Double-press the Digital Crown to see a transcript of the past 15 seconds of conversation. The Apple Watch chimes and displays an animation to indicate it’s in use, then shows the transcript for 30 seconds.

Also: Is cellular on Apple Watch worth it? 4 ways people use it – and why I opt out

Live Rewind is built for those head-in-the-clouds moments when you miss a tidbit of information and can’t go back and ask what a speaker said. I think about how useful this could be in a college lecture or boardroom setting, where dozens of people’s conversations and questions prevent someone from asking a clarifying question about what was discussed.

The user can send the snippet to the Siri app to save it or ask about it (if they want to look up the definition of a mentioned term or get more information on the history of a mentioned topic, for example). If the user doesn’t act on it, the snippet is deleted. Any snippet you save is encrypted through iCloud. The audio buffer updates continuously, and unused audio is automatically deleted. It’s processed on the device and not sent to Apple.

Think of the Secure Exclave as a private island on the S11 chip where the Apple Watch Series 12 and Ultra 4 process audio. A secure audio buffer processes the raw audio, and a secure pairing mechanism privately enables the connection between a paired Apple Watch and iPhone.

Also: The Apple Watch Ultra 4 just hit its lowest price ever ahead of Black Friday

For Siri Recap, the S11 chip listens to detect whether the watch wearer is part of a current conversation. Once detected, audio enters the Secure Exclave, where it’s encrypted and sent to the Secure Exclave on the iPhone. The iPhone turns that audio into condensed text, essentially editing the conversation to remove filler words or irrelevant information, and then it’s sent to private cloud compute. Private cloud compute creates a recap, delivered to your iPhone’s Siri app.

This process ensures that no one, including Apple, can access the audio data.

Don’t want your Apple Watch to listen to you? Siri Recap and Live Rewind are off by default, according to Apple.

If your Apple Watch prompts you to enable Audio Intelligence during setup, you can choose which features to turn on.

On its support page, Apple said you can “turn on Siri Recap in the Watch app on iPhone.” Once it’s enabled, you can “turn it on or off at any time from Control Center.” To enable Live Rewind, Apple said to “open the Watch app, tap Siri, then tap Live Rewind and turn on ‘Double Click Digital Crown.’”

I haven’t tested these controls myself. I’d expect you can follow the same steps to switch Live Rewind off, but I haven’t confirmed that yet.

#3196. Motorola’s $1,600 Signature 27 Is Throwing Every Ultra-Level Phone Feature Together

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

Our expert, award-winning staff selects the products we cover and rigorously researches and tests our top picks. If you buy through our links, we may earn a commission.

Motorola's new Signature 27 has one of the fastest wired charging speeds we've seen for a US phone.

After teasing it during Qualcomm’s Snapdragon Summit in September, Motorola’s $1,600 Signature 27 phone will be unveiled on Thursday, and it clearly wants to make a big impression for that high starting price.

Even with the ongoing RAM shortage leading to higher prices for most phones, it would be understandable to think a $1,600 candybar-style phone sounds extravagant. It is. But it’s actually priced competitively against the 512GB model of the Samsung Galaxy S26 Ultra (also now $1,600 following its own fall price increase).

The Signature 27’s biggest feature could be its 200-megapixel periscope telephoto camera, which is capable of a 3x optical zoom and what Motorola calls a 100x Super Zoom Pro. That camera is joined by a 50-megapixel wide camera, a 50-megapixel ultrawide camera and a 50-megapixel front camera. An Event-Based Vision action sensor will also be included to assist with photographing fast-moving subjects.

But particularly eye-opening to me — as someone who’s constantly tracking how quickly phones can recharge — is that the Signature 27 will have 90-watt wired charging. For context, the Galaxy S26 Ultra and the iPhone 18 Pro Max charge at 60-watt speeds, with both phones being among the fastest we’ve tested. The Signature includes a 7,000-mAh silicon carbon battery, which is a newer battery technology that’s able to pack more capacity into less space.

The phone will have a 6.8-inch 1.5K-resolution display that runs at a 120Hz refresh rate, but has an absurdly high 12,000-nit peak brightness. By comparison, many phones we’ve tested lately have included 2,000- and 3,000-nit brightness levels that make it easy to see the screen in sunny environments.

Powering it will be Qualcomm’s new Snapdragon 8 Elite Extreme Gen 6 processor, which Qualcomm says will be particularly helpful for gaming at high-graphics settings, recording video at 8K resolution as well as 4K at 60 frames per second and for on-device AI tasks. The phone’s audio system is created with a partnership with Bang and Olufsen, which we’ll have to hear but should help tune the phone well for music and movies.

The Signature also gets several Android 17 features that debuted on Google’s Pixel 11 series, including Rambler for voice transcription that uses AI to remove “umm”s from the text as well as understanding commands. There will also be a Create My Widget feature for having Gemini create personalized homescreen widgets, and the ability to use American Sign Language for texting. Motorola’s own Qira AI assistant will also be available on the Signature 27, which Motorola says will work across Lenovo devices.

Like the Razr Fold, the Signature 27 will get seven years of software and security updates — which brings Motorola firmly in line with what Google and Samsung provide to their flagship Pixel and Galaxy phones. The Signature will come in two Pantone colors: the dark coal smoke and the green capulet olive. I am interested in feeling both phones because the coal smoke model is described as having a “tactical weave finish” akin to materials used for cars while the olive is said to have a textile-inspired finish that may be closer to the vegan leather backings we’ve seen on the Razr line.

The Signature 27 may be expensive, but I do see where there may be an audience. With the recent retreat of OnePlus from the US phone market, fans of that brand may be looking for a new gamer-friendly phone alternative with both a high-end processor and fast phone charging. #3195. Want an iPhone Duo for the holidays? Apple’s latest stock update isn’t reassuring

Our gifting experts are obsessively searching for holiday gifts that are unique, thoughtful and suitable for any budget.

The iPhone Duo likely won't make it into Santa's sleigh this year. Here's what Apple had to say about it.

Apple is unsure when it will have more of its foldable iPhone Duo in stock for customers to purchase ahead of Black Friday and the holiday shopping season.

During Apple’s earnings call on Monday, Nov. 2, Apple’s chief operating officer, Sabih Khan, told investors that the company couldn’t say when supply of its new iPhone Duo would catch up with current demand.

Also: iPhone Duo hands-on: Some magical touches

“iPhone Duo is constrained as of today … We’re working hard to get this revolutionary new product into the hands of our customers as quickly as possible. But at this time, it’s really hard to predict when supply and demand will be in balance,” Khan told investors.

The stock and shipping delays were among the broader concerns on an earnings call riddled with questions about rising memory chip costs driven by the AI industry, according to reports from TechCrunch.

Also: iPhone Duo shortage watch: Changing wait times, buying limits, launch-day odds

Last month, the iPhone Duo (Apple’s priciest smartphone to date) sold out shortly after its official launch on Oct. 23. Apple told the Financial Times that demand for the new Duo was “nothing short of extraordinary” after the smashing sell-outs, though veteran techies like Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman posited that Apple knew it would encounter supply chain issues, yet it was still the plan all along.

Those who didn’t initially jump to preorder the new device or wait in line at an Apple store are still facing shipping times that extend into 2027. Some outlets are even reporting that carriers like Verizon have offered gift cards as apologies for the extended delays.

Apple CEO John Ternus signaled the company’s effort to meet demand for the iPhone Duo, announcing that Apple will be “deepening” its partnership with Perryman, a titanium producer supplying pieces for the device.

Also: iPhone Duo screen cracks: Serious issue or overblown? What we know

“We’ve been thrilled with the early response from reviewers and customers, and we are working hard to get iPhone Duo into customers’ hands as quickly as we can,” Ternus said during his opening remarks on the earnings call.

While the iPhone Duo snafu is a rare event for Apple, which traditionally has a strong reputation for a smooth supply chain, rising demand for memory chips is raising hardware costs across the industry, and it’s something Apple can’t circumvent. On the call, Khan noted that Apple has had to increase prices on numerous products, though he said those decisions were made rather “reluctantly.”

Back in June, MacBooks and iPads saw price increases of up to 25% due to rising hardware and chip costs.

As Apple works to iron out its kinks, customers may be looking elsewhere. Reports from Korea indicate that Samsung Galaxy Z Fold 8 sales jumped 20% in the week after the iPhone Duo became available, and recent reports of cracked displays are another strike for Apple.

Also: Want an iPhone Duo before 2027? Try this

So, Santa may not be able to deliver the iPhone Duo this year, but Samsung’s foldables may make it onto Christmas lists across the globe instead.

Grab your Walkman and press play on Kate Bush

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Wired headphones are having their moment. As we turn to more physical media and collect more vinyl and cassette tapes, we need to get our hands on the best ways of listening to them. Is streaming dying? Well, no, not by any means. But more and more people who have invested in physical media need a way to listen to their music.

Anyone you talk to who had a music collection in the '80s and early ‘90s will tell you the same thing — the Sony TPS-L2 Walkman and the MDR-3 changed the audio game. You could take your music with you anywhere and look pretty stylish while listening.

In line with the retro audio revival, thanks to a trend of digital fatigue, Sony has reimagined its iconic 1979 headphones with the release of the MDR-3R.

In looks, there’s not much that separates the headphones back then from the headphones now. They’ve had minor upgrades to make them suited to modern music listening, but side by side they look virtually identical.

The headphones are featherlight at just 1.3 ounces, making them the lightest headphones in the Sony lineup. They have a flexible headband adjuster, too, to get your ideal fit.

They have the same classic earpads that come in blue and orange, with both included with purchase of the headphones. The wire has been updated to have a USB-C input, making it compatible with modern devices. There are also in-line controls with a microphone, making them feel like modern wired headphones without compromising the overall look.

You’re likely wondering how these headphones might sound. Since they’re essentially a replica, not much has changed, but Sony says minor adjustments have been made to retain the classic sound and make the headphones suited to more modern music.

Get instant access to breaking news, the hottest reviews, great deals and helpful tips.

The MDR-3R headphones keep the classic analog warmth of the originals with a few tweaks. The 23mm driver is based on the 1979 version, but offers a wider frequency range, so the bass is more manageable for the cans.

I haven’t listened with these headphones as of yet, so I can’t speak from first-hand experience, but if they’re anything like the Gadhouse Wesley Headphones, we can expect crackly warmth with a nostalgic feel, but these retro headphones have 40mm dynamic drivers.

So, how much will these cans be setting you back? Well, they’re actually pretty affordable at $59. They can easily complement the NW-WM1AM3 or the NW-WM1ZM3, Sony’s new Walkman devices.

This is also cheaper than other retro-style headphones on the market, since the Gadhouse Wesley Headphones cost $89.

But the exciting headphones launch isn’t all that Sony has in store for us. Fully embracing the influence Max Mayfield has had on us over the last few years, the MDR-3R headphones are also launching in a Stranger Things edition.

This design has a black headband with the choice of black or red earpads in the box. These cost a little more at $79, and $20 may seem a little steep simply for a different colorway, but Stranger Things fans will love this ode to the show.

Tomo Sano: Thanks for having us. Maybe just on gross margins, which improved significantly to 28.2%, 650 basis points. While your full year guidance is 25%-26%, could you unpack a little bit more about the margin expansions behind by several factors, and how should we think about the margins going forward into the back half to stay at the high level? Thank you.

Chris Thome: Yeah. Thanks for the question. Margins were a little bit higher than our normal run rate for the quarter, and that really was a function of mix as well as higher volumes. But primarily, the impact on the margin was lower material receipts. If you recall, in the second quarter of last year, we had about $10 million of extraordinarily high material receipts, which carry with them lower margins. So, you have a little bit lower than normal margin in the prior year quarter. We have a little bit higher than normal margin in the current quarter. So, we would expect that to more normalize as the year progresses.

However, it was ahead of our expectations, which is why we bumped our gross margin guidance by about 50 basis points on the bottom and top end.

Matt Malone: Yeah. What we are seeing there is we are seeing improved execution. We are seeing more favorable pricing start to come out of the backlog. We had talked before about we had to get lower margin jobs out of the backlog, and that process has been unwinding. It is a little bit of pricing, it is a little bit of improved execution, as Chris mentioned, and then it is a little bit of just mix versus material receipts.

Chris Thome: More specifically on the mix, right? Space obviously is a lot higher in the current year, which carries with it higher margins, as you know. Additionally, FlackTek was higher this quarter versus the prior year and versus the sequential quarter, and they have a higher margin business as well. One thing that may not be intuitive, within our defense business, we are starting to enter into some higher margin programs, now that we have some of the older orders off the books. It is not only the mix within the markets, but within defense itself as well.

Tomo Sano: Thank you. Then on cash flow, please. Operating cash flow was very strong in Q2, partially reflecting the timing with the receivable collections and customer deposits. What level of cash generation should we expect in the future quarters? Also, just related to that, any comments on M&A pipelines and any areas or comments appreciated. Thank you.

Chris Thome: Yeah, sure. We had an exceptionally strong cash flow quarter. The teams did a great job on receivables collection. As you know, our business is very cash flow positive, as many of our contracts we are able to bill for the materials ahead of time before we actually have to pay for them. With that said, they can also be very lumpy. We had some receivables push out from the first quarter to the second quarter, which is why the second quarter was so high. As you know, we typically like to speak to EBITDA as far as our cash flow generation, just because of the lumpiness of our cash and our working capital.

We literally can have a $5 million or a $10 million payment that shifts from one quarter or one year to the next, which can kind of skew the results from quarter to quarter, which is why we don't provide cash flow guidance and prefer to talk to adjusted EBITDA. As far as M&A.

Matt Malone: Yeah, when we look at what we're going to, I'll just say what we're prioritizing with the cash that we have, since we have no debt. First priority is continued investment in organic growth. We see that as the highest avenue for return for our shareholders, and specifically, we continue to have that 20% hurdle rate. The next in line is M&A, or it would be debt, but we don't have any, so the third in line is M&A. I'll just say, pipeline remains full. We're only focused on extremely strategic opportunities that meet the criteria that we've laid out in our investor slide deck.

Yeah, the pipeline remains full, conversations are active, and we're excited about potential opportunities on the horizon.

Tomo Sano: Great. Thank you very much. Congrats on the quarter.

Operator: As a reminder, to ask a question, please press star one. The next question is from Robert Brooks from Northland Capital Markets. Please go ahead.

Robert Brooks: Hey, good morning, team. Thank you for taking my question. As we think of the increasing needs for more power dense items in high-stress environment, that really kind of plays right into your favor and what you guys specialize in, right? I was just curious to hear, any new orders you would like to highlight so far in year-to-date for your fiscal 2027 that exemplify that thesis in action?

Matt Malone: Yeah. Something that just gets me jazzed. Bobby, I will talk through a few examples at a high level. The first, specifically I want to hone in on even a sub-sector of nuclear. If you look at microreactors, I am talking containerized reactors that could be deployed at a hyperscale level. Look, it is not going to happen overnight, but we do still feel optimistic. Barber-Nichols does design some of the most, and produce some of the most power-dense rotating machines on the market. With the microreactor, power density matters. You have got to be able to fit the rotating machine that cools the reactor within the shipping container.

We are seeing a number of opportunities that have entered into our design environment and now production environment that meet those needs. That is one example in the microreactor space. The next area where we're seeing it is on the Defense side. If you look specifically, you hone in and you say radar, we've had some opportunities this year that have converted that have to do with increasing the visibility on the battlefield from a directional radar platform to 360 degrees. I would specifically say we've talked about that at our investor day, but what's happening is it's starting to scale to low rate and now rate production. We're starting to see the scaling effect of that.

Lastly, on the Space side, Barber-Nichols has had heritage on the Space side with complex rotating machines, and more specifically, power-dense rotating machines for now 20+ years. We're seeing opportunities in space to cool. I'll say we have had bookings and opportunities to cool launch vehicles as well as satellite systems, as well as astronaut backpacks. Some of that's been a long conversation. Some of it's converted more recently. I would just say it's an area that power-dense electrified rotating machines is the differentiator, and we're seeing it connect with the market need.

Robert Brooks: That's really helpful color there. Just as we maybe step back or expand the view, obviously you have a really strong position within supplying U.S. Navy programs. I was just curious to get a sense of maybe what are the key hurdles for you guys to clear to win Defense business with American allied Navy programs? Is that something that's not really on the table and you kind of focus that there's better opportunities domestic?

Matt Malone: No, it's a great question. We do it today. The nice thing is we do it through the folks that buy it. Our integrator, our prime, or upstream is actually the one that then regulates it to where it goes to foreign allies. We basically have increased content. Use shipbuilding as an example. It gets integrated at a prime, and then it could go to AUKUS, which is other different avenues for usage. Other examples of that, we do supply spare parts for different submarine solutions globally. I would just say, it is a part of our business today, and we continue to see opportunity there for growth.

Robert Brooks: That's great to hear. Then maybe just the last one for me on the capa... like, it seems like you're not necessarily capacity constrained today, but the Arvada expansion is more about better, not about throughput, but about growing the business in the future. I was a little confused there. I just want to clear up my understanding.

Matt Malone: Okay, think of it this way. We're not capacity constrained today, but when you overlay the backlog that's been growing for seven straight quarters, you get to a situation in the future where current capacity doesn't meet it. So you essentially have to build ahead to meet the capacity constraints, because you can't build a facility overnight. It's just leveling up to meet the backlog overlay in our portfolio, and that's what we've done really well for the last number of years.

Robert Brooks: That's definitely the case. Appreciate the time, and congrats on another strong quarter.

Operator: This concludes the question and answer session. I'd like to turn the floor back over to Matthew Malone for closing comments.

Matt Malone: Thank you. Overall, we are pleased with the solid start to the first half of the year. With that said, we recognize there is still significant work ahead, and we remain focused on disciplined execution, profitable growth, and getting better every day as we work towards becoming a top quartile performer in creating value for our customers and shareholders. As always, please reach out with any questions. Thank you, everyone, for joining us today and your interest in Graham.

Operator: This concludes today's teleconference. You may disconnect your lines at this time. Thank you for your participation.
